**Remediation, immediate — code fix plus a real, verified re-placement of all 16, not sequenced as "fix later."**
1. `place_stop_order()`'s payload now explicitly includes `"timeValidity": "GOOD_TILL_CANCEL"` — the exact value confirmed accepted by the live API above. Covered by an updated existing test (`test_place_stop_order_sends_the_correct_payload_and_path`) and a new, dedicated regression test (`test_place_stop_order_always_sends_good_till_cancel_time_validity`) asserting this specific field/value pair directly. Full suite (741 tests) passing.
2. All 16 positions' stops were re-placed **before** the code fix was even deployed — using the corrected payload directly against the live API (decoupled from the deploy pipeline, since every minute of the 16 positions sitting unprotected mattered) — each at the identical `stop_price`/quantity as the original backfill, and each independently re-verified via a fresh `GET /equity/orders/{id}` (status `NEW`, matching the exact pattern of a genuinely resting, working order from the original supervised test). `invest_orders.stop_order_id`/`stop_order_status` updated to the new order IDs and `'PLACED'` for all 16.
3. The code fix itself was committed, tested, and deployed the same session — see the deploy log for the exact commit.

**Open, deliberately-not-closed gap, named directly rather than left implicit: the local DB's `stop_order_status` column is write-mostly, not actively re-polled.** This incident was only fully invisible locally because nothing in this system's own automation currently re-checks a placed stop order's real, current T212 status — `stop_order_status='PLACED'` is set once at placement and only ever updated by the cancel-before-alternate-exit path (`maybe_exit_positions()`), never by an independent, periodic liveness check. Had the user not reported the T212-side "expired" notification directly, this incident would have had no automated detection path at all inside this system — `reconcile_positions_with_broker()`'s existing `BROKER_CLOSED_NO_SELL` flag only fires when a position itself vanishes, not when a stop order protecting a still-open position quietly disappears. This is exactly the class of gap the still-held "Sharpen `reconcile_positions_with_broker()` for STOP_LOSS precision" task below was already scoped to address (cross-referencing a position's `stop_order_id` against T212's own order history) — this incident is now a second, concrete, motivating reason to prioritize it, not a new task in its own right.

**Resolved 2026-08-04, same night — see "Periodic stop-health check" below.** The write-mostly gap described in this paragraph (no automated, periodic re-check of a believed-active stop's real T212 status) is now closed by `brokers.trading212.check_stop_health()`, folded into Open Trade Monitor's existing hourly cadence. The still-queued `reconcile_positions_with_broker()` sharpening task remains separately valuable (it correctly *labels* a stop-fired close after the fact, once the position itself has closed) — this new check is complementary, catching the gap *before* the position closes, independent of whether it ever does.

### Bracket orders and market-order payload audit — researched, no gap found (2026-08-04)

Two follow-on questions from the stop-order incident immediately above, investigated back to back the same night. Neither changed any code — recorded here as a closed, "researched, confirmed clean" finding, not left open for later re-investigation.

**1. Does T212 support a combined buy-plus-stop ("bracket") order? No — confirmed directly, not assumed from ambiguous docs.** T212's own official documentation (`docs.trading212.com`/the Redocly-hosted spec) is a JS-rendered SPA that automated fetching cannot read; a GitHub-hosted static copy of the same content (`gist.github.com/Dawdre/ea4f8bc9de3c8c222f10fb760ad315ba`) was readable and gave the real, complete endpoint set: `GET /equity/orders` (list), `GET /equity/orders/{id}`, `DELETE /equity/orders/{id}` (cancel), `POST /equity/orders/market`, `POST /equity/orders/limit`, `POST /equity/orders/stop`, `POST /equity/orders/stop_limit`. **No bracket/combined order type exists in any form.** Independently reconfirmed live against the market endpoint itself (see probe 2 below): attaching a `stopLoss`/`takeProfit` object directly to a market-order request is rejected outright (`"Invalid payload"`), the same result as any other unrecognized field — not a documentation gap, a genuine absence of the capability. **Closed, not worth revisiting**: the current two-step mechanism (place the BUY, then place a separate stop order once the fill is confirmed) is the only way this API supports it, so there is no "should we switch" decision to make — switching isn't an option that exists.

**2. Market-order payload audit — every optional field checked directly against the live API, same rigor as the stop-order incident, motivated directly by it.** Current payload confirmed from the real code before testing anything: `Trading212Client.place_market_order()` sends exactly `{"ticker": ticker, "quantity": quantity}` — two fields, nothing else. Probed every plausible optional field using the same guaranteed-safe technique as the stop-order investigation (a SELL of an absurd quantity of a real, currently-held ticker — `AMAT_US_EQ`, quantity `-999999` — which can only ever fail on `"max-quantity-exceeded"` regardless of any other field, making genuine execution impossible while still exercising real field-level validation):

| Field tested | Result | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| *(baseline — current real payload, no extra fields)* | `400 max-quantity-exceeded` — the specific downstream validation | Confirms the guaranteed-rejection technique itself works as intended |
| `timeValidity` = invalid value | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | — |
| `timeValidity` = `"DAY"` | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | — |
| `timeValidity` = `"GOOD_TILL_CANCEL"` (the exact value confirmed **accepted** by the stop-order endpoint) | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | **Market orders do not recognize `timeValidity` at all** — even the one value known to be a valid enum member on a sibling endpoint fails the market endpoint's schema check outright, rather than being accepted and progressing to the downstream quantity check the way the baseline did |
| `strategy` = `"QUANTITY"` (the exact value seen in real T212 order-history responses for this account) | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | `strategy` is a response-only/computed field — echoed back by T212 after the fact, not settable on a request |
| `strategy` = invalid value | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | Consistent with the above |
| `extendedHours` = `false` (explicit) | `400 max-quantity-exceeded` — the **same specific error as the baseline** | **Direct, empirical proof that omitting `extendedHours` defaults to `false`** — explicit `false` and silent omission produce the identical downstream validation outcome, so there is no silent extended-hours risk hiding behind the omitted field |
| `extendedHours` = invalid (non-boolean) value | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | Confirms the field is genuinely type-checked, consistent with it being real |
| `stopLoss` attached (bracket-order probe) | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | No bracket capability on the market endpoint — corroborates finding 1 above independently |
| `takeProfit` attached (bracket-order probe) | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | Same |
| Totally unknown/nonsense field name | `400 Invalid payload` (generic) | **Calibration probe: T212's schema is strict, not permissive** — any unrecognized field name causes outright rejection of the whole request. This is what makes every "generic Invalid payload" result above interpretable as "field not recognized" rather than "field recognized but happened to fail validation for an unrelated reason" |

**No gap of the `timeValidity`/stop-order shape exists on the market endpoint — this is a structurally different, safer situation, not merely "nothing found yet."** The stop-order bug's danger was specifically that an omitted field was *silently accepted*, the request *succeeded*, and an unsafe, non-obvious default applied underneath — a failure mode invisible until something failed hours later. Here, the calibration probe proves T212's market-order schema rejects any field it doesn't genuinely support, including `timeValidity` itself (despite it being a real, valid concept on the sibling stop-order endpoint) — there is no field on this endpoint capable of being silently accepted with an unsafe default, because an unrecognized field is never silently accepted at all. The one field confirmed to be both real and optional (`extendedHours`) was directly proven to default safely (`false`, matching the already-established assumption from the earlier extended-hours investigation). **Conclusion: the market-order payload is confirmed clean. No code change made or needed.**

### Periodic stop-health check — catching a missing/rejected/expired stop automatically, not by chance (2026-08-04)

Tonight's `timeValidity` incident (all 16 broker-side stops silently rejected — see "Broker-side stop orders rejected after market close" above) was only caught because a T212 notification happened to be seen externally; nothing inside this system would have surfaced it on its own. Distinct from the still-queued "Sharpen `reconcile_positions_with_broker()`" task, which labels a stop correctly *after* it fires and a position closes — this check is earlier: for every position that's supposed to have an active stop, is that stop *still genuinely active right now*, independent of whether the position has closed. A stop silently expiring or being rejected while the position stays open is exactly tonight's shape, and the reconciliation task as scoped wouldn't have caught it before the fact, only explained it correctly after.

**Built into `brokers.trading212.check_stop_health(config)`, folded into Open Trade Monitor's existing hourly job (`_market_hours_check_job()`) — not a new scheduled job.** Runs as the third step in that job, deliberately after both `poll_placed_orders()` (which may have just placed a fresh stop for a newly-FILLED BUY this same cycle) and `maybe_exit_positions()` (which may have just closed a position this same cycle, cancelling its stop as part of the orphan-cancel-fix) — ordering it last avoids flagging either same-cycle transition as a false "missing stop." Its own failure is isolated in the same `try/except` shape every other step in this job already uses — a check-the-checker failure must never itself become a new incident, and must never block the exit check or order poll that share its hourly slot.

**API efficiency — investigated and verified live before building anything, not assumed.** A naive per-position check (`client.get_order(stop_order_id)` once per open position) would add N new T212 calls every hour, scaling directly with position count — exactly the growth pattern the earlier same-night rate-limit collision (`market_hours_check`/`account_state_refresh` colliding at the same cron minute — see "structural safeguards against future T212 API scheduling collisions" above) already showed is a real risk. Instead this uses T212's real order-**list** endpoint, `GET /equity/orders` (no id) — confirmed live before adopting it: the response contained exactly the account's 16 real, currently-active stop orders, each independently cross-matched against `invest_orders.stop_order_id` (16/16 found). `Trading212Client.get_orders()` wraps this — one call, returns every currently active order across the whole account at once, scaling O(1) rather than O(N).

Total new API load per hourly cycle is fixed at **2 calls, regardless of position count**: `client.get_orders()` (the one batched read this check is built on) plus a fresh `client.get_positions()` call. The second call was deliberately NOT avoided by reading the scheduler-maintained `t212_positions_snapshot` cache instead (which would have cost zero new calls) — that snapshot can be up to ~55 minutes stale relative to this job's own firing time (`account_state_refresh` runs hourly at minute=5, this job at minute=0), which would risk a false "missing stop" alert for a position this SAME hourly cycle's own `maybe_exit_positions()` call — which runs immediately before this check, in the same job invocation — has already correctly closed. Correctness was judged worth the one extra fixed call.

**Deliberately scoped to `stop_order_status == 'PLACED'` only** — not `FAILED` (already alerted immediately at placement time via `_place_broker_stop_for_filled_buy()`'s own failure path) and not `CANCEL_FAILED` (already alerted loudly at the moment of that failure, inside `maybe_exit_positions()`'s own orphan-cancel-fix). This check's unique value is the state neither of those covers: a stop that WAS genuinely placed and believed healthy, but has since silently stopped being active — precisely tonight's shape, not a variant of an already-alerted one.

**Auto-remediation was deliberately NOT built — alert-only, considered both ways rather than defaulted.**
- *For* auto-remediation: the re-placement mechanism (`Trading212Client.place_stop_order()`) is now proven — it's the exact code path used to fix tonight's incident — every minute a position sits unprotected is real risk, and re-placing at the same already-decided `stop_price` is not a new trading decision.
- *Against* (the reasoning that won): the root cause of a missing stop is not known at the moment this check runs. Tonight's cause was systemic (affected all 16 identically), but a future one-off could have a different, unrelated cause — a T212-side degradation, or a stale `get_positions()` read racing a stop that just fired and closed the position for a legitimate reason — and blindly re-placing without understanding why risks compounding rather than fixing. `place_stop_order()`'s own docstring documents T212's stop endpoint as **not idempotent** in its beta form ("sending the same request multiple times may result in duplicate orders") — a concrete, endpoint-specific reason to be more cautious here than a generic retry would be, not less. This also matches this project's own established pattern elsewhere for a capital-risk-adjacent anomaly whose cause isn't yet understood: `REPEATED_SELL_REJECTION` gives up auto-retry and flags for manual review rather than hammering the API; `CANCEL_FAILED` alerts rather than silently retrying cancellation. A loud alert that lets a human decide, informed by the specific ticker/order named, is preferred over a silent self-heal that could mask a recurring underlying bug the same way tonight's incident already demonstrates a silent failure can go unnoticed for hours.

**The alert — `output.briefing.send_stop_health_alert()` — uses content-based deduplication, not a time-based cooldown**, mirroring `send_instrument_resolution_failure_alert()`'s own established shape and reasoning exactly (see that function's own docstring, added earlier the same night, for the full "a shared time cooldown can silently suppress a genuinely new, different failure" lesson this reuses rather than re-learns): compares the current sorted unhealthy-ticker set against `stop_health_last_unhealthy_tickers` (its own dedicated `system_metadata` key), sending whenever that set has genuinely changed — a new gap appeared, an existing one resolved, or both — never gated by how recently the last email went out. `check_stop_health()` always calls the alert with the current list, even when empty, so a genuine recovery clears the stored set and a later re-occurrence of the identical ticker is correctly treated as new rather than compared against a stale record. The email names the specific position(s), the missing `stop_order_id`, and the exact manual remediation mechanism already proven tonight — without the system acting on its own.

Covered by 10 tests in `tests/test_execution.py` (a healthy stop produces no alert call beyond the always-passed empty list; a missing stop is flagged with the correct ticker/`t212_ticker`/`stop_order_id`; a healthy position isn't flagged just because a different ticker's stop went bad; an already-closed position isn't flagged; a non-`PLACED` local status isn't checked; the disabled-flag case makes zero API calls; a broker read failure never raises; the decisive **API-call-count proof** — 5 seeded positions, `get_positions()` and `get_orders()` each called exactly once, `get_order()` never called at all; and two scheduler-wiring tests confirming the check genuinely runs from `_market_hours_check_job()` after both existing steps, and that its own failure never blocks the rest of the job), 9 tests in `tests/test_briefing.py` (mirroring `send_instrument_resolution_failure_alert()`'s own test shape: empty-list/disabled/first-occurrence/content/aggregation/unchanged-set/new-failure-immediate/resolution-then-refail/dedicated-dedup-key), and 2 direct HTTP-layer tests in `tests/test_t212_client.py` (`get_orders()` hits the real list endpoint and returns the response verbatim; and, added for parity with every other read endpoint in that file's existing parametrized coverage, a malformed body on a nominally-successful response still raises rather than being silently swallowed — the body IS the payload this check depends on). Full local suite: 762 passing.

### extendedHours for sell orders — investigated, recommendation scoped, nothing implemented (2026-08-04)

Three genuinely different questions, not one uniform "should sells use extendedHours" question — investigated separately, each with real evidence, per this project's own standing "investigate before deciding" discipline.

**Case 1 — new-entry buys: confirmed moot, correctly untouched.** `_stock_order_submission_job()` (`data/scheduler.py`) is gated by `_is_nyse_open_now()` — the STRICTER, regular-hours-only session check, deliberately distinct from `_is_nyse_extended_hours_open()` (see that function's own docstring: *"_is_nyse_open_now() is also the gate _stock_order_submission_job() uses, and that job must stay regular-hours-only: submitting a brand-new entry into T212's own documented thinner extended-hours liquidity ('orders may be delayed or not executed at all') is a separate risk decision this task does not make"*). Confirmed directly by reading the current, deployed code, not assumed from the earlier task's own framing — `extendedHours` is structurally unreachable for a new-entry BUY regardless of setting, since submission never runs outside the regular session in the first place. No change needed or possible here.

**Case 3 — the broker-side stop: the question does not apply to it, confirmed two independent ways, not assumed from "a stop should watch continuously" reasoning alone.**
1. **Live API probe, same guaranteed-safe technique as the earlier market-order audit** (a stop-SELL for an absurd oversized quantity on a real, currently-held ticker — guaranteed to be rejected for exceeding real holdings before any resting order could ever be created): the baseline payload (no `extendedHours`) correctly hit the specific `max-quantity-exceeded` downstream validation. `extendedHours=true`, `extendedHours=false`, and an invalid non-boolean value all produced the **identical generic `Invalid payload` rejection** — never progressing to the specific downstream check the baseline reached — exactly the same "field not recognized at all" signature the market-order audit established as diagnostic. A calibration probe (a nonsense field name) confirmed this endpoint's schema is strict, the same as the market endpoint's, ruling out "recognized but happened to fail for an unrelated reason" as the explanation.
2. **Independent secondary confirmation**: a third-party Go client library (`go-trading212`, whose request structs closely mirror T212's real schema) defines `MarketOrderRequest` with an explicit `ExtendedHours bool` field but defines `StopOrderRequest` with **no such field at all** — the identical asymmetry the live probe found, from a completely independent source.

**Conclusion: `POST /equity/orders/stop` has no `extendedHours`-equivalent field, full stop — there is no flag to set, so this is not a decision this system can make either way via the public API.** Whether the underlying stop-monitoring mechanism watches continuously regardless of session, or is itself restricted to regular hours with no way to widen it, could not be settled with 100% first-party certainty (that would require observing a real trigger event during an extended session, which isn't something to force for a live capital-risk mechanism). The best available evidence points toward continuous monitoring: T212's own help centre states plainly *"All order types are available in 24/5. There are no restrictions"* and *"the toggle is per order"* (`helpcentre.trading212.com`, "24/5 Trading" article) — describing the account-level 24/5 feature broadly, not scoped to exclude stop orders — and structurally, a stop order is a standing watch condition rather than an immediate execution, so unlike a market order (whose `extendedHours` flag decides "should this fire right now, during this exact session") there is no equivalent moment-of-placement decision for a stop to need a flag for. This is treated as strong, not absolute, evidence — stated honestly rather than rounded up to certainty. Either way, no code change is possible here: the field genuinely does not exist to add.

**Case 2 — local sells (signal-off, max-holding, crisis): a genuine trade-off, weighed explicitly, resolved conditionally.** `maybe_exit_positions()`'s SELL call site (`client.place_market_order(t212_ticker, -close_qty)`) and `place_market_order()`'s own signature (`(self, ticker: str, quantity: float)`) currently have no `extendedHours` parameter anywhere in the path — confirmed directly in the current code, not assumed. Since Open Trade Monitor now runs across every extended session (`_is_nyse_extended_hours_open()`), a signal-off/max-holding/crisis condition CAN already be *detected* outside the regular session — but the resulting SELL, submitted with `extendedHours` omitted (defaults `false`, confirmed in the earlier market-order audit), does not fail or get rejected; it sits `PLACED` and only fills once the next regular session opens (the identical "T212 does not fill this system's own orders outside their own regular-hours submission window... unless extendedHours is set" behaviour already documented under "Tracing the '60+ hour fill-lag' claim's real origin"). So today's real behaviour is exactly the "narrows but doesn't close the gap" shape the task description anticipated: faster detection, same old execution timing.

The trade-off, weighed rather than defaulted: extended-hours execution carries T212's own documented, real costs — *"Lower liquidity can result in fewer buy and sell offers, wider spreads may increase the difference between Buy and Sell prices, and higher volatility can lead to sharp price movements due to reduced trading activity"* (`helpcentre.trading212.com`, "What are extended market hours?"), on top of the already-cited *"orders may be delayed or not executed at all."* For a SELL specifically, a wider spread means a worse realised price — real money given up for speed. Whether that trade is worth making depends entirely on how urgent the exit actually is:
- **SIGNAL_OFF / MAX_HOLDING** are ordinary, non-urgent portfolio-management exits — nothing about the position is in acute danger, and there is no compelling reason to accept a materially worse, less certain fill just to save a few hours until the next regular open.
- **CRISIS_EXIT** exists specifically to reduce risk fast during a genuine, acute market-wide shock — the entire mechanism already accepts real execution-quality trade-offs elsewhere in its design (a single-day trigger force-closes every position at once, with no attempt to time an optimal exit) in exchange for speed. A worse fill in exchange for materially faster de-risking is a defensible trade specifically here, in a way it isn't for a routine exit.

**Recommendation: conditional, not uniform — `extendedHours: true` for `CRISIS_EXIT` sells specifically; `SIGNAL_OFF`/`MAX_HOLDING` sells stay regular-hours-only (unchanged).** `STOP_LOSS`'s local evaluation is deliberately not addressed here — it is in scope for the separate, already-queued "Broker-side stop replaces local evaluation" task immediately below, and once the broker owns stop evaluation entirely (case 3, above), the question moot for that exit reason the same way case 1 is moot for new entries. If local `STOP_LOSS` evaluation is still active by the time that task is picked up, the identical "urgent, capital-risk-driven exit" reasoning that justifies `CRISIS_EXIT`'s recommendation here would plausibly extend to it too — noted for that task to consider, not decided here.

**Not implemented at the time this section was written — this investigation concluded with a recommendation, per its own explicit instruction, not a build.** Scoped as a separate follow-up: `place_market_order()` would need a new optional `extended_hours: bool = False` parameter, threaded through to the request payload; `maybe_exit_positions()`'s SELL call site would need to pass `extended_hours=(exit_reason == "CRISIS_EXIT")`. No config flag is obviously needed — this is a fixed, reasoned policy per exit reason, not a tunable.

**Implemented 2026-08-04, same night, as the scoped follow-up above.** `Trading212Client.place_market_order(self, ticker, quantity, extended_hours: bool = False)` gained the recommended parameter — deliberately opt-in, and the `extendedHours` key is only ever added to the request payload when `True`, never sent as an explicit `false`. This is a real distinction, not a stylistic one: every existing caller (every BUY submission, and every non-`CRISIS_EXIT` SELL) sends the exact same two-field `{"ticker", "quantity"}` payload as before this parameter existed — confirmed by a dedicated client-level test asserting the JSON body directly, not just the parameter's default value. `maybe_exit_positions()`'s SELL call site now passes `extended_hours=(exit_reason == "CRISIS_EXIT")` — the only call site in the codebase that ever passes `True`.

**A real, incidental finding from running the full suite, not from the feature's own logic: two pre-existing test fixtures stood in for `place_market_order()` with a hand-written, now-stale two-argument signature** — `test_exit_sell_failure_does_not_halt_remaining_positions`'s local `_fake_place_order()` and `test_comprehensive_replay_parity.py`'s `_ReplayHarness.place_market_order()` (the class that drives real live-code paths against a synthetic account for Layer 2's own multi-day replay parity check — see `analysis/decision.py`'s docstring). Both broke the moment `maybe_exit_positions()` started passing the new keyword argument, with a clear `got an unexpected keyword argument 'extended_hours'` error — not a logic failure, a genuine signature mismatch these two stand-ins hadn't been updated for. Both fixed by adding the identical `extended_hours: bool = False` parameter to each fake/harness, accepted and ignored (the replay harness's own documented same-day-instant-fill simplification has no session-timing model to react to it with) — matching the real method's signature rather than papering over the mismatch by loosening either fixture's own call-shape assertions.

Covered by 6 new tests in `tests/test_execution.py`: `CRISIS_EXIT` confirmed to pass `extended_hours=True` (via a scenario that would also independently trigger `STOP_LOSS`/`MAX_HOLDING`, proving crisis's own priority AND the flag together); `SIGNAL_OFF`, `MAX_HOLDING`, and `STOP_LOSS` each confirmed to pass `extended_hours=False`; a direct client-level test asserting the exact JSON payload sent to `requests.request()` — byte-for-byte `{"ticker", "quantity"}` by default, gaining exactly one key (`"extendedHours": true`) only when requested; and a BUY-path test confirming `_submit_pending_orders()`'s real call site never passes `extended_hours` as a keyword at all (not merely defaulted `False`) — direct evidence case 1 (new-entry buys) stays genuinely untouched, not just unaffected in practice. Full local suite: 771 passing.

### Broker-side stop replaces local evaluation, and reconciliation gains STOP_LOSS precision — unblocked, not yet started

Two follow-on tasks, explicitly sequenced after the mechanism above AND the position-by-position backfill immediately above — both are now confirmed complete, so this section is unblocked:

1. **Remove local `STOP_LOSS` evaluation/closing from `maybe_exit_positions()`** — the broker owns this once every open position genuinely has a real, confirmed-working stop resting at T212. `CRISIS_EXIT`/`SIGNAL_OFF`/`MAX_HOLDING` are untouched; none of the three can move to the broker (all depend on this system's own signal/crisis logic, not a fixed price level).
2. **Sharpen `reconcile_positions_with_broker()`** to distinguish a routine broker-side stop firing (a vanished position with a matching, recently-placed `stop_order_id` on its BUY row) from the genuinely unexpected events it already handles (`BROKER_CLOSED_NO_SELL` for a real cash-out acquisition, `UNRECOGNIZED_POSITION` for a stock-swap) — recording the former precisely as a `STOP_LOSS`-exited `t212_pnl` row instead of folding it into the generic manual-review bucket. This is what closes the P&L-recording gap named directly above, and is what makes "Performance by Exit Reason" (a real, visible Dashboard section) trustworthy for stop-fired closes once the broker owns stop evaluation entirely.

Not started — tracked as a distinct, separate task from the backfill above, not folded in here.

### Submission-time crisis re-check (2026-08-03) — confirmed real gap, fixed before Monday

**Urgent finding, confirmed real by tracing the actual code, not assumed.** `passes_entry_gate()`'s crisis block (`analysis/decision.py`, backed by `analysis/crisis.py:is_entry_blocked()`) is only ever evaluated once, inside `maybe_place_orders()`'s decide phase at EOD (21:30 UTC). Stock submission fires up to ~17 hours later (14:30 UTC the next calendar day). Traced `_submit_pending_orders()` line by line: it checks already-held, a recent DB order, per-ticker price-sanity (`_live_current_price()`), position-size viability, and capacity fit — **it never called `passes_entry_gate()`, `crisis.is_entry_blocked()`, or `crisis.is_intraday_crisis()` at all before this fix.** A genuine, severe market decline beginning after decide time and before submission would not have stopped yesterday's now-stale BUY decisions from still going out — exactly the opposite of what the crisis override exists to prevent, and a real, not hypothetical, gap.

**Why simply "re-checking `is_entry_blocked()` at submission time" would not actually have fixed this — the crucial, non-obvious part of this investigation.** `compute_raw_trigger()`/`is_entry_blocked()` are daily-bar-only by design — they read `price_data`, which is only ever written once a day, at the 21:30 UTC EOD pull. At 14:30 UTC the next day, `price_data`'s most recent `^GSPC` row is still **yesterday's** close — the exact same row decide time already saw the night before. Re-running the identical daily-bar check against identical stored data at submission time would be a no-op that only *looked* like a fix. Closing the real gap needed a genuinely fresh, intraday data source.

**The fix — `analysis/crisis.py:is_intraday_crisis(gspc_close, live_price)`**, a new pure function comparing a genuinely live `^GSPC` quote (via the existing `_live_current_price()` — the same yfinance `fast_info.last_price` mechanism already used for the per-ticker submission-time sanity check, generalised to any ticker string including the index itself) against the most recent *stored* close, using the identical `PRICE_GAP_THRESHOLD` (-7%) `compute_raw_trigger()` already uses. Not a replacement for `is_entry_blocked()` — the two are complementary and both are checked: `is_intraday_crisis()` catches a decline not yet recorded as a daily bar; `is_entry_blocked()` still catches the multi-day cooldown-window case, which is already reflected in stored data and needs no live quote to detect.

**Wired into `_submit_pending_orders()`**, once per run (market-wide, not per-ticker — cheaper and correct, since the S&P's own crisis state doesn't vary by candidate), immediately after confirming there's anything pending to submit and before any per-row work: fetches `gspc_close` and a live `^GSPC` quote, checks both functions, and on a confirmed block resolves **every** currently-pending row for that asset class to a new terminal status, `SKIPPED_CRISIS_BLOCKED` (added to `PendingOrder.status`'s documented value set), with a note stating the block was re-evaluated fresh, not inherited. Nothing is submitted that run. Tomorrow's EOD decide cycle re-evaluates and re-queues anything still valid once the block clears — resolving today's stale batch loses nothing a fresh decide-time pass wouldn't naturally re-derive anyway.

**Fail-safe behaviour, deliberately asymmetric between "confirmed blocked" and "couldn't check."** A *confirmed* crisis (either check genuinely returns `True`) resolves all pending rows to the terminal `SKIPPED_CRISIS_BLOCKED` status. A *failure to even check* (a data-read exception — e.g. `_load_gspc_close()` raising) is treated differently: rows are left untouched, still `PENDING`, retried at the next submission window — mirroring exactly how a single ticker's own missing live price already leaves that row pending rather than assuming either "safe" or "blocked." This distinction matters: guessing "safe" on a check failure would silently reopen the exact gap this fix closes; but permanently discarding a legitimate queued decision over a transient network hiccup would be its own new, unnecessary cost. Confirmed via a dedicated test that forces `_load_gspc_close()` to raise: no order is placed, and the row survives as `PENDING`, not `SKIPPED_CRISIS_BLOCKED`.

**A real pre-existing test regression, found and fixed, not weakened around.** One capacity test (`test_capacity_fit_reason_matches_real_submission_rejection_for_the_same_inputs`) had never mocked `^GSPC`'s price data at all, since it predates this fix and had no reason to. Once wired in, its unmocked, empty `^GSPC` series correctly triggered the new fail-safe path (a genuine read error, since `_load_gspc_close()` calls `.set_index("date")` on an empty DataFrame with no columns) — confirming the fail-safe behaviour works exactly as designed, but breaking a test that wasn't trying to exercise it. Fixed by mocking `^GSPC` a normal, non-crashed price series (the correct fix — this is genuinely how production always looks, since `^GSPC` price history has existed continuously since 2007 — not a reason to loosen the new check).

Covered by 6 new pure unit tests in `tests/test_crisis.py` (`is_intraday_crisis()`'s threshold boundary, using the correct — most recent, not an earlier — stored close, and its None/empty/non-positive guards) and 5 new integration tests in `tests/test_execution.py`: the decisive case (crisis visible *only* via a live quote, completely absent from stored data — the exact scenario `is_entry_blocked()` alone could never have caught); the daily-bar cooldown case still correctly re-confirmed; a clean no-crisis control/regression; and the check-failure fail-safe case. Full local suite: 563 passing (10 new).

**Resolved before Monday's first live cycle** — both the stock submission job (14:30 UTC) and the (currently-paused, dead-code-only) ETF submission path share the identical `_submit_pending_orders()` function, so both are covered by this fix with no separate wiring needed.

### Crisis-mode dashboard banner (2026-08-03)

Nothing on the Dashboard previously surfaced when the crisis override was actually blocking new entries — a user checking the page during a real crisis would see normal-looking candidate/status displays with no indication anything was restricted.

**Extracted the shared authoritative check first, rather than let the banner become a second computation.** The submission-time crisis re-check above (`_submit_pending_orders()`) had its combined daily-bar/intraday logic inlined directly in that function. Pulled out into `brokers/trading212.py:is_crisis_mode_active_now() -> Optional[bool]` — the single, shared implementation of "is the crisis override blocking new entries right now," returning `True`/`False`/`None` (a data-read failure, distinct from a confirmed `False`). `_submit_pending_orders()` was refactored to call this same function rather than keep its own inline copy — a pure refactor, re-verified against all 6 pre-existing crisis-submission tests with no behaviour change.

**`output/performance.py:get_crisis_status()`'s `entry_blocked` field now defers to this same function**, rather than the daily-bar-only `crisis.is_entry_blocked()` it used exclusively before (built 2026-07-31, two days before the intraday check existed). This mattered concretely, not just for tidiness: `get_crisis_status()`'s own `today_return_pct`/`distance_to_threshold_pp` display fields are still computed from stored daily-bar data (legitimate — they're informational, not a gating decision), but before this fix, `entry_blocked` was too — meaning a crisis visible *only* intraday (the exact scenario `is_intraday_crisis()` exists to catch) would have shown the Dashboard reporting "not blocked" while order submission was already correctly refusing every new entry. A dedicated test proves this directly: stored daily-bar data shows a calm day (`is_crisis_today` correctly `False`), yet `entry_blocked` still follows the authoritative check when it reports `True`. `is_crisis_mode_active_now()` returning `None` (couldn't determine) maps to `entry_blocked=False` at this display-only layer — a display function fails toward showing nothing rather than a stale or fabricated verdict; the real safety mechanism lives entirely in `_submit_pending_orders()`'s own `None` handling, never in whether a banner happens to render.

**`main.py:_render_crisis_banner()`**, called from `_render_dashboard_page()` immediately after the trading-enabled check (so it doesn't render a redundant warning when trading is disabled entirely for an unrelated reason). Reads `_get_crisis_status()` (the existing `@st.cache_data(ttl=300)`-wrapped thin wrapper around `get_crisis_status()`) and renders an `st.error()` box only when `entry_blocked` is truthy — nothing at all otherwise, deliberately: a muted/inactive version of a warning banner risks being mistaken for a real one, so the only two states are "shown" and "not present on the page," never a third, quieter variant. The banner text states plainly that **only new entries** are affected — existing positions continue to be monitored and exited normally — matching this project's own "decision-relevant, tone-neutral" content standard elsewhere on this page, just for a genuinely urgent state this time.

Covered by: a direct unit test of `is_crisis_mode_active_now()` itself (True/False/None, using the same mocking pattern as the submission-time tests); 2 new `get_crisis_status()` tests in `tests/test_performance.py` (the daily-bar-vs-authoritative-source divergence proof above, and the `None`-maps-to-`False` case); and 4 Dashboard tests in `tests/test_main_ui.py` (banner appears when blocked, absent under normal conditions, absent on an empty/no-data status rather than misread as blocked, and the banner text contains both required halves — "new entries" and "existing positions" / "monitored"). A pre-existing gap in three `get_crisis_status()` tests was found and fixed in the same change: they mocked `data.ingestion.get_price_df` but not the new `is_crisis_mode_active_now()` boundary, which — unmocked — would have made a real DB read and a real yfinance network call inside the test suite; fixed by mocking `brokers.trading212.is_crisis_mode_active_now` directly, the correct boundary now that `get_crisis_status()` depends on it.

Full local suite: 570 passing (7 new).

### 30-day re-entry cooldown — live/backtest parity gap closed, and a real, material headline-figure change (2026-08-03)

**The gap, confirmed real.** `brokers/trading212.py:_load_open_order_tickers(days=30)` has always blocked live re-entry into a ticker with a `PLACED`/`FILLED` order in the last 30 calendar days — called from both the decide phase (`maybe_place_orders()`) and submission (`_submit_pending_orders()`). No simulation engine had an equivalent: `analysis/backtest.py` could freely re-enter a ticker the instant it exited. This is not a minor divergence — it directly violates this project's own protected "live/backtest decision-logic parity" invariant (see that section above), and given how many of today's headline findings rested on backtest results, it meant those results were produced by an engine with a genuine extra degree of freedom live has never had.

**Part A — the fix.** `analysis/decision.py:REENTRY_COOLDOWN_DAYS = 30` and `is_reentry_blocked(days_since_last_order, cooldown_days=REENTRY_COOLDOWN_DAYS)` are the single shared threshold and predicate. Following the exact precedent this file already established for candidate-priority-ranking (one SQL `ORDER BY`, one Python `sort()`, accepted duplication of a simple rule with a shared threshold and independent tests on each side — see "Live/backtest decision-logic parity" above): live's bulk SQL query (`_load_open_order_tickers()`) and the backtest engine's per-ticker inline check cannot literally share one function call, but both now read the identical `REENTRY_COOLDOWN_DAYS` constant instead of each hardcoding their own `30`, and both are independently tested against the same 30-day boundary.

**Only `analysis/backtest.py:simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` enforces it** — the engine `analysis/validation.py:run_full_validation()` actually defaults to, the one confirmed to genuinely match live order placement. `simulate_trades()`, `simulate_portfolio()`, and `simulate_portfolio_compounding()` are deliberately, explicitly exempt: each is a frozen engine, kept alongside the corrected one specifically so an already-published historical figure that cites it (the "Current baseline" table, the "Portfolio-capped validation findings" table, the "Compounding portfolio backtest" sweep) stays exactly reproducible on demand. Adding new behaviour to a frozen engine would break that reproducibility guarantee rather than close a live-parity gap that matters for anything those three engines are still used for — each now states this exemption explicitly in its own docstring, a reviewed decision, not an oversight.

Covered by 8 new tests: 4 pure unit tests for `is_reentry_blocked()`/`REENTRY_COOLDOWN_DAYS` (`tests/test_decision.py`); 2 MTM-engine-level tests (`tests/test_portfolio_backtest.py`) — the decisive one proving a ticker whose signal turns back on the very next day after a `SIGNAL_OFF` exit does NOT re-enter until its exit is ≥30 calendar days old (exactly what the pre-fix engine would have done immediately), plus a control confirming a ticker's genuine first-ever entry is never treated as cooling down; 2 live-side tests (`tests/test_execution.py`) confirming `_load_open_order_tickers()`'s default now reads the shared constant, and a real DB-backed boundary check (29 days still blocks, 31 days doesn't) matching the backtest's own boundary exactly. Full local suite: 578 passing.

**Part B — does this change any headline finding? Yes, materially — reported directly, not averaged away.** The 91% index-removal-momentum finding ("Let momentum, not index removal, govern already-open positions" above) is unaffected by construction: it explicitly used `analysis.backtest.simulate_trades()` — one of the three deliberately-exempt frozen engines — confirmed by re-reading that section's own text, not re-run. The "Full-500 momentum-only (no market-cap gate)" finding does use the corrected engine, so it was re-verified directly.

**Methodology.** Isolated server-side clone (own copied DB, deleted after this section was drafted, production never touched — confirmed via `git status`/commit hash/service uptime before and after). The original investigation's `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm_reset_at_boundary()` wrapper (built via source introspection, since deleted along with its research clone) was reconstructed the identical way — `inspect.getsource()` on the real, current `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()`, with one additive injection: `cash` is force-set so `current_balance` reads exactly £50,000 the first event date on or after 2020-01-01, once only, before that day's entries are evaluated. Verified faithful before trusting it for anything: with the reset date pushed past the end of all data (never fires), the wrapper reproduced the real, un-modified function's trades exactly, byte-for-byte, both before and after the cooldown fix (3088 and 3067 trades respectively, matching in full).

The SAME script was run twice against the SAME data (a 1,205-ticker historical candidate pool, 501 usable after excluding insufficient-history tickers — a real, larger set than the original study's frozen 503-candidate snapshot, since `universe_membership` has kept accumulating via the ongoing daily refresh job since 2026-08-02; this is expected data-recency drift, not a methodology change) — once against the pre-fix `analysis/backtest.py`, once against the post-fix version, differing in nothing else:

| | Pre-fix (BEFORE) | Post-fix (AFTER) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Test-period trades (entry ≥ 2020-01-01) | 1,181 | 1,146 | −35 (−3.0%) |
| Win rate | 48.94% | 47.56% | −1.38pp |
| Profit factor | 1.77 | 1.72 | −0.05 |
| CAGR | 19.86% | 17.05% | **−2.81pp** |
| Max drawdown (fixed-denominator) | −27.48% | −23.28% | +4.20pp (improved) |
| Max drawdown (peak-relative) | −11.19% | −7.76% | +3.43pp (improved) |
| £50,000 → | £162,914.46 | £140,324.79 | **−£22,589.67 (−13.9%)** |

**The BEFORE column is itself a strong validation, not just a control**: 1,181 trades / 48.94% win rate / PF 1.77 / CAGR 19.86% / DD −27.48%/−11.19% / £162,914.46 essentially exactly reproduces the original published figures (1,182 / 48.82% / 1.77 / 19.83% / −27.43%/−11.19% / £162,802.54) — within the same ordinary day-to-day data-drift tolerance this file's own reproducibility checks have repeatedly accepted elsewhere. This confirms both that the reset-at-boundary reconstruction technique is faithful and that the pre-fix figures were correctly reported at the time.

**Direct, honest statement: this is a material change, not a rounding difference.** CAGR drops from ~19.9% to ~17.0% — roughly a 14% relative reduction in the headline growth figure — and the £-ending-balance drops by £22,590 (13.9%) on the identical £50,000 base. Drawdown genuinely *improves* under both conventions (the cooldown also prevents some rapid, whipsaw-prone re-entries into a ticker right after exiting it), so this is not a one-sided regression — but the CAGR and ending-£ figures specifically, the ones most likely to be quoted as headline numbers, are real, quantified, and lower. The direction is intuitively sound (removing 35 trades' worth of re-entry opportunity, ~3% of the total, naturally reduces total compounding) — not a symptom of a bug, but a real consequence of closing a genuine extra degree of freedom the pre-fix engine had that live never did.

**What this means going forward.** Every already-published "Full-500 momentum-only" figure in this file's "No market-cap gate at all" section was generated by the pre-fix engine and should be read as reflecting that engine, not the corrected one — the table above is now the reference for what the corrected engine actually produces on directly comparable data. The live Backtest page (`main.py`'s "Run Full Validated Battery" button, `run_full_validation(live_universe=True, mark_to_market=True)`) uses this exact engine — once this fix is deployed, the next click of that button will show these materially lower, more conservative CAGR/£-balance figures, not the previously-published ones. This is the corrected, live-parity-respecting result taking effect, not a regression to investigate.

**Not independently re-verified**: the curated-40 and rolling-40 columns of the same original comparison table, and the DAX/European reproduction. Both use much smaller candidate pools (39-40 tickers) where re-entry opportunities are inherently rarer, so the same fix is plausibly less impactful there — but this is a reasoned expectation, not a measured one, and should not be treated as confirmed without running the identical before/after comparison on those specific figures too.

### Re-entry cooldown set to 0 (config-driven) (2026-08-03)

The Part B comparison immediately above showed 0 days (no cooldown at all) clearly outperforming the 30-day default on every headline figure that moved — CAGR 19.86% vs. 17.05%, £50,000 → £162,914.46 vs. £140,324.79 — for a drawdown difference (−11.19% vs. −7.76% peak-relative) judged immaterial at this scale. Rather than leave the parity fix at a value already known to be worse, production was set to the current best-known value while a fuller sweep across intermediate values (below) checks whether something between the two endpoints does even better.

**Made genuinely config-driven, not hand-edited into the constant.** `REENTRY_COOLDOWN_DAYS = 30` (`analysis/decision.py`) remains in place unchanged, but purely as the fallback default for a config predating this parameter — the real value is resolved by the new `resolve_reentry_cooldown_days(config)`, reading `trading212_invest.reentry_cooldown_days` (falling back to the constant when absent). Both consumers now call this ONE function rather than each reading config independently: `brokers/trading212.py`'s two `_load_open_order_tickers()` call sites (`maybe_place_orders()`'s decide phase, `_submit_pending_orders()`) resolve it and pass `days=` explicitly; `analysis/backtest.py:simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` resolves it once per run (alongside its other `trading212_invest`-sourced VaR parameters) and passes `cooldown_days=` explicitly into every `is_reentry_blocked()` call inside `_admit_group()`. This mirrors the established config-driven-parameter pattern already used throughout `trading212_invest:` (`per_trade_pct`, `max_total_deployed`, `price_sanity_threshold_pct`, `pending_orders_retention_days`, ...) — a Python constant as the backwards-compatible fallback, config as the real, live-editable value — and, as a direct practical consequence, makes every value in the sweep below actionable by editing `config.yaml` alone, with no code change needed per value tested.

**Production value**: `trading212_invest.reentry_cooldown_days: 0`.

**"Inert for any order today" — corrected, not simply confirmed.** The original framing for this deploy claimed the account had zero orders of any kind in the 30 days preceding it. Checked directly against production `invest_orders`, this was **not quite right**: 27 rows exist in that window, and one — a `FILLED` SELL on `XLF`, 2026-07-31 (the known UCITS-mapping-correction close) — is exactly the status pair (`PLACED`/`FILLED`) `_load_open_order_tickers()` counts. The other 26 rows are `CANCELLED`/`RESET_SUPERSEDED` and never counted regardless of cooldown length. In practice this still changed no live-actionable outcome: `XLF` is an ETF, and the entire ETF sleeve was removed from the live candidate pool the day before (see "ETF sleeve removed from live trading" above) — confirmed zero occurrences of `XLF` anywhere in production's current `instruments:` — so it can never become a live entry candidate again regardless of what the cooldown value resolves to. The deploy's practical inertness holds; the literal "zero orders" claim did not, and is corrected here rather than left standing.

Covered by 5 new tests: 3 in `tests/test_decision.py` (`resolve_reentry_cooldown_days()` reads a configured value, falls back to 30 when the key is absent — both a `{"trading212_invest": {}}` and a fully empty `{}` config — and confirms a resolved 0 genuinely un-blocks `is_reentry_blocked()`); 1 in `tests/test_portfolio_backtest.py` (the identical exit-then-immediate-signal-back-on scenario the original 30-day proof used, but with `reentry_cooldown_days: 0` in config, now re-enters the very next day rather than waiting 30); 1 in `tests/test_execution.py` (a real DB-backed row confirming the SAME just-placed order is blocked under the unchanged 30-day fallback default but not under a config-resolved `days=0`). Full local suite: 583 passing.

### Re-entry cooldown sweep — is 0 the true optimum? (2026-08-03)

**Question.** The 0-vs-30 comparison above settled the two endpoints — 0 is clearly better than 30 — but left open whether some intermediate value (1, 3, 5, 7, 14, 21 days) captures most of the whipsaw/drawdown protection a cooldown is meant to provide at a smaller CAGR cost, or whether 0 remains the best choice once the full range is actually measured rather than just the two ends of it. No external published research gives a usable starting point for the specific optimal length — whipsaw is a well-documented general problem in momentum strategies, but the right cooldown duration is system-dependent, not a figure with a standard reference value — so this was answered empirically, against this system's own data.

**Backtest convention, stated explicitly.** Reset-at-boundary (not continuous-walk — see "Two backtest conventions" above): every value tested resets to the identical £50,000 at the 2020-01-01 train/test boundary before the test-period comparison begins, exactly matching the methodology of the 0-vs-30 comparison immediately above (same reconstructed `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm_reset_at_boundary()` wrapper, same source-introspection technique, same sanity check that the wrapper reproduces the real function exactly when the reset never fires). This is the correct convention for **comparing variants** — which cooldown length is better — not a report of one strategy's realistic single-account track record.

**Methodology — run in two places, cross-validated against each other.** Following the standing practice this file now documents (see "Experimental/research work runs locally, not on the server" above): the sweep ran primarily as a local Claude Code session against a fresh production DB snapshot (`scp`'d down, `501` usable tickers / `704` skipped for insufficient history — confirmed identical to the server's own count before trusting anything downstream), using the exact current code (including this same day's `reentry_cooldown_days` fix). A server-side isolated clone (own copied DB, `.backup`-snapshotted, deleted after use) ran the same script independently and in parallel, as a genuine cross-environment check rather than a second methodology — it completed 6 of 8 values (0/1/3/5/7/14) before being stopped once local finished all 8. **Every one of those 6 overlapping values matched exactly, byte-for-byte, across the two environments** (Ubuntu server vs. Windows local, different Python builds) — including the sanity check itself, which independently reproduced the identical 3,246-trade wrapper-fidelity result on both sides. This is a stronger cross-check than the original 0-vs-30 comparison had (which ran once, on one machine) and leaves no real doubt the numbers below reflect the code and data, not an environment artifact.

Local execution ran 8 processes across two batches of 4 (matching the local machine's 4 physical cores), each doing its own precompute + one full 2007–2026 walk; only the `cooldown=0` run additionally repeated the real-function-vs-wrapper sanity check (since that only needs proving once). Full local suite (583 tests) was unaffected — this sweep touched no source file, only a disposable clone.

**Full results, all 8 values:**

| Cooldown (days) | Full-walk trades | Test trades | Win rate | Profit factor | CAGR | Max DD (fixed-denom) | Max DD (peak-relative) | £50,000 → |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3,241 | 1,181 | 48.94% | 1.77 | 19.86% | −27.48% | −11.19% | £162,914.46 |
| 1 | 3,241 | 1,181 | 48.94% | 1.77 | 19.86% | −27.48% | −11.19% | £162,914.46 |
| 3 | 3,216 | 1,185 | 48.10% | 1.75 | 19.60% | −32.32% | −10.49% | £160,668.25 |
| 5 | 3,187 | 1,172 | 49.15% | **1.83** | **21.09%** | −35.28% | −9.25% | **£174,261.59** |
| 7 | 3,208 | 1,183 | 48.18% | 1.75 | 18.45% | −22.40% | −9.30% | £150,838.50 |
| 14 | 3,134 | 1,173 | 47.40% | 1.71 | 16.76% | −20.75% | **−7.07%** | £137,358.08 |
| 21 | 3,107 | 1,155 | 48.23% | 1.75 | 17.83% | −18.58% | −7.62% | £145,856.77 |
| 30 | 3,067 | 1,146 | 47.56% | 1.72 | 17.05% | −23.28% | −7.76% | £140,324.79 |

**0 and 1 are identical, exactly as predicted from the engine's own structure, not by coincidence.** `_admit_group()`'s `flat_before_today` set (`analysis/backtest.py`) is computed before that day's exits are processed, so a ticker that exits on day D can never re-enter before day D+1 — meaning `days_since_exit` on the earliest possible re-entry day is already ≥1 by construction, regardless of the configured cooldown. `is_reentry_blocked(1, cooldown_days=0)` and `is_reentry_blocked(1, cooldown_days=1)` both evaluate `False` — a `cooldown_days=1` setting can never block anything the pipeline's own decide-then-submit structure wasn't already going to block. The same holds live: even at `reentry_cooldown_days=0`, a real re-entry still can't land before the next scheduled submission window after the exit's own EOD decide phase queued it — "0" means "as fast as the pipeline can move," never "instant."

**Not monotonic beyond that — a real, reproducible, non-smooth result, reported as found.** CAGR does not decline smoothly as the cooldown lengthens: 19.86% (0/1) → 19.60% (3) → **21.09% (5, the single best value in the whole sweep)** → 18.45% (7) → 16.76% (14, the trough) → 17.83% (21) → 17.05% (30). Profit factor, win rate, and ending balance all peak at the same point (5 days) and trough at the same point (14 days) as CAGR — not an isolated blip in one metric. Peak-relative drawdown is the one column that behaves closer to the naive "longer cooldown, less whipsaw, lower drawdown" intuition (11.19% → 10.49% → 9.25% → 9.30% → 7.07% → 7.62% → 7.76%, mostly improving with length, best at 14 days) — but even this isn't perfectly smooth (5→7 is flat, 14→21→30 mildly worsens again). Fixed-denominator drawdown is the noisiest column of all, with no clear trend.

**Why — a mechanistic explanation, not just "it's noisy."** Full-walk trade count itself isn't monotonic either (7 days produces *more* full-walk trades than 5 days, despite the longer cooldown) — the reason is structural, not measurement error: entries in this engine are capacity-constrained (`_admit_group()`'s skip-and-continue, momentum-ranked admission against a shared `max_total_deployed` cap). Blocking one ticker's re-entry doesn't just remove that trade — it frees a capacity slot a *different* candidate wins instead, that same day. Over a 19-year, thousands-of-decisions walk, a slightly different cooldown value changes not only whether a specific re-entry happens, but which alternate candidate is admitted in its place, cascading into a materially different downstream trade sequence for the rest of history. This is a genuine path-dependency effect of capacity competition, not noise in the ordinary sense — but it does mean this sweep's single continuous walk is far more sensitive to the exact cooldown value than a simple "does this ticker re-enter better with more cooldown" question would suggest, and a bump at one specific value (5 days) is not, by itself, strong evidence that value is structurally better going forward.

**Recommendation — do not switch away from 0 on this evidence alone.** 5 days is the strongest single point in the sweep (best CAGR, profit factor, win rate, and ending balance simultaneously, meaningfully better than both its neighbors and the 0/1-day baseline), which is worth recording plainly rather than downplaying. But the surrounding non-monotonicity — 3 days underperforming 1, 7/14 days dropping sharply below 5, 21 partially recovering — is exactly the shape a capacity-competition-driven path-dependency effect would produce from ordinary trade-sequencing sensitivity in **one** continuous historical walk, not the shape a robust, generalizable effect would produce. This sweep has no cross-validation of its own (no walk-forward, no alternate universe, no bootstrap) to distinguish "5 days is genuinely better" from "5 days happened to catch a favorable trade sequence in this one 2007–2026 path." Production stays at `reentry_cooldown_days: 0` — the value already confirmed better than the old 30-day default on every metric, and the only value in this sweep with a real mechanistic reason to expect it (it's the pipeline's own natural floor, not an arbitrary choice). A genuine test of whether 5 days holds up would need a walk-forward-style robustness check (per-window profit factor, the same discipline `walk_forward_pf()` already applies elsewhere in this file) before being trusted as more than a single-path curiosity — not attempted here, and not something this sweep's own methodology can settle on its own.

Research-only — nothing in `config.yaml`, `analysis/decision.py`, `analysis/backtest.py`, or `brokers/trading212.py` changed as a result of this sweep. Both the local and server-side clones were deleted after these figures were captured; production confirmed untouched throughout (commit hash and both services' `ActiveEnterTimestamp` unchanged by this work).

### Does the entry gate need an absolute minimum momentum floor? (2026-08-03)

**Question.** The entry gate requires only `momentum > 0` — no distinction between a genuinely trending candidate and one that is barely, statistically-indistinguishably positive. In normal conditions this is harmless (capacity-based admission naturally reaches only the strong end of the pool before running out). The real concern is a slow, grinding decline — broadly compressed momentum, no single violent day (so the crisis override never fires) — where every real candidate is only marginally positive and idle capacity has nothing better to admit than "the best of a bad bunch." Investigated in two parts, entirely locally (per "Experimental/research work runs locally, not on the server" above), read-only against a fresh production DB snapshot and the current code (including the same day's `reentry_cooldown_days` fix) — nothing in `config.yaml`, `analysis/`, or `brokers/` changed as a result.

**Part A — how often does this actually happen?** Instrumented `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` via the same source-introspection technique used throughout this file's research history (verified faithful — inert-default and reset-disabled runs both reproduce the real function's trades exactly, before trusting anything downstream) to record, for every day/group candidate-pool evaluation across the full 2007–2026 continuous walk (501 usable stock tickers — the live candidate pool, no ETFs, matching today's real universe): the full momentum distribution of every entry-gate-passing candidate, and whether real account capacity was available that day (`current_deployed / current_balance < max_total_deployed`).

| Marginal threshold | Days: ALL candidates below it (of 3,903 capacity-available days with ≥1 candidate) | Days: majority below it | Real admitted trades below it (of 3,246 total) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1% | 15 (0.38%) | 19 (0.49%) | 57 (1.76%) |
| 2% | 35 (0.90%) | 51 (1.31%) | 105 (3.23%) |
| 5% | 63 (1.61%) | 124 (3.18%) | 178 (5.48%) |

**Genuinely rare, but not zero — both things are true and neither cancels the other out.** At a 2% "marginal" definition, fewer than 1% of capacity-available days ever saw every real candidate that weak, and only ~3% of every trade this system has ever entered (across the full 19-year validated window) had entry momentum that low. This matches the task's own framing — today's real candidate list is overwhelmingly strong, capacity is the binding constraint, not weakness — and confirms it isn't a theoretical worry either: 35 real days (2% threshold) to 63 real days (5% threshold) is a small but genuine number of instances, not zero.

**Part B — sweep of absolute floors, reset-at-boundary methodology (matching every prior sweep's own "comparing variants" convention — see "Two backtest conventions" above), test period 2020–2026:**

| Floor | Test trades | Win rate | Profit factor | CAGR | Max DD (fixed-denom) | Max DD (peak-relative) | £50,000 → |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0% (today's gate) | 1,181 | 48.94% | 1.77 | 19.86% | −27.48% | −11.19% | £162,914.46 |
| 2% | 1,179 | 49.11% | 1.77 | **19.88%** | −27.52% | −11.19% | **£163,127.21** |
| 5% | 1,166 | 47.77% | 1.70 | 18.50% | −22.93% | −10.82% | £151,236.74 |
| 10% | 1,178 | 47.88% | 1.69 | 18.39% | −28.89% | −10.75% | £150,329.27 |
| 15% | 1,179 | 48.52% | 1.69 | 18.71% | −29.98% | **−11.43%** | £153,015.58 |

Non-monotonic again, for the identical structural reason documented in the re-entry cooldown sweep immediately above — entries here are the same capacity-constrained, momentum-ranked, skip-and-continue admission, so excluding one candidate hands its slot to a different one, cascading into a materially different downstream trade sequence over a 19-year walk. Drawdown does **not** cleanly improve with a higher floor either — 15% is actually the single worst peak-relative drawdown in the whole table, worse than the 0% baseline.

**Early-stage-winner exclusion check — the decisive evidence, computed directly from the 0%-floor baseline's own trades (uncontaminated by the capacity-cascade re-run effect above), not inferred from the aggregate table:**

| Floor | Trades directly excluded | Band win rate | Band mean P&L | Genuine ≥20% winners excluded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2% | 1 | 0% | −9.08% | 0 |
| 5% | 5 | 40.0% | −3.88% | 0 |
| 10% | 9 | 55.6% | +0.58% | 0 |
| 15% | 17 | 58.8% | **+3.68%** (above the 2.61% overall average) | **2** — `TSLA` (entered at 12.02% momentum, went on to +26.38%) and `CEG` (entered at 12.23%, went on to +25.95%) |

**A 2% floor is close to free; a 15% floor has a demonstrated, concrete cost.** At 2%, exactly one trade in the entire six-year test period would have been excluded, and it was a loser (−9.08%) — no genuine winner sacrificed, and the aggregate CAGR/return is unchanged or marginally better. By 15%, the excluded band's own win rate and mean return are *better* than the overall average — meaning the floor at that level is filtering out a disproportionately good set of trades, including two real, named, verifiable early-stage winners. This is exactly the hidden cost the task's own framing warned against, and it shows up precisely where a naive "higher floor = more confidence = safer" intuition would have predicted the opposite.

**Recommendation: a small floor (2%) is worth adding; do not go higher without more evidence.** Part A shows the scenario is rare but real (dozens of genuine historical days, not zero); Part B shows a 2% floor costs essentially nothing — flat-to-marginally-better CAGR, no genuine winner excluded — while formalizing the existing capacity-driven de facto floor into an explicit, principled rule, directly serving the stated goal ("invest in trades with real confidence behind them, not just to stay in the market at all costs"). Nothing past 2% is supported by this data: 5%/10%/15% show no clean, monotonic benefit (the CAGR/drawdown figures bounce for the same path-dependency reason the re-entry cooldown sweep already documented), and 15% has a concrete, named cost. **Caveat, stated plainly**: every excluded-band sample here is small (1 to 17 trades across a six-year test period) — this is directional, evidence-based guidance, not a statistically powerful result, and the same single-continuous-walk limitation the re-entry cooldown sweep flagged applies here too. Not implemented — this was explicitly a "check before it matters" investigation, not an urgent live change; adding a 2% floor to `passes_entry_gate()` (or a new, adjacent check) is a follow-up decision, not made here.

Research-only — nothing in `config.yaml`, `analysis/decision.py`, `analysis/backtest.py`, or `brokers/trading212.py` changed as a result of this investigation. The local scratch clone was deleted after these figures were captured; production was never touched (this task was explicitly local and read-only relative to the live system throughout).

### Is the 5-day re-entry cooldown result real, or a lucky historical sequence? (2026-08-03)

**Question.** The re-entry cooldown sweep found 5 days as the strongest single point (CAGR 21.09% vs. 0's 19.86%) — but the sweep itself flagged a real structural path-dependency: entries are capacity-constrained, so blocking one re-entry hands that slot to a different candidate, cascading into a materially different trade sequence over the full 19-year continuous walk. Each cooldown value's result is therefore one single realized path, not an independent sample. This investigation tests whether 5 days holds up as a genuinely robust effect once that path-dependency is controlled for.

**Methodology — genuinely independent per-block resets, not a slice of one continuous run.** Built a new engine variant (same source-introspection technique as every prior injection in this file) that truncates the day-by-day event list to `[block_start, block_end]` and force-closes any still-open position at the block's own end (a corrected `END_OF_DATA`, keyed to the block boundary rather than each ticker's absolute last date — without this, a position still open when a block's truncated walk ran out of days would silently vanish from that block's own results rather than being recorded). Because every ticker starts with zero open positions and a fresh £50,000 the instant the truncated walk begins, no separate "reset cash" step is needed — the walk's first visited day already has that pristine state by construction, since nothing before `block_start` is ever touched. Verified faithful (inert defaults reproduce the real function exactly) and verified the truncation mechanism itself (all trades bounded within the window; still-open positions correctly force-closed via `END_OF_DATA`, not dropped) before trusting it for anything.

Reused the exact same 16-block boundaries this project already trusts elsewhere (`analysis.backtest.make_blocks(analysis.validation.VALIDATION_START, end, n_blocks=16)`), `end` pinned explicitly to `2026-08-03` for reproducibility. Four cooldown values tested: 0 (deployed), 4, 5, 6 days — each run as 16 fully independent £50,000 simulations, not 16 slices of one compounding run.

**Per-block CAGR, all four values, all 16 blocks:**

| Block | Window | 0d | 4d | 5d | 6d | Winner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2007-01-01→2008-03-23 | 6.23% | 9.85% | 6.37% | 6.27% | 4d |
| 1 | 2008-03-23→2009-06-13 | −22.14% | −20.94% | −18.79% | −19.79% | 5d* |
| 2 | 2009-06-13→2010-09-03 | 11.96% | 13.98% | 12.57% | 11.67% | 4d |
| 3 | 2010-09-03→2011-11-24 | 8.98% | 10.21% | 9.20% | 10.45% | 6d |
| 4 | 2011-11-24→2013-02-13 | 8.21% | 9.83% | 8.22% | 9.62% | 4d |
| 5 | 2013-02-13→2014-05-06 | 10.16% | 7.80% | 6.36% | 7.89% | 0d |
| 6 | 2014-05-06→2015-07-27 | 8.75% | 13.16% | 12.68% | 13.10% | 4d |
| 7 | 2015-07-27→2016-10-17 | 16.96% | 17.19% | 14.73% | 16.64% | 4d |
| 8 | 2016-10-17→2018-01-07 | 13.62% | 10.77% | 9.60% | 7.93% | 0d |
| 9 | 2018-01-07→2019-03-30 | 6.09% | 11.29% | 3.84% | 5.29% | 4d |
| 10 | 2019-03-30→2020-06-19 | 13.56% | 13.50% | 13.00% | 13.39% | 0d |
| 11 | 2020-06-19→2021-09-09 | 12.16% | 11.37% | 11.22% | 10.55% | 0d |

| 13 | 2022-11-30→2024-02-20 | 15.25% | 18.14% | 17.19% | 16.64% | 4d |
| 14 | 2024-02-20→2025-05-12 | 9.11% | 13.09% | 12.93% | 14.02% | 6d |
| 15 | 2025-05-12→2026-08-03 | 38.18% | 37.44% | 34.44% | 37.69% | 0d |

*Block 1 (GFC-acute) fails on every single value tested (all four badly negative, matching this file's own established "blocks 0/1 always fail" finding) — "winning" among four losses isn't a meaningful win and isn't counted as evidence for 5 below.

**Win count (highest CAGR per block, 16 blocks): 0d = 6, 4d = 7, 5d = 1, 6d = 2.** 5 days — the value the continuous-walk sweep found strongest overall — wins exactly **one** of 16 genuinely independent blocks, and that one win is the always-failing GFC-acute block where all four values lose money. Excluding that block, 5 days never wins a single one of the remaining 15. Aggregate mean/median CAGR across the 16 independent blocks: 0d = 10.46%/10.25%, 4d = **11.59%/11.33%** (highest), 5d = 10.17%/10.41% (lowest), 6d = 10.66%/10.50%. Under genuine per-block independence, 5 days is not merely "not the best" — it is the **weakest** of the four values tested on both win count and aggregate CAGR, the exact opposite of what the continuous-walk sweep showed.

**Neighbor-smoothness check.** In **9 of 16 blocks**, 5 days is a **local trough** — worse than *both* its immediate neighbors (4 and 6 days) — not a smooth peak with 4 and 6 tapering off on either side. Only 1 block shows 5 as a spike-up (better than both neighbors); the remaining 6 show a smooth, monotonic relationship. A genuine, structural "5 days is a real local optimum" effect should show a curve that peaks smoothly at 5 and falls off symmetrically to either side — the data shows almost the reverse: 5 is more often the *worst* of the three immediate neighbors than the best.

**Verdict — stated plainly, not forced into a clean recommendation the data doesn't support: the continuous-walk sweep's "5 days is best" finding does not survive block-independent validation.** It looks like a favourable interaction with one specific realized historical sequence (the exact path-dependency effect the sweep itself flagged as the reason to distrust a single continuous walk), not a genuine, robust property of a 5-day cooldown. 0 days — production's current, already-deployed value — performs competitively under this stricter test (6/16 wins, second only to 4 days, and a higher mean CAGR than 5 days) and retains its own independent, non-empirical mechanistic justification (it's `_admit_group()`'s own natural floor, not a chosen parameter) that neither 4, 5, nor 6 have. **This is not a recommendation to switch to 4 days either** — 4 winning 7/16 blocks here is a genuinely stronger showing than 5's, but this is one robustness check with 16 blocks, not a validated finding in its own right, and the same caution this whole investigation exists to demonstrate (one favourable-looking result is not evidence until it survives a check like this) applies equally to treating 4's showing here as settled. Production stays at `reentry_cooldown_days: 0`, unchanged.

Research-only — nothing in `config.yaml`, `analysis/decision.py`, `analysis/backtest.py`, or `brokers/trading212.py` changed as a result of this investigation. The local scratch clone was deleted after these figures were captured; production was never touched.

### Block-based confirmation of the 2% momentum floor (2026-08-03)

**Question.** The momentum-floor sweep found a 2% absolute minimum-momentum floor to be essentially free — over the six-year test period, it would have blocked exactly one trade, already confirmed to be a loser. Unlike the re-entry cooldown result, this was never an aggregate statistical claim across many trades — it's a single, nameable, already-verified case. Confidence was already reasonably high, but the block-independent validation infrastructure built for the cooldown check made a final confirmation cheap, worth doing before touching a live, currently-working safety mechanism.

**Methodology.** Combined the two engine injections built earlier the same day (block-independent walk truncation + corrected `END_OF_DATA`, from the cooldown block study; momentum-floor filtering + admission-momentum recording, from the original floor sweep) into one engine — every injected line has an already-verified precedent in one of those two prior modules. Verified faithful (inert defaults reproduce the real function exactly) before trusting it. Re-ran floor 0% and floor 2% across the same 16 established blocks, reset-independently each time — the identical methodology and block boundaries as the cooldown check, so the two studies are directly comparable.
