- Signal/regime/module-score context — `signal_type`, `confluence_score`, and `regime` come from the BUY row (the entry decision); the five per-module scores (`trend_score`, `mean_reversion_score`, `volatility_score`, `volume_score`, `macro_score`) are looked up retroactively from the nearest `signals` row on or before the BUY's fill date, since `t212_invest_orders` only stores the aggregate `confluence_score`, not the per-module breakdown.
- `exit_reason` — copied directly from the SELL row's `exit_reason` column (see `T212InvestOrder` above).

Writes one row per newly-closed pair to the `t212_pnl` table (`T212Pnl` model), keyed on a `(buy_order_id, sell_order_id)` unique constraint. Idempotent by design: a Python-side pre-filter checks already-reconstructed pairs before attempting inserts, with the DB unique constraint (`on_conflict_do_nothing`) as a defensive backstop, so calling this repeatedly (it runs on every exit-check cadence) only ever writes rows for positions closed since the last call. "Never raises" contract — any DB error is logged and swallowed, matching the rest of `brokers/`'s automation functions.

**Date comparisons use SQLite's `date()` function, not raw `<=`.** A Python `datetime` with `microsecond=0` stringifies without a fractional-seconds component (e.g. `"2026-06-20 00:00:00"`), while SQLAlchemy's `DateTime` column always stores one (`.000000`). Since SQLite stores dates as TEXT and compares lexicographically, a raw `date <= :d` comparison silently excludes same-day rows more often than not — `date(date) <= date(:d)` normalises both sides to day granularity first, which is all that matters anyway since both `price_data` and `signals` are daily-bar tables.

Called from `maybe_exit_t212_positions(config)` and `maybe_exit_stock_positions(config)` — placed immediately after the `enabled` + credentials checks, **before** either function's `if not positions_by_ucits: return` / `if not positions_by_t212: return` early-return guard. This ordering matters: that guard fires exactly when there are currently zero open positions, which is precisely the state right after a position has just closed — reconstructing "after the position-checking logic" would mean it never actually runs for the single-position case. Since both exit functions already run on every hourly trade-alert cycle and from the EOD run (see "Exit timing" above), reconstruction effectively runs on the same cadence with no dedicated scheduler job of its own.

### Email alerts

`output/briefing.py` provides email functions that all send **HTML emails with plain-text fallback** via a shared `_smtp_send(subject, text_body, html_body, config)` helper. `_smtp_send` builds a `MIMEMultipart("alternative")` message, attaches both text and HTML parts, reads `smtp_pass` from config or `os.environ.get("SMTP_PASSWORD", "")`, and handles the SMTP connection/login/sendmail in one place. All HTML uses inline CSS only (no flex/grid, `bgcolor` attribute on TD elements for Outlook compatibility).

- `send_weekly_summary_email(config)` — gathers data via `_gather_weekly_data(config)` (DB-only, no external API calls). `_build_weekly_email_html(data, config)` produces HTML sections: Market Regime & Overlays, Signal Snapshot, Last Week's Performance, T212 Positions Closed This Week, Signal Accuracy Progress (HTML progress bar), Macro Pulse, Watch List. Plain text built separately by `_build_weekly_email(data, config)`. Sends stamped to `system_metadata` under `last_weekly_summary_sent`. Respects `notifications.weekly_summary.enabled` independently of `notifications.email.enabled`. The "Open Trades" section it used to include was removed along with manual CFD trade logging (see "Removed: manual CFD trade logging" above); "Closed This Week" and "Signal Accuracy Progress" both source from `t212_pnl` via `get_t212_closed_positions()` (see "Trade lifecycle" above), not the legacy `trades` table.
- `send_test_email(config, ...)` — `_build_test_html(config, regime, last_analysis, open_trade_count)` produces a status table + confirmation strip. Bypasses the enabled flag; always sends. Returns a success string with recipient addresses. `open_trade_count` is now the count of open T212 Invest positions (`len(_get_t212_invest_brief_cards(config))`), not CFD trades.
- `send_vix_spike_alert(vix_pct, vix_current, vix_prev, config)` — sent by the hourly job's VIX spike check when VIX rises >20% intraday vs. the previous close (once per calendar day).

Manual CFD trade alert emails (`send_alert_email()`, `should_send_alert()`, `_build_alert_html()`, `_options_block_html()`, and their exclusive helpers `_option_row_h()`, `_stop_distance_str()`, `_current_regime()`, `_next_analysis_run_uk()`, and the `_STATUS_EMAIL_LABELS`/`_REGIME_SIGNAL_NOTES`/`_STATUS_PRIORITY` constants) were removed along with the CFD alerting loop in `_trade_alert_job()` — see "Removed: manual CFD trade logging" above. `STATUS_COLOURS`, `STATUS_ICONS`, and `_pnl_color()` are kept — they're still used by `main.py:_render_trade_card()` (T212 cards) and the weekly summary email respectively.

When writing raw SQL against the `correlations` table in email or scheduler code, use the actual column names: `divergence` (not `status_30d`), `z_score` (not `z_score_30d`), `pair_score` (not `expected_direction`).

### yfinance MultiIndex handling

`yf.download()` for a single ticker returns a MultiIndex column DataFrame in yfinance ≥ 0.2.x. `ingestion.py` flattens this with `df.columns = [col[0] for col in df.columns]` before processing. Any new code that calls `yf.download` for a single ticker must do the same.

## Deployment (Ubuntu 22.04 / cloud VM)

The app runs as a systemd service behind a Caddy HTTPS reverse proxy.

### First-time setup on a fresh VM

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/YOUR/investment-research.git /root/investment-research
cd /root/investment-research

# 2. Run the one-time setup script (takes ~5 min)
bash setup.sh research.yourdomain.com
```

`setup.sh` installs Python 3.11, compiles the TA-Lib C library from source, installs Caddy, installs all packages system-wide via `python3.11 -m pip`, writes `.streamlit/config.toml`, and registers both `investment-research.service` (Streamlit web UI) and `investment-research-scheduler.service` (standalone scheduler daemon) with systemd. It also creates a symlink so the scheduler daemon inherits credentials from the same secrets drop-in file as the web UI service. There is no virtualenv — packages are installed at the system level.

### Password-protecting the dashboard

Caddy's `basicauth` directive guards the app. After `setup.sh` runs:

```bash
caddy hash-password          # enter your password, copy the hash output
nano /etc/caddy/Caddyfile    # replace REPLACE_WITH_HASH (and 'admin' if desired)
systemctl reload caddy
```

### Managing server credentials

API keys and passwords live in a systemd drop-in override file that is never touched by deploys:

```
/etc/systemd/system/investment-research.service.d/secrets.conf
```

```ini
[Service]
Environment=FRED_API_KEY=...
Environment=SMTP_PASSWORD=...
Environment=T212_API_KEY=...
Environment=T212_API_SECRET=...
```

After editing: `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart investment-research && systemctl restart investment-research-scheduler`. The `investment-research.service` template in the repo has blank placeholders — never put real values there. The drop-in takes precedence and is unaffected by `deploy.sh` or `git pull`.

The scheduler daemon inherits the same credentials automatically. `setup.sh` and both deploy scripts create `/etc/systemd/system/investment-research-scheduler.service.d/secrets.conf` as a symlink pointing at the web UI drop-in — only one secrets file to manage.

### Ongoing deploys (from Windows)

The easiest path is a plain `git push origin main` — the pre-push hook calls `deploy.ps1` automatically (see [Git hooks](#git-hooks) below). To deploy without that hook, or from a machine where it isn't installed:

```bash
bash deploy.sh          # Git Bash — VM_IP is hardcoded in the script
```

```powershell
.\deploy.ps1            # PowerShell — gitignored, local-only; SSH key at ssh-keys\
```

Both scripts push to GitHub first, then SSH into the VM to `git pull`, reinstall any new packages, copy both service files to `/etc/systemd/system/`, ensure the secrets symlink exists for the scheduler service, run `systemctl daemon-reload`, and restart both `investment-research` and `investment-research-scheduler`. Service file changes in the repo take effect automatically on the next deploy.

**Two systemd services must both be restarted on every deploy** — there is no way to update just one:

- `investment-research` — the Streamlit web UI.
- `investment-research-scheduler` — the standalone APScheduler daemon (`scheduler_daemon.py`) that fires all ten scheduled jobs even when no browser is connected (see "Status page and startup automation" above).

Both processes import the same modules independently at startup and keep their own in-memory copy of the code until restarted. **If a deploy restarts `investment-research` but not `investment-research-scheduler`, the scheduler daemon keeps running the pre-deploy code** — including stale versions of `analysis/regime.py`'s `is_entry_allowed()` / `resolve_entry_signal()` and `brokers/trading212.py`'s order-placement logic. Since the daemon (not the web UI) is what actually places T212 orders on the EOD/pre-market/US-open schedule, this means newly-deployed regime gates, entry-signal overrides, or any other order-logic change silently fail to apply — orders keep being placed under the old rules until the daemon itself is restarted. `deploy.sh`, `deploy.ps1`, and `setup.sh` all restart/enable both services for exactly this reason — never edit them to restart only `investment-research`.

After any deploy that touches order logic, verify both services picked up the same code by checking their start times match the deploy:

```bash
ps aux | grep -E "streamlit|scheduler_daemon" | grep -v grep
systemctl status investment-research investment-research-scheduler
```

### Git hooks

`setup-hooks.sh` installs a pre-push hook that auto-deploys whenever you push to `main`. Run once after cloning:

```bash
bash setup-hooks.sh
```

The hook runs `pytest` from the project root first. A failing suite aborts the push (exit 1) with `❌ Tests failed — push aborted. Fix failing tests before deploying.` — nothing reaches GitHub or the server. A passing suite prints `✅ Tests passed — pushing now; deploy to platform.example.com will follow in the background.` and exits 0, letting the outer `git push` (the one you actually ran) proceed and push the commits itself. See "Running tests" above for what the suite covers and how it stays self-contained.

The hook does **not** push to GitHub itself — it schedules the SSH deploy as a detached background job (`nohup ... & disown`) that sleeps 15 seconds before running, giving the outer `git push` time to land on GitHub first, then SSHes in to `git pull` and restart the service. Output is appended to `/tmp/investment-research-deploy.log` on the local machine rather than the terminal, since the hook has already exited by the time it runs. (An earlier version of this hook pushed to GitHub from inside itself before deploying, which raced the outer `git push`: the hook's own push advanced `origin/main`, so the outer push — still holding the old remote SHA it read at hook-invocation time — got rejected with `cannot lock ref`. Not pushing from the hook at all removes the race.) To skip both the tests and the deploy for a single push: `git push --no-verify`.

### Deployment timing

Every scheduled job (see `start_scheduler()` in `data/scheduler.py`) fires at a fixed UTC (or, for the weekly summary, Europe/London) time and several place or submit live broker orders. A deploy that lands mid-job — `git pull` mid-way through, or `systemctl restart` killing the process mid-run — leaves the service running a half-updated version of the code or reading a half-updated `config.yaml` for the remainder of that run, and can commit broker order decisions based on that transitional state. The scheduled job windows most at risk:

| Window (UTC) | Weekdays only? | Job |
|---|---|---|
| 06:45–07:15 | Yes | `etf_order_submission` (07:00, submits queued ETF entries during LSE hours); `monday_premarket` (07:00, Mondays only — cancels stale weekend orders first, then re-runs the order pipeline) |
| 13:15–14:00 | Yes | `stock_order_submission` (13:30, submits queued stock entries during NYSE's regular open) |
| 21:00–22:00 | Yes | `membership_refresh` (21:15) and `scheduled_eod` (21:30, full data refresh + order placement) — EOD is the highest-risk job, the one that places T212 orders |
| 07:45–09:15 (Sun) | No — Sunday only | `weekly_summary` — fires at 09:00 *Europe/London*, not a fixed UTC time (08:00 UTC in BST, 09:00 UTC in GMT); the window covers both possible times with a buffer rather than the script computing today's DST state at runtime |

**Corrected 2026-08-02 — this table, and the two deploy scripts' own blackout checks, were stale in three ways, found and fixed together:** (1) the 06:45–07:15 and 13:15–14:00 windows still named the "pre-market analysis"/"US open analysis" jobs removed 2026-07-31 (see "Pre-market/US-open scheduled runs removed") — both time slots are still genuine order-placing windows today, just under the newer `etf_order_submission`/`stock_order_submission` names (see "Exchange-aware order submission"); (2) the Sunday window (previously 09:45–10:15) assumed a fixed 10:00 UTC weekly-summary time that predates that job moving to 09:00 Europe/London (see "Weekly summary email — Sunday 09:00 UK local time") — 10:00 UTC never matched either DST case, and the old window didn't even bracket the 09:00 GMT case correctly; (3) none of the three weekday windows ever checked day-of-week at all, so all three fired as false positives every Saturday/Sunday — confirmed directly by dry-running the range logic against injected times/weekdays, not assumed, before trusting the fix. A real deploy on Sunday 2026-08-02 at 13:26 UTC hit exactly this: the (then-stale) 13:15–14:00 window showed active, and proceeding required manually re-deriving that the underlying job no longer applied — this fix makes that judgment automatic instead of something every future Sunday/Saturday deploy has to re-derive from scratch.

**Blackout warning (`deploy.sh` / `deploy.ps1`):** both deploy scripts check the current UTC time before doing anything else. `deploy.sh` compares `date -u +%H%M`/`date -u +%u` against the ranges above (weekday-gated via a small `is_weekday()` helper for the three non-Sunday windows); `deploy.ps1` uses `[System.DateTime]::UtcNow`/`.DayOfWeek` the same way. If the current time falls inside any window, the script prints a warning naming the specific job and its run time (e.g. `⚠️  WARNING: Stock order submission job runs at 13:30 UTC weekdays — deploying now risks order logic running on transitional state.`), followed by `Note: deploy restarts BOTH investment-research and investment-research-scheduler.`, and prompts `Continue anyway? (y/N):`. Any answer other than `y`/`Y` aborts with exit code 1 before either script touches git or SSHes into the server — nothing is deployed. This is a warning, not a hard block, because some deploys (urgent hotfixes) legitimately need to go out regardless of the clock. The reminder matters more than usual here: a deploy that skips restarting the scheduler daemon is worse than no deploy at all — the web UI shows new code while the daemon keeps placing orders under the old logic (see "Ongoing deploys" above).

**Missed EOD catch-up (`data/scheduler.py:_check_missed_eod_run()`):** the inverse safety net — if a restart (from a blackout-window deploy or otherwise) causes the 21:30 EOD job itself to be skipped for the day, this runs at scheduler startup, after all jobs are registered, and detects it. It requires both: `last_full_refresh` (in `system_metadata`) is more than 20 hours old — a run from earlier the same day doesn't count as missed — and the current UTC time is between 21:45 and 23:59 — the 15-minute grace period after 21:30 plus the rest of the post-EOD window. Inside that window with a stale timestamp, it logs `"Missed EOD run detected — running catch-up pipeline now"` and runs `_run_analysis_pipeline(config, get_all_tickers(config), "full")` in a background daemon thread so `start_scheduler()` returns promptly. Outside the window it skips silently — the next scheduled job (tomorrow's 07:00 pre-market or 21:30 EOD) will pick up stale data naturally. A `None` `last_full_refresh` (fresh install, no data yet) also skips silently, and the existing weekend guard (no EOD job is ever scheduled Saturday/Sunday) is preserved. This replaced an earlier, looser version (`_maybe_catch_up_missed_eod`) that used a 26-hour threshold OR'd with an unbounded "past today's EOD time" check and re-ran the full `_eod_job` (data pull + FRED + T212 snapshot) rather than just the analysis/signal/order pipeline.

**Recommendation:** for deployments affecting order logic (`brokers/trading212.py`, `data/scheduler.py`, `analysis/confluence.py`, `config.yaml`), deploy before 21:00 UTC or after 22:00 UTC on weekdays.

### Key files

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `setup.sh` | One-time server bootstrap (no virtualenv; installs packages system-wide) |
| `investment-research.service` | systemd unit for the Streamlit web UI |
| `investment-research-scheduler.service` | systemd unit for the standalone scheduler daemon (fires jobs at boot, no browser required) |
| `scheduler_daemon.py` | Entry point for the scheduler daemon — calls `init_db()` + `start_scheduler()` then sleeps in a heartbeat loop |
| `Caddyfile` | Caddy reverse-proxy template (gitignored — contains domain/hash) |
| `.streamlit/config.toml.example` | Reference for the server config created by `setup.sh` (actual file is gitignored) |
| `deploy.sh` | Git Bash deploy script (VM_IP hardcoded; SSH key at `ssh-keys/`) |
| `deploy.ps1` | PowerShell deploy script — gitignored (local-only, contains SSH key path) |
| `setup-hooks.sh` | Installs the pre-push git hook; run once after cloning |
| `config.yaml` | Runtime config — **actually git-tracked** (not in `.gitignore`, despite this file previously documenting it as gitignored/server-managed). Secret fields (`macro.fred_api_key`, `notifications.email.smtp_password`) are committed as blank placeholders — real values are supplied only via env vars (`FRED_API_KEY`, `SMTP_PASSWORD`, `T212_API_KEY`, `T212_API_SECRET`) in the server's systemd secrets drop-in, never written into this file. Verify those fields stay blank before committing any change here. |

### TA-Lib: Windows vs Linux

`requirements.txt` has both package names commented out with explanations. `setup.sh` installs `TA-Lib` (Linux wrapper) after compiling the C library. Windows dev installs `TA-Lib-Precompiled` manually if needed; all analysis modules have pure-pandas fallbacks so it is optional on both platforms.

### Useful server commands

```bash
journalctl -u investment-research -f              # web UI live logs
journalctl -u investment-research-scheduler -f   # scheduler daemon live logs
systemctl status investment-research             # web UI service health
systemctl status investment-research-scheduler   # scheduler daemon health
systemctl restart investment-research-scheduler  # restart scheduler (e.g. after config change)
systemctl reload caddy                           # apply Caddyfile changes without downtime
```

## Adding a new analysis module

1. Create `analysis/your_module.py` with a `compute_your_module(df, config) -> dict` returning `{"score": int, ...raw_values}`.
2. Call it in `analysis/engine.py:analyse_ticker()` and merge its raw values into `indicator_values`.
3. Call it in `analysis/confluence.py:score_ticker()` and add its score to `module_scores`.
4. Add `"your_module"` with a weight to every regime dict in `analysis/regime.py:REGIME_WEIGHTS` — weights must still sum to 1.0 per regime.
5. Add `your_module_score` to the `Signal` model in `data/database.py`, to `_apply_migrations()`, and to the upsert in `confluence.py:_persist_signal()`.
6. Add any new raw-value columns to the `Indicator` model and to `_apply_migrations()`.
7. Update `total_signal_modules` in `config.yaml`.

Note: `analysis/correlations.py` is an exception to the pattern — it operates on pairs of assets rather than a single ticker's DataFrame, so `compute_all_pairs()` is called once at the end of `run_analysis()` rather than inside `analyse_ticker()`, and `compute_correlations(ticker, config)` fetches its own data internally rather than accepting a pre-fetched `df`.

## The live trading universe — fully dynamic, no manual curation (rewritten 2026-08-03)

**This section used to describe a manual `watchlist:` config-editing workflow (add a ticker, set a `tradeable` flag, place it in a sector group). That workflow, that config section, and the flag no longer exist.** `config.yaml` has no `watchlist:` section at all any more — only `reference_tickers:`, a short, fixed list of monitoring-only instruments (`^GSPC`, `GBPUSD=X`, `EURUSD=X`) that never gets an execution mapping and essentially never changes. The live stock-trading universe is not configured anywhere — it is derived automatically, every day, from real S&P 500 index membership.

**How a ticker actually becomes tradeable.** `analysis/universe.py:get_live_stock_candidates()` returns every ticker this system has ever discovered as a genuine (former or current) S&P 500 constituent, filtered down to genuine membership *as of today* via `is_member()`. The discovery side, `refresh_membership_from_source()`, re-fetches a public, point-in-time S&P 500 membership dataset (`fja05680/sp500` on GitHub — see `analysis/universe.py`'s own module docstring for the verification this source received before being trusted) once a day, 15 minutes ahead of the EOD job (the `membership_refresh` scheduler job, 21:15 UTC). **There is no onboarding step for a new S&P 500 addition and no code change for a removal** — a stock added to the real index today becomes a live candidate the moment tomorrow's membership refresh discovers it; a stock removed from the index stops being one the same way. `passes_entry_gate()` (`analysis/decision.py`) still requires a positive 12-month-momentum signal and a clear crisis-override window before any of this turns into an actual entry — membership alone only ever determines *candidacy*, never a decision to buy.

**No discretionary exclusions — this is a stated design decision, not an oversight.** `analysis/universe.py`'s own docstring is explicit: a stock is eligible on any date it was a genuine index constituent, nothing else. TSLA, META, and GOOGL are all live candidates, included from their real membership dates. An earlier version of this system excluded these three names (plus TSM) for subjective "socio-political/geopolitical risk" reasons — that exclusion is deliberately not reproduced in the current design, and should not be reintroduced without a fresh, explicit decision; see the module's own docstring for the full reasoning, not just this summary. TSM itself is absent from the universe for a genuinely different, objective reason: Taiwan Semiconductor is a foreign private issuer, and foreign companies are structurally ineligible for S&P 500 inclusion — it has no membership window in the source data at any date, unrelated to the earlier subjective exclusion.

**A separate, deliberately frozen universe exists purely for backtest/research reproducibility — do not confuse the two.** `analysis/universe.py:ALL_TICKERS`/`ETF_TICKERS`/`STOCK_MEMBERSHIP` is a hand-curated, static set (33 broad ETFs + 40 US large-cap stocks, one of which — `GOLD`, Barrick Gold — is deliberately kept with an empty membership window since it was never a genuine constituent, kept only so a specific historical backtest figure stays reproducible) used only by the frozen research/backtest engines this file's own "V2 architecture" and later sections validate against. It is intentionally *not* kept in sync with the live universe — changing it would silently invalidate every already-published backtest figure that cites it. There is no live-trading reason to ever add a ticker here; doing so is a deliberate, rare research action (e.g. reproducing or extending an already-published study), not a routine "add an asset" task.

**What, if anything, genuinely still needs a manual edit today:** adding a new *reference* ticker (a fixed monitoring/conversion instrument like `^GSPC` or a currency pair) to `reference_tickers:` — genuinely rare, since the three there today cover the crisis-override index and the two FX conversions the system currently needs. There is no other manual asset-management step in the live system.

## Status page scheduler-health/job-recency fixes (2026-08-03)

Two rounds of fixes on the same underlying root cause, found via real production evidence rather than code review alone: `stock_order_submission` (the job that actually places live orders, added 2026-08-02 — see "Exchange-aware order submission" above) and `weekly_summary` were both genuine, currently-registered jobs that several Status-page consumers of "the complete job set" simply didn't know about — each consumer had its own hardcoded or partially-stamped notion of what jobs exist, and none of them had been updated when the two newer jobs were added.

**Round 1 — the Scheduler Health table.** `main.py`'s `_JOB_LABELS` dict and the daemon-mode job-list reconstruction (`_static_jobs`/`_extra_static` in `_render_status_page()`, used whenever the standalone scheduler daemon — not the in-process fallback — is what's actually running, i.e. normal production) were both missing `stock_order_submission` and `weekly_summary` entirely, and mislabeled `scheduled_eod`/`membership_refresh` as `"Mon–Fri"` when both jobs were changed 2026-08-02 to fire *every calendar day* with internal NYSE-calendar gating (`_is_scheduled_trading_day()`). Fixed: both jobs added with correct schedule labels; the stale `day_of_week="mon-fri"` reconstruction removed from `scheduled_eod`/`membership_refresh`'s daemon-mode trigger rebuild so the "Next Run" column is never wrong on a weekend/holiday.

**Round 2 — real production evidence exposed a second, independent instance of the same root cause.** 16 real positions were opened on a Monday at 14:30 UTC / 15:30 BST (the `stock_order_submission` job genuinely firing), yet the Status page's "Last Scheduled Run" card, the Pipeline table's "2 · Order Logic" row, and the sidebar's "Last scheduled run" caption — all three read the identical `system_metadata` key, `last_scheduled_run`/`last_scheduled_run_name` — still showed that same Monday's earlier 07:00 UTC / 08:00 BST Monday Pre-Market job as the most recent event. Traced to the source: `last_scheduled_run`/`last_scheduled_run_name` were only ever stamped by `_eod_job()` and `_monday_premarket_job()` (`data/scheduler.py`) — `_stock_order_submission_job()` and `_weekly_summary_job()` never touched either key at all, despite both being real, currently-registered jobs. Fixed by adding the identical stamping call (`set_metadata("last_scheduled_run", ...)` / `set_metadata("last_scheduled_run_name", "...")`) to both, in a `try/except` matching the existing pattern exactly — stamped unconditionally once each job genuinely fires (mirroring `_monday_premarket_job()`, which has no internal no-op gate), not only when the job actually placed an order — "the job ran" is the signal this key represents, not "the job did something." A third consumer of the same key (the sidebar's "Last scheduled run" caption in `main.py`) reads it directly with no separate list of its own, so it self-healed with no additional code change once the source was fixed — confirmed by grepping the whole repo for every reader of `last_scheduled_run`, not assumed.

**A second, independent bug found in the same investigation: the price-pull/order-logic staleness thresholds were calendar-day-naive, not NYSE-trading-day-aware.** Real evidence: the "Last Data Refresh"/"1 · Price Data Refresh" widgets showed **STALE** for a refresh only one real NYSE trading day old (Friday's EOD run, as of the following Monday) — a genuine 63+ hour gap, but only one real trading day — directly contradicting the same page's own "Data Coverage" section, which already correctly uses a genuine NYSE-trading-day count (`_price_coverage()`'s own per-ticker logic, unaffected by this bug and left as-is) under the stated "Fresh (≤3 trading days)" convention. The cause: `main.py:_age_level()` was a flat elapsed-hours count (48h/96h for price refresh, 48h/72h for order logic, plus an ad hoc, only-partially-weekday-aware 14h/26h check for the "Last Scheduled Run" card specifically) with no concept of a weekend or market holiday at all — an inconsistency between two widgets on the same page describing the same underlying concept two different ways.

**Fix.** `main.py:_nyse_trading_days_since(ts)` — a new, genuinely calendar-aware count (`pandas_market_calendars`, NYSE specifically, since that's the only calendar this system's live decisions depend on since the ETF sleeve's removal — see "ETF sleeve removed from live trading" above) of trading sessions strictly after `ts`'s date, through today. `_trading_day_age_level(ts, warn_td=3, error_td=6)` maps that count to ok/warn/error using the same "≤3 trading days = fresh" threshold already established elsewhere on the page, so the whole Status page now agrees with itself on what "stale" means. `_pipeline_row()`'s signature changed from `(label, ts, warn_h, error_h, desc, ...)` to `(label, ts, level, desc, ...)` — callers now precompute the level via whichever rule actually fits that row, rather than the row-rendering function assuming one hardcoded rule for everything it renders; both Pipeline rows and both of the "Last Data Refresh"/"Last Scheduled Run" cards now call `_trading_day_age_level()`. The old `_age_level()` was deleted outright once its last caller was removed — confirmed genuinely unused via a full-repo grep before deleting, not assumed — matching this project's standing practice of not leaving confirmed-dead code in place.

**Test-isolation hazard found and fixed while adding coverage for the scheduler-side stamping fix.** The two new `set_metadata()` calls in `_stock_order_submission_job()`/`_weekly_summary_job()` are NOT mocked by several pre-existing tests in `tests/test_scheduler.py` that call these functions directly (`test_weekly_summary_job_calls_send_weekly_summary_email`, `test_weekly_summary_job_never_raises_on_failure`, `test_stock_order_submission_job_calls_submit_pending_stock_orders`, `test_stock_order_submission_job_never_raises_on_failure`) — running them unmocked calls the real `data.database.set_metadata()`, which resolves its own DB path via `data.database._load_config()` (a separate function from `data.scheduler._load_config()`, which these tests DO mock) and genuinely opened and wrote to this machine's real local `database/investment_research.db` file during a test run, confirmed directly via the file's mtime changing and the actual `last_scheduled_run`/`last_scheduled_run_name` rows it overwrote. Fixed by adding `mocker.patch("data.scheduler.set_metadata")` to all four pre-existing tests, plus two new dedicated tests asserting the stamping calls themselves. The local DB's `last_scheduled_run`/`last_scheduled_run_name` values were left as the test-run's own overwritten values rather than fabricating a "restored" prior value with no real source of truth to restore from — this is a local, non-authoritative research-copy database (see "Experimental/research work runs locally, not on the server" above), not the live production database on the server, so the practical impact is limited to this one local file's own display accuracy.

Covered by 2 new tests in `tests/test_scheduler.py` (`test_weekly_summary_job_stamps_last_scheduled_run`, `test_stock_order_submission_job_stamps_last_scheduled_run`) and 3 new tests in `tests/test_main_ui.py` — all three constructed against real, independently-computed NYSE calendar dates (`pandas_market_calendars`, not a frozen/mocked "today") so they pass regardless of which real calendar day the suite happens to run on: a genuinely-1-trading-day-old refresh renders OK (not STALE), a genuinely-many-trading-day-old refresh still renders OVERDUE (confirming the fix isn't just "always OK"), and a freshly-stamped `last_scheduled_run_name` from a job other than EOD/Monday-premarket renders correctly on the Order Logic row. Full local suite: 588 passing.

## SNDK's real resolution, and the Candidate Queue's disappearing-resolved-row bug (2026-08-03)

**Part A — what actually happened to SNDK, confirmed directly against the real production database and the live scheduler service log, not guessed.** SNDK — Sunday night's top-ranked candidate by momentum (+2699.8%, already confirmed genuine, not a split-adjustment artifact, per the same night's earlier investigation) — was correctly, deliberately skipped by the submission-time price-sanity check, exactly as designed (see "Exchange-aware order submission" above). SSHing into the production server and querying `pending_orders` directly for `ticker='SNDK'` returned two real rows: an earlier one (`id=272`, decided 2026-08-02 21:31:10 UTC) resolved to `SUPERSEDED` at 21:49:06 UTC ("cleared for fresh re-run 2026-08-02 following urgent capacity/split-adjustment verification" — the same-night queue-clear documented under "Urgent pre-submission verification" above), and the final one (`id=590`, decided 2026-08-02 21:50:29 UTC) resolved to `SKIPPED_PRICE_MOVED` at 2026-08-03 14:30:02 UTC with `resolution_note`: *"price moved +3.11% since decision (decided 1214.83 -> now 1252.56), exceeds 3% sanity threshold"*. `invest_orders` has zero rows for SNDK — no order was ever placed. Cross-checked against the real `investment-research-scheduler` systemd journal for that exact window: `2026-08-03 14:30:02 WARNING Skipping SNDK (SNDK1_US_EQ) submission — price moved +3.11% since decision (decided 1214.83 -> now 1252.56), exceeds 3% sanity threshold` — matching the DB row exactly. The same submission run also skipped WDC (-4.33%), LITE (+3.96%), and STX (-5.03%) for the identical reason — the exact same extreme-momentum names flagged in the same night's earlier investigation, all volatile enough to move past the 3% threshold between Sunday's decision and Monday's submission. **Not** a capacity rejection, **not** an instrument-resolution issue, **not** a bug of any kind — the mechanism (`brokers/trading212.py`'s submission-time price-sanity check, `price_sanity_threshold_pct`) worked exactly as designed.

**Part B — the real bug: the dashboard's query, not the filter widget itself, silently excluded every resolved row.** `output/performance.py:get_pending_candidates()` — the sole backing function for the Dashboard's Candidate Queue table — was hardcoded to `WHERE status = 'PENDING'`. The moment SNDK's row resolved to `SKIPPED_PRICE_MOVED`, it vanished from every consumer of this function, even though the row was (and is) still sitting in `pending_orders`, fully within its unrelated, unchanged 30-day retention window (`purge_old_pending_orders()`). The status-filter `st.multiselect` itself was never hardcoded to `PROJECTED_*` values — its options are already derived dynamically via `cdf["Status"].unique()` — it simply never had a non-`PROJECTED_*` value to offer, because the query upstream had already filtered every one of them out before the dropdown ever saw the data. Confirmed directly: querying the real production `pending_orders` table with the `WHERE status = 'PENDING'` filter removed returns SNDK's both rows (SUPERSEDED and SKIPPED_PRICE_MOVED) exactly as expected.

**The fix — a query-scope fix only, explicitly not a retention change.** `get_pending_candidates()` now selects every `pending_orders` row regardless of status (removing the `WHERE status = 'PENDING'` clause), adding `status`/`resolution_note` to the SELECT so a resolved row's own final outcome — and why — is directly visible on the dashboard without needing to SSH into the server, as this investigation had to. `purge_old_pending_orders()` and its 30-day window (`trading212_invest.pending_orders_retention_days`) are completely untouched — this function simply stops re-filtering out rows that policy has already decided to keep for the full window.

**Two real, secondary correctness issues found and fixed while broadening the query, both a direct consequence of resolved rows now coexisting with pending ones in the same table:**
1. **Per-row status lookup, not per-ticker.** `main.py`'s old `cdf["Status"] = cdf["ticker"].map(lambda t: projected_by_ticker.get(t, ...))` was safe under the old PENDING-only query (a ticker could have at most one PENDING row at a time, per the existing `_has_pending_order()` dedup guard), but breaks the moment a ticker can have several historical rows in view at once — exactly SNDK's real case (a SUPERSEDED row and a later SKIPPED_PRICE_MOVED row for the same ticker). Fixed: `cdf["Status"]` is now computed per row (`cdf.apply(..., axis=1)`) — a genuinely-`PENDING` row still gets the live re-projected status; any other row shows its own real, final status directly, never borrowed from a different row for the same ticker.
2. **Momentum-strength bands, re-scoped per decision-date cohort.** `_compute_momentum_strength_bands()`'s whole design (see "Dashboard candidate-queue momentum-strength label" above) is explicitly "relative to today's own pool" — computing one set of bands across the whole table would now silently mix multiple days' momentum distributions together once historical rows from earlier days are shown alongside today's. Fixed via `cdf.groupby("decided_date")["momentum_pct"].transform(...)` — each day's candidates are still judged only against that same day's own real pool, preserving the original per-day design intent rather than degrading it as a side effect of this fix.

A `Note` column (the row's `resolution_note`) was added to the table — the specific missing piece that would have let this exact investigation be answered from the dashboard itself rather than requiring an SSH session. Both status-related captions were reworded: the "projection, not a guarantee" caption now states explicitly that it applies only to a still-`PENDING` row's `PROJECTED_*` status — any other status shown is a real, final, historical outcome, not a projection; the Strength caption now says "that candidate's own decision-date cohort" rather than "today's."

Covered by 2 new tests in `tests/test_performance.py` (`get_pending_candidates()` returns every status ordered by momentum, and returns the real `status`/`resolution_note` columns — seeded with SNDK's actual real-world figures) and 4 new tests in `tests/test_main_ui.py`: a resolved candidate (SNDK, `SKIPPED_PRICE_MOVED`) appears with its real status and note rather than disappearing; the filter dropdown genuinely offers resolved statuses (`SKIPPED_PRICE_MOVED`, `REJECTED_CAPACITY`) alongside `PROJECTED_ADMIT`, and filtering to one narrows correctly; a ticker with two historical rows (SNDK's own real shape) shows each row's own distinct status, not one bleeding into the other; and an explicit test confirming a row from several days ago (well within the unchanged 30-day retention) is shown exactly like a same-day one — proving this is a visibility fix, not a retention change. Full local suite: 593 passing. No database write of any kind was needed for this fix (pure query/UI logic) — no `.backup` was required, matching this project's own established distinction for code-only changes.

## Monday pre-market cancellation — confirmed to only ever touch real broker orders, never queued candidates (2026-08-03, investigated urgently, no bug found)

Raised urgently the same night as the tomorrow-gating fix (see "`_eod_job()`'s two independently-gated steps" above): once a Friday-queued candidate's real submission window can legitimately stretch past a single weekend (a Monday holiday pushing it to Tuesday or Wednesday, still sitting validly `PENDING` the whole time), does `_monday_premarket_job()`'s "cancel stale weekend orders" step risk cancelling that still-valid, not-yet-submitted candidate simply because it's old enough to span a weekend — which would silently and permanently prevent genuine trades, worsening every week this went unnoticed?

**The direct answer, confirmed by reading the real code, not inferred: no bug.** `_cancel_stale_weekend_orders()` (`data/scheduler.py`) operates exclusively on `invest_orders` — its SELECT is `FROM invest_orders WHERE status = 'PLACED' AND direction = 'BUY' AND placed_at < :cutoff`, and its UPDATE is `invest_orders SET status = 'CANCELLED' ... WHERE id = :row_id`. Neither statement references `pending_orders` at all. `invest_orders` rows only ever exist once an order has genuinely been placed with T212 (a locally-queued, not-yet-submitted decision lives exclusively in `pending_orders`, a structurally separate table with no overlap) — so this step can only ever cancel a real, broker-placed, still-unfilled order sitting stale over the weekend, exactly its documented intent, never a locally-queued candidate still waiting for its real 14:30 UTC submission window.

**The second half of the job — `_run_analysis_pipeline(config, get_all_tickers(config), run_type=RUN_ANALYSIS_ONLY)` — was checked with equal rigor, since it's the part that runs immediately after cancellation and could in principle interact with the queue.** Traced directly: `RUN_ANALYSIS_ONLY = "analysis_only"`, and `brokers/trading212.py:maybe_place_orders()`'s own `run_type != "full"` branch (`if run_type != "full": maybe_exit_positions(config); ...; return`) calls **only** `maybe_exit_positions(config)` and returns immediately — the BUY/decide-and-queue phase (the only code in that function that ever writes to `pending_orders`) sits entirely below that early return and is never reached. A still-`PENDING` row is therefore untouched twice over: neither of `_monday_premarket_job()`'s two steps ever writes to `pending_orders` in `analysis_only` mode.

**The "Order Logic" step's real purpose, and whether it's redundant — reported honestly, both halves.** Its substantive work (`maybe_exit_positions()`) genuinely duplicates what the hourly `trade_alert_check` job (`00:00–21:00 + 23:00 UTC` weekdays, which includes 07:00 UTC Monday) already does every hour — both calls re-evaluate the identical exit conditions (crisis/stop-loss/signal-off/max-holding) around the same wall-clock time on a normal Monday. This overlap is harmless, not a correctness risk: `maybe_exit_positions()` is safe to call twice in quick succession (a real exit fires once; the second call's own duplicate-SELL guard, `_has_recent_sell_order()`, simply finds nothing new to do). Two things the Monday job does that the hourly job does **not**: the instrument-resolution-failure check/alert (`_run_analysis_pipeline()`'s own body, run on every scheduled pipeline call) and stamping `last_scheduled_run`/`last_scheduled_run_name` — so it is partially, not wholly, redundant. Not changed as part of this investigation — the task's own scope was confirming safety, not de-duplicating a harmless overlap; a future cleanup could fold the instrument-resolution check into the hourly job and drop the Monday job's own exit-check call, but that's a separate, non-urgent task.

**Verified with real, direct test coverage, not just re-reading the code.** `tests/test_scheduler.py:test_monday_premarket_stale_order_cancellation_never_touches_pending_orders` seeds both a genuinely stale broker order (`invest_orders`, 33.5h old) and a still-valid, not-yet-due locally-queued candidate (`pending_orders`, also 33.5h old — deliberately the same age as the broker order, to prove age alone doesn't matter) side by side, runs the real `_monday_premarket_job()`, and confirms the broker order is correctly cancelled while the `pending_orders` row is byte-for-byte unchanged — same status, same content, nothing resolved. `tests/test_execution.py:test_analysis_only_run_type_never_touches_pending_orders` independently confirms the same guarantee one level lower, directly against the real (unmocked) `maybe_place_orders(config, run_type="analysis_only")`: a seeded `PENDING` row survives byte-for-byte, complementing the pre-existing `place_market_order.assert_not_called()` coverage with a `pending_orders`-level assertion the task specifically asked for. No code change was needed — this was a confirm-and-document task, not a fix — so no deploy was required either; the two new regression tests were still committed and pushed so this guarantee stays enforced going forward. (Superseded the same day by "Monday Pre-Market removed entirely" immediately below, once a follow-up check found the cancellation half was itself no longer necessary either — the two new tests this paragraph describes were removed as part of that full removal, since their subject no longer exists; see that section for the final, current test count.)

## Monday Pre-Market removed entirely (2026-08-03)

**Superseded the same-day partial fix immediately above** (which kept the stale-order-cancellation half and only dropped the redundant exit-check re-run) — a follow-up, urgent re-check found the cancellation half was itself no longer necessary either, for a structural reason specific to this system's current architecture, not merely "confirmed still safe."

**Why cancellation stopped being needed.** `_cancel_stale_weekend_orders()` existed to guard against a real V1-era risk: the old architecture placed a BUY order immediately at EOD decide time (21:30 UTC) — a Friday-evening order could sit unfilled all weekend, since T212 doesn't fill market orders outside trading hours, and a lot can change by Monday (geopolitical events, Sunday futures pricing, macro news). The current decide-then-submit architecture (see "Exchange-aware order submission" above) closed this gap structurally, not just incidentally: a decision queued at EOD is never submitted at EOD — it waits for stock submission at 14:30 UTC, hours *into* the NYSE session, with several hours of trading remaining before that day's close. A market order placed mid-session, against a liquid instrument, during real trading hours, has no structural reason to still be unfilled by end of day, let alone by the following weekend — the specific scenario this job guarded against (an order sitting unfilled *into* a weekend) cannot arise under this architecture regardless of which day of the week it is. This holds independently of the Part B finding below.

**Full removal, not a second partial fix.** `_monday_premarket_job()`, `_cancel_stale_weekend_orders()`, and `_STALE_ORDER_HOURS` were deleted entirely from `data/scheduler.py`; the scheduler registration (`id="monday_premarket"`, `day_of_week="mon"`, `hour=7`) was removed from `start_scheduler()`. The earlier same-day partial fix's own extraction — `_check_and_alert_instrument_resolution_failures()`, pulled out of `_run_analysis_pipeline()` specifically so the (now also removed) Monday job could call it directly without re-triggering the redundant exit check — was reverted back to its original inline form inside `_run_analysis_pipeline()`, since its sole reason for existing as a separate function (a second caller) no longer applies; keeping a single-caller abstraction around after the reason for it evaporates is exactly the kind of premature structure this project's own conventions warn against. `_run_analysis_pipeline()` itself, and its two remaining real callers (`_eod_job()`, and `main.py`'s manual "Order Logic Only" Status-page button), are completely unaffected — the instrument-resolution-failure check and `last_run_type`/`last_scheduled_run` stamping still happen on every EOD run exactly as before, just via the original, unextracted code path.

**Confirmed nothing else depends on the removed job.** The instrument-resolution-failure alert and `last_scheduled_run` stamping — the two pieces the same-day partial fix had specifically preserved from the old "Order Logic" step — are both still covered independently: `_eod_job()` (daily, including every Monday) already runs the identical instrument-resolution check via `_run_analysis_pipeline()`, and `last_scheduled_run`/`last_scheduled_run_name` are now stamped by four other jobs (`_eod_job()`, `_stock_order_submission_job()`, `_weekly_summary_job()`, and the removed job's own former stamp is simply one fewer source among several — see "Status page scheduler-health/job-recency fixes" above). No gap opened by this removal.

**Status page fully updated, not left showing a removed job.** `main.py`'s `_JOB_LABELS` dict, the Scheduler Health table's daemon-mode reconstruction (`_extra_static`), the "Next Scheduled Run" soonest-of comparison, and the "Scheduled Runs" section's own dedicated Monday card were all removed — the now-unused `_next_monday_at()` helper was deleted too, confirmed via full-repo grep before removing it (its only two call sites were both in the code just removed). The "Scheduled Runs" section's column layout was adjusted from `st.columns(len(_RUN_DISPLAY) + 1)` (reserving a trailing slot for the Monday card) back to `st.columns(len(_RUN_DISPLAY))`, matching there being one real scheduled-runs entry (EOD) left to display.

**Verification.** `tests/test_scheduler.py`'s entire Monday-premarket test section (6 tests exercising the now-deleted functions directly, plus their shared `_seed_order`/`_monday_mocks` helpers and the now-unused `_frozen_utcnow` datetime-freezing helper) was removed, replaced by a single `test_scheduler_never_registers_monday_premarket_job` mirroring the exact "confirmed removed, stays removed" pattern already used for the Tue-Fri pre-market/US-open jobs and the ETF-submission job (`sched.get_job("monday_premarket") is None`, `not hasattr(scheduler, "_monday_premarket_job")`, `not hasattr(scheduler, "_cancel_stale_weekend_orders")`). `tests/test_t212_client.py`'s end-to-end regression test for the empty-DELETE-body bug (`test_cancel_stale_weekend_orders_records_cancelled_when_t212_returns_empty_body`) — which specifically exercised the now-removed function as its real-world call site — was removed too, since the underlying guarantee it proved (`cancel_order()` correctly treats an empty 200/204 DELETE response as success, not failure) remains fully covered by the simpler, still-valid `test_cancel_order_with_empty_body_on_success_does_not_raise`, which exercises `Trading212Client.cancel_order()` directly with no scheduler-layer scaffolding — keeping a redundant end-to-end test around for a call site that no longer exists would have been dead weight, not defense in depth. Full local suite: 588 passing, confirmed directly (not assumed from arithmetic) by re-running the whole suite after every change in this section.

## Tracing the "60+ hour fill-lag" claim's real origin (2026-08-03)

This figure had been cited multiple times in this file — as a reason for caution around the broker-side stop-loss investigation's framing, and as the stated justification for the Dashboard's "Placed, Unconfirmed Exits" section's reassuring caption — always as "already documented elsewhere in this codebase," never freshly re-investigated. Traced directly, end to end, rather than continuing to treat it as settled.

**Origin, found precisely via `git log -S`.** The claim was first written in commit `0db34ed` (2026-07-06 08:34:15 +0100), "Fix duplicate SELL when a PLACED T212 order ages past the dedup window": *"Production data showed T212's demo account can leave a SELL sitting in PLACED for 60+ hours before poll_placed_orders() sees it resolve (XLU/XLE/EWG/PDBC, all placed 2026-07-03 16:00 UTC)."* The commit's own text already noted, honestly, that the corresponding BUY fills for the same four tickers took 9–10h to resolve too, and interpreted that as "suggesting this is a demo-account fill-latency characteristic, not a polling bug on this side" — a reasonable-sounding inference, but, traced further, one that outran what the evidence available at the time could actually support.

**The methodological gap, found by comparing this commit against the very next one.** `poll_placed_orders()`'s status field (`FILLED`, at whatever moment our own polling notices it) is the *only* signal `0db34ed` could have used to write "XLU and XLE only resolved to FILLED the morning of 2026-07-06" — because the mechanism capable of checking T212's own *authoritative* fill timestamp, `Trading212Client.get_order_history()`/`_historical_fill()` (`GET /equity/history/orders`, which retains the true fill price/quantity/timestamp indefinitely), did not exist yet. It was added in commit `216afb5`, **24 minutes later**, the same morning (08:58:39 +0100), "Fix permanent NULL fill_price on closed T212 positions blocking P&L" — a *different* bug entirely (a stuck-`NULL` fill price silently excluding closed positions from `t212_pnl`), which happened to affect two of the exact same four orders (`XLU` order id 11, `XLE` order id 13). In other words: the claim that "T212 itself took 60+ hours to fill these orders" was written using a measurement tool (our own status-poll timing) that cannot actually distinguish "T212 took 60 hours to fill this" from "our own polling only just noticed" — the tool that *could* make that distinction didn't exist until less than half an hour after the claim was written, for an unrelated reason.

**What happened to the corrected data — also checked directly, not assumed.** `216afb5`'s own text states the two `NULL`-fill-price rows were "manually corrected with their real fill price/timestamp fetched live from `get_order_history()`" (see "Resolved data gap" above) — meaning someone, at the time, genuinely did look at T212's own authoritative fill timestamp for `XLU`/`XLE` specifically. But neither that commit nor any later one records the *specific* recovered timestamp value anywhere — only that the correction was applied. Queried the current production database directly for these exact rows (`invest_orders WHERE ticker IN ('XLU','XLE','EWG','PDBC') AND placed_at LIKE '2026-07-03%'`): **zero rows returned.** The `invest_orders` table has been reset/recreated multiple times since (the full V1→V2 removal, the account reset, and others documented elsewhere in this file), and no surviving backup reaches back far enough — the earliest backup file on the server is dated 2026-07-30, three-and-a-half weeks after the event. **The original evidence, and even the corrected version of it, no longer exists anywhere on this system.** This is stated plainly rather than glossed over: the specific 2026-07-03 example this claim was built on cannot be re-examined today, by anyone, under any method.

**Real, current, directly-gathered evidence instead — the best available substitute for the exact original example.** Queried every row currently in production's `invest_orders` with `status = 'FILLED'` (17 rows total, spanning 2026-07-31 through 2026-08-03 — the entire real history the current V2 system has produced): **every single one resolved from `PLACED` to `FILLED` within 1–8 seconds of being placed** — including all 16 of today's real stock BUY fills from the 14:30 UTC submission run (e.g. `MU`: placed 14:30:20.444714, filled 14:30:20.000; `KLAC`: placed 14:34:55.575286, filled 14:34:55.000). Separately checked the 6 `CANCELLED` SELL rows from the 2026-07-31 false-`INDEX_REMOVAL` incident (see "Membership-window bug" above) — these were manually cancelled by a human roughly 49 minutes after being placed, once the underlying bug was discovered, consistent with human-intervention timing rather than any organic multi-hour broker-side delay. Also checked real production logs from today's own hourly job runs for evidence of a genuine, silent polling gap that could independently explain a multi-hour reporting lag: T212 rate-limiting was directly observed (`"T212 rate limited — waiting 4s/8s/16s (attempt N/3)"`), but `_request()`'s own exponential-backoff retry resolves (or exhausts) within well under a minute per attempt — nowhere near the scale of a multi-hour, let alone 60-hour, gap.

**Direct answer: most likely a reporting/measurement artifact, or at minimum an unverifiable claim as originally stated — not a confirmed, ongoing genuine execution-delay characteristic of this account.** The claim was written using a tool that could not, by construction, distinguish the two possibilities it was purporting to describe, and the one piece of evidence (the manually-corrected real fill timestamps for `XLU`/`XLE`) that genuinely could have settled the question either way was never recorded and no longer exists to check. Every real, currently-observable fill on this account — the only evidence actually available today — resolves in seconds, not hours, which argues against "T212 demo-account fills are characteristically slow" as an ongoing reality, though it cannot rule out that the original July 3rd batch experienced some genuinely unusual, one-off circumstance specific to that day (this was, after all, the same general period this file documents several other real, confirmed T212 integration bugs from — pricing, mapping, exception handling — see "Live pricing bug, exception isolation, and ETF mapping audit" above, albeit from 2026-07-31, after this specific incident).

**Consequence for reasoning built on this claim tonight, stated plainly rather than left implicit.**
- **The broker-side stop-loss investigation** (see "Broker-side stop order" above) never actually cited the specific "60+ hours" figure in its own text — checked directly by re-reading it — so nothing in that investigation's own conclusions needs revising on this basis. Its general caution ("this only protects a position if this project's own scheduled check runs and fires correctly — and this exact session already found multiple real cases of scheduled logic silently not running as intended") rests on the membership-window and pricing bugs found *elsewhere* tonight, not on this claim, and remains exactly as valid as those two findings are — unaffected either way.
- **The Dashboard's "Placed, Unconfirmed Exits" section** *did* directly state the "60+ hours... documented lag... not a stuck order needing manual intervention" framing as settled fact in its own caption. This has been corrected (`main.py`) to state plainly that the specific figure could not be re-verified and should not be relied on as a reason to dismiss a genuinely lingering row, while still explaining the real, legitimate reason a row can be a few minutes old and completely routine (poll timing). This is a real, user-visible wording change, not just a documentation note — a future engineer or user reading that caption will no longer be told a specific, unverifiable number as if it were established fact.

Investigation only — no production order-handling code changed (the poll/dedup logic `0db34ed` itself fixed remains correct and unaffected; only the *evidentiary basis* for one specific claim about *why* it was needed was re-examined). No database write was made or needed beyond the read-only queries above. Full local suite: 588 passing.

## "Trade Alerts" renamed to "Open Trade Monitor"; "Pipeline" merged into "Scheduler Health" (2026-08-03)

Two display-only changes to the Status page, done together since both touch the same part of it.

**Rename.** The hourly job labeled "Trade Alerts" is `trade_alert_check` (`data/scheduler.py:_trade_alert_job()`) — it actively evaluates crisis/stop-loss/signal-off/max-holding exit conditions via `maybe_exit_positions()`, places real SELL orders when one triggers, polls order status, and reconciles positions against the broker. Arguably the single most safety-critical recurring job in the system — the thing that actually protects capital hour by hour — "Alerts" read as a passive notification feed, not that. Relabeled to **"Open Trade Monitor"** in both places the Scheduler Health table's job-label lookup can resolve it from (`main.py`'s `_JOB_LABELS["trade_alert_check"]`, used when a real in-process APScheduler is running, and the daemon-mode `_extra_static` reconstruction used when only the standalone scheduler daemon's heartbeat is detected), plus the two prose captions that referenced the old name: the Dashboard's "Placed, Unconfirmed Exits" caption ("hourly via the Open Trade Monitor job") and the Status page's own "Scheduled Runs" caption (below). Purely a label change — `_JOB_LABELS`' dict *key* (`"trade_alert_check"`), the underlying job id, its registration/schedule, and `data/scheduler.py`'s own log line ("Trade alert check starting…") are all untouched. The Log Viewer's `"Scheduler"` category filter keyword `"trade alert"` was deliberately left as-is for the same reason — it's a substring match against that unchanged log text, not the UI label.

**What Pipeline showed that Scheduler Health didn't — checked directly, not assumed clean to delete.** The old "Pipeline" section (a standalone two-row table: "1 · Price Data Refresh", "2 · Order Logic") showed two genuinely useful data points Scheduler Health's job-list table didn't carry: `price_desc` (ticker coverage detail — "All N tickers up to date" / stale-ticker names / missing-ticker names) and `order_desc` (`last_run_type`-derived "Last run: Full Refresh"/"Order Logic Only"/"Not yet run"). Both of these are produced by exactly one job — `scheduled_eod` ("End of Day") — which pulls prices *and* runs the order-decide pipeline in the same run. There was no genuine split across two different Scheduler Health rows to make (the task's own tentative "map onto End of Day and Stock Order Submission" framing turned out not to fit the real code: `_stock_order_submission_job()` never touches `last_run_type` at all). Both details are folded into a single new `_eod_detail = f"{price_desc} · {order_desc}"` string, rendered in a new **Description** column on the "End of Day" row only (empty for every other job row) — added to `_sched_row_html()`/`_sh_head` in both the in-process and daemon-mode rendering branches, so the detail shows up correctly regardless of which scheduler mode the page detects. Column widths were rebalanced to make room (Job 22%→16%, Schedule 28%→20%, Next Run 25%→18%, In 12%→9%, Status 13%→10%, Description new at `flex:1`, roughly 25% of the row).

**Pipeline fully removed** — `st.markdown("### Pipeline")`'s rendering block (the `_THEAD`/`rows`/`_TFOOT` HTML assembly) and the now-zero-caller `_pipeline_row()` function are both deleted outright, not left disabled, matching this project's standing practice for confirmed-superseded UI (same precedent as the GARCH stop loss/HMM regime gate code removals). `price_desc`/`order_desc`'s own computation (reading `_price_coverage(config)` and `get_metadata_str("last_run_type")`) is unchanged and kept exactly where it was — only its *consumer* changed, from the deleted Pipeline block to the new `_eod_detail` string.

**A pre-existing inconsistency was found and is flagged here, not fixed as part of this task — deliberately out of scope.** Pipeline's own OVERDUE/STALE/OK badge for "1 · Price Data Refresh" was driven by `_trading_day_age_level()` (the newer, genuine NYSE-calendar-aware staleness check — see "Status page scheduler-health/job-recency fixes" above). Scheduler Health's "End of Day" row has always used a separate, older, cruder mechanism for its own OVERDUE badge — `_eod_overdue()`, a flat 26-hour-elapsed threshold plus a hand-rolled weekday/Monday exemption. These two functions can disagree on whether the same underlying `last_refresh` timestamp counts as stale, and after this merge they now sit in the same row (the badge from `_eod_overdue()`, the Description text's own staleness framing implicitly informed by whatever `price_desc`/`order_desc` say) without being reconciled. This task's instructions were explicit — display only, no behavior change — so `_eod_overdue()`'s formula was deliberately left untouched; recorded here as a genuine follow-up candidate, the same class of "two independently-tracked staleness signals for the same question" issue this file has already found and fixed once at the top-level-widget layer (see "Status page scheduler-health/job-recency fixes" above) — just not yet closed at this specific row.

**Placement.** The merged, enriched Scheduler Health section now renders in Pipeline's former position — immediately after the pr1/pr2/pr3 top-level cards ("Last Data Refresh"/"Last Scheduled Run"/"Next Scheduled Run") and the `price_desc`/`order_desc` computation, well before "Scheduled Runs" — rather than staying in its old, further-down position. Verified directly via a dedicated test asserting `at.markdown` element order (Scheduler Health's own "### Scheduler Health" heading must appear before "### Scheduled Runs"'s), not just that both sections happen to exist somewhere on the page.

**Tests.** Three pre-existing tests in `tests/test_main_ui.py` depended on Pipeline's removed HTML structure via a `_pipeline_row_badge()` helper (parsing OK/STALE/OVERDUE out of the Pipeline table's concatenated markdown) — rewritten to check the still-existing "Last Data Refresh"/"Last Scheduled Run" top-level `_status_card()` cards instead, via a new `_status_card_level()` helper that extracts a card's `border-left:3px solid {colour}` hex and maps it back through `main._LEVEL_COLOUR` — the exact same underlying `_trading_day_age_level()` staleness mechanism those tests were built to validate, unaffected by this merge. Four new tests: Pipeline's heading/row text confirmed absent; "Open Trade Monitor" present and "Trade Alerts" absent (seeding a fresh `scheduler_heartbeat` so the daemon-mode job-row rendering branch — not the "Scheduler is not running" fallback — actually executes, since job labels only render once the scheduler is detected active); the "End of Day" row's Description column showing both the price-coverage text and the `last_run_type`-derived label; and the section-ordering check described above. Full local suite: 592 passing (588 + 4 new), confirmed by a full run, not arithmetic.

No underlying job behavior changed anywhere in this task — `_JOB_LABELS`' dict key, job ids, schedules, `_eod_overdue()`'s formula, and `data/scheduler.py` itself are all untouched; this was display-only, confirmed by the full test suite passing with zero changes to any scheduler/broker file.

## Status page restructuring — sections relocated/removed now that the Dashboard and Instruments pages exist (2026-08-03)

Several Status page sections predated the Dashboard (2026-08-02) and the current Instruments page (2026-08-02/03), and had come to genuinely overlap with them. Not a blanket removal — each section was checked individually against what those two pages already show, and only the genuinely duplicated pieces were removed; everything else moved or was de-emphasized in place.

**Manual Controls → a bottom "Danger Zone".** Both buttons ("Refresh Data + Orders Now", "Order Logic Only") can trigger real T212 order placement immediately — the single most consequential action available anywhere on this page — but previously sat inline between "Data Coverage" and "Email Notifications" with no visual distinction from routine informational sections. Moved to the literal bottom of the page (after Log Viewer, immediately before the footer), inside an `st.container(border=True)` with a red-left-border, red-tinted heading card ("⚠ Danger Zone") above the two buttons — the closest genuine equivalent this component library allows to GitHub's own destructive-action pattern, since Streamlit's real bordered containers don't expose a custom border colour via the public API; the red visual weight comes from the heading card inside the border, not the border itself. Functionally identical — same two button keys (`status_full_refresh`, `status_run_orders`), same click behaviour, only placement and surrounding styling changed.

**Email Notifications — removed entirely, no banner, no expander.** This section only ever showed static From/To/relay-host/enabled-flag text read from config — no action, no live state, nothing that changed day-to-day. Its own caption additionally understated the real alert surface ("order-placement error alerts only," when this codebase's alerting has grown to five distinct alert types across several modules — see CLAUDE.md's various alert-mechanism sections) — a factual error not worth fixing since the whole section is gone.

**T212 Invest Account — split, not removed wholesale.** Checked directly what this section actually contained before deciding what to cut:
- **Kept — genuine configuration/methodology**: the ENABLED/NOT ENABLED and DEMO/LIVE badges, candidate count, `per_trade_pct`/`max_total_deployed` figures, and the VaR-sizing-parameters caption (confidence/lookback/max-risk/floor) — none of this is live account *state*, all of it is how the system is configured to behave. Also kept: the "not enabled"/"credentials not found" setup guidance, the `t212_invest_error` banner + Clear button (an operational alert, not a duplicated metric), and the "Refresh Account" button + "Last updated" caption — this last one is a genuinely useful *action* (it refreshes the same underlying T212 snapshot both this page and the Dashboard read), not "state" itself, so removing the metrics it used to feed didn't mean removing the button too.
- **Removed — genuine Dashboard duplication**: the four `st.metric()` cards (Account Value, Available Cash, Invested, Open Positions) and the deployed-capital progress bar, which read the identical `t212_account_snapshot`/`t212_positions_snapshot` metadata the Dashboard's own account-balance cards (`_get_account_summary()`) already display prominently at the top of that page. A short caption now points to where these live instead ("Account value, cash, invested, and open-position count are on the **Dashboard** page...").

**Recent Orders → moved to the Dashboard**, a relocation for organisation, not a de-duplication — `invest_orders` (this table) and `pending_orders` (the Candidate Queue table already on the Dashboard) are genuinely different tables answering different questions (real, permanent trade history vs. the transient pre-trade decision queue), so there was no actual overlap to remove, only a better home for real trade information to live alongside the Dashboard's other real-trade sections (Top Trades, Placed/Unconfirmed Exits). The inline raw-SQL query that used to live directly in `main.py`'s Status-page code was extracted into `output/performance.py:get_recent_orders(limit=10)`, following this module's own established one-reader-per-table-shape convention (`get_pending_candidates()`, `get_unconfirmed_exits()`) rather than left duplicated inline in the UI layer. Rendered on the Dashboard between "Top Trades" and "Candidate Queue" — grouping real trade/order history together contiguously before the pre-trade decision queue.

**Instrument Mapping → moved to the Instruments page**, joined directly onto the existing per-ticker table rather than kept as a second, disconnected table. `_render_instruments_page()` now builds a `resolutions_by_ticker` dict from `load_all_instrument_resolutions()` and adds four columns to the same Ticker/Name/Yahoo-Finance table: **Resolution Status**, **T212 Instrument**, **Currency**, **Note** — colour-coded VERIFIED/FAILED/PENDING exactly as the old Status-page expander did. A ticker with no resolution row at all (every reference ticker; a live S&P 500 candidate not yet evaluated) shows "—", never a fabricated status. A summary caption ("N verified · M failed — needs review · K pending retry") sits alongside the existing "X of Y instruments shown" caption rather than in a separate expander label. `load_all_instrument_resolutions()`'s own docstring was updated to point at its new consumer.

**Nothing genuinely useful was lost — confirmed by checking each section's actual content before cutting anything**, not assumed from its heading alone. The one place this mattered directly: the T212 Invest Account section's live-metrics block and its "Refresh Account" button/caption were adjacent in the same code path, and it would have been easy to remove both together as "the account block" — checked specifically and kept the button, since it's a distinct action with no Dashboard equivalent, not itself a duplicated display.
