## Price-sanity threshold — momentum-skew investigation, asymmetric variant recommended (2026-08-03)

**Question.** Live evidence the same night: 4 of the top handful of candidates by momentum (SNDK, WDC, LITE, STX — all "Very Strong," all top-ranked) were skipped by the submission-time price-sanity check (`brokers/trading212.py:_submit_pending_orders()`, `price_sanity_threshold_pct`, default 3%), all for the identical reason — price moved more than 3% between the EOD decision and next-day submission. Structural hypothesis: the stocks with the most extreme trailing momentum are mechanically also the most likely to have the most extreme day-to-day volatility, making them systematically more likely to trip a fixed percentage threshold. Tested empirically before considering any change, per this project's own standing discipline — no threshold was changed based on reasoning alone.

**Methodology, stated explicitly per this file's own conventions.** Reset-at-boundary (not continuous-walk — see "Two backtest conventions" above): this is a comparison between variants (which threshold/direction is better), so every variant resets to a fresh £50,000 and zero open positions at each of the project's own established 16 block boundaries (`analysis.backtest.make_blocks(2007-01-01, 2026-08-01, n_blocks=16)`), never carrying train-period luck into a later block. Run entirely locally (isolated `git worktree` at `../sp500invest-price-sanity-sweep`, own copied production DB verified current against the server — 526,934,016 bytes, byte-identical, coverage confirmed through 2026-07-31/08-01), per this project's own "Experimental/research work runs locally" and git-worktree standing practices — zero risk to the live system throughout.

**The real live universe, not the frozen 73-ticker research set** — `analysis.universe.get_live_stock_candidates(as_of=2026-08-01)`, the identical `live_universe=True` methodology `analysis.validation.run_full_validation()`/the Backtest page use, since the mechanism under test only ever applies to the genuinely dynamic live candidate pool the SNDK/WDC/LITE/STX incident actually happened in. 503 candidates, 500 usable (3 excluded for insufficient history — the same `FDXF`/`HONA`/`Q` gap already documented elsewhere in this file).

**Daily-bar modeling choice for "price at submission time," stated explicitly since this backtest has no intraday data.** `decided_price` = the signal day's own close (exactly what the existing engine already uses as `entry_price` — unchanged). The submission-time price proxy is that ticker's **next trading day's open** — genuinely closer to live's real timing (decide at EOD close, stock submission ~mid-morning the next trading day, hours before that day's own close) than using the next day's close would be. A candidate that fails the check is skipped entirely for that day (never enters at that day's close), exactly mirroring live's `SKIPPED_PRICE_MOVED` (a dead decision, never retried) — the day-by-day walk's own re-consideration of a still-eligible ticker the following day reproduces live's real "the next EOD decide cycle re-queues it if the signal is still on" behaviour for free, no extra bookkeeping needed. A candidate that **passes** still enters at that day's own close (the existing engine's unchanged convention) — the filter only ever gates *whether* entry happens, never repricing an admitted entry to the next-day open, so the skew/performance question under test is never conflated with a second, unrelated change to execution-price convention.

**Fidelity verified before trusting the modified engine for anything.** The research engine (`simulate_with_price_sanity()`) is a line-for-line copy of the real `analysis.backtest.simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` (exit priority via `evaluate_exit_reason()`, entry gate via `passes_entry_gate()`, momentum-priority skip-and-continue admission, VaR sizing, re-entry cooldown — all identical, imported directly from `analysis.decision`/`analysis.volatility`/`analysis.universe`, never reimplemented) with only two additions: the price-sanity filter itself, and block-truncation with END_OF_DATA force-close at each block's own end (the exact technique already validated in "Is the 5-day re-entry cooldown result real?" above). With the filter disabled (`price_sanity_threshold=None`) over the full continuous 2007-2026 walk, the modified engine reproduced the real, unmodified `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` **exactly — 3,246 trades both sides, 0 field mismatches** — before any threshold variant was trusted.

**Sweep design.** 11 variants × 16 blocks = 176 independent runs: `uncapped` (no filter, the true baseline), `symmetric_{2,3,5,7,10}pct` (blocks on any move beyond the threshold, either direction — today's live 3% behaviour), `asymmetric_{2,3,5,7,10}pct` (blocks only on a **drop** beyond the threshold — a rise, however large, never blocks, on the theory that a rise confirms the momentum thesis rather than invalidating it). Parallelized across the local machine's cores (`ProcessPoolExecutor`, 6 workers — per this project's own "run compute-heavy research locally" standing practice), completed in 2,107s (~35 minutes) with zero errors. For every candidate actually reached in the ranked per-day admission loop (not merely "in the pool" — a candidate never reached due to capacity exhaustion never takes the price check at all, so correctly excluded from the denominator), recorded whether it was that day's own top-decile by momentum (relative to that day's real candidate pool, mirroring `main.py:_compute_momentum_strength_bands()`'s own convention) and whether the price-sanity filter blocked it — giving a genuine, apples-to-apples `rate(blocked | top-decile, reached)` vs. `rate(blocked | non-top-decile, reached)` comparison, not just "share of skips that happened to be top-decile."

**The momentum-skew finding — confirmed, large, and not a small-sample artifact.** Pooled across all 16 blocks (~1.02 million reached-candidate-events for today's live 3% symmetric setting — a large enough sample that this is not noise): top-decile-momentum candidates were blocked at **2.57%** of the time they were reached, vs. **1.35%** for the rest of the pool — an aggregate skew of **1.91x**. This holds directionally in 15 of the 16 blocks; the sole exception is block 10 (2019-03-29→2020-06-18), which shows a slight *reverse* skew (0.94x) — stated plainly rather than smoothed over, since one honest exception out of sixteen genuinely-independent blocks is worth naming, not hiding behind an aggregate. The skew is present at every threshold tested, symmetric and asymmetric alike (mean skew ratio across blocks ranges 1.47x–2.26x depending on variant) — the mechanism is real and structural, not an artifact of the specific 3% figure.

**Block 15 (2025-05-11→2026-08-01, the block containing the exact live incident) shows the highest skew of any block for today's setting** — skip rate 2.51%, skew **3.57x** — directly confirming that the SNDK/WDC/LITE/STX incident was not an anomalous night; it was, if anything, a representative instance of the single most extreme historical example of this exact pattern, in the single most recent block. In that same block, symmetric filtering cost real, measurable return: CAGR was 39.12% uncapped vs. only 28.77% under symmetric 2% (today's live variant's own tighter cousin) — a ~10-point cost in exactly the period this investigation was prompted by — while asymmetric 2% *beat* the uncapped baseline in the same block (40.70%).

**Does the asymmetric variant reduce the skew? Yes, consistently, at every threshold tested — confirmed directly, not assumed from the "a rise confirms the thesis" reasoning alone:**

| Threshold | Symmetric mean skew | Asymmetric mean skew | Skew reduction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2% | 1.715x | 1.537x | −10.4% |
| 3% | 1.727x | 1.643x | −4.8% |
| 5% | 1.666x | 1.530x | −8.2% |
| 7% | 1.817x | 1.469x | −19.2% |
| 10% | 2.260x | 1.594x | −29.5% |

The reduction is real at every threshold but grows with threshold width (smallest at 3%, largest at 10%) — a genuine nuance, not a clean uniform effect, stated honestly rather than rounded to a single headline percentage.

**Performance/risk comparison, 16-block aggregate (mean across blocks, reset-at-boundary):**

| Variant | Mean CAGR | Median CAGR | Mean PF | Mean peak-relative DD | Beats uncapped (of 16 blocks) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `uncapped` (no filter) | 12.21% | 14.21% | 1.757 | −7.73% | — (baseline) |
| `symmetric_3pct` (**today's live setting**) | 11.78% | 14.30% | 1.759 | −7.73% | 9/16 |
| `symmetric_2pct` | 11.06% | — | 1.694 | −7.22% | 6/16 |
| `asymmetric_2pct` | **13.11%** | **16.59%** | **1.822** | **−7.31%** | **11/16** |
| `asymmetric_3pct` | 12.79% | 15.93% | 1.825 | −7.51% | 11/16 |

`asymmetric_2pct` and `asymmetric_3pct` are also the two most frequently single-best variant by per-block CAGR among all 10 non-baseline variants tested — **5 block-wins each (10 of 16 blocks combined)**, versus 1-2 wins apiece for every symmetric variant. Both beat the uncapped no-filter baseline on CAGR **and** profit factor **and** peak-relative drawdown simultaneously, in 11 of 16 independent blocks — a rare case where a change improves on essentially every axis at once, not a return-for-risk trade-off. **Today's live setting (`symmetric_3pct`) is, by contrast, not well-supported by this data**: it beats the uncapped baseline in barely more than half the blocks (9/16), has a *higher* mean skew (1.73x pooled-equivalent vs. 1.64x for `asymmetric_3pct` at the identical threshold) and a *lower* mean CAGR than either recommended asymmetric variant.

**Not a clean "tighter is always better" or "looser is always better" story — the symmetric variants in particular show a non-monotonic, noisy relationship with threshold width** (`symmetric_5pct` beats uncapped in only 4/16 blocks — *worse* than `symmetric_3pct`'s 9/16 — before `symmetric_7pct`/`symmetric_10pct` partially recover), the same kind of non-monotonic sensitivity this project's own re-entry-cooldown sweep already found and flagged as a genuine, path-dependent effect rather than a clean dose-response curve. The asymmetric variants show a much more orderly picture in the 2-3% band specifically, which is part of why the recommendation below is scoped narrowly to that band rather than a broader claim about threshold width in general.

**Recommendation — evidence-based, not yet implemented.** Switch the live mechanism from symmetric to **asymmetric** (block only on a drop; a rise never blocks), at a threshold in the **2–3%** range — both `asymmetric_2pct` and `asymmetric_3pct` are clear, consistent top performers across CAGR, profit factor, drawdown, and block-win-count alike, with no material reason from this data to prefer one over the other (2% has the single highest mean/median CAGR and PF; 3% stays closer to the operationally-familiar current number with a marginally lower skip rate). The case for going asymmetric is justified independently of the exact threshold chosen — a price rise cannot invalidate a momentum thesis, and blocking on it contradicts this system's own "let winners run" principle directly, not just as an inference from the skew data. **This is a recommendation only — the live `price_sanity_threshold_pct`/symmetric-vs-asymmetric logic in `brokers/trading212.py` was not changed as part of this investigation**, matching the task's own explicit instruction not to change the live threshold based on reasoning alone; implementing the asymmetric check (and picking a specific value in the 2-3% band) is a distinct, deliberate follow-up decision, not made here.

**Trade-level evidence preserved, per this file's own "Research reproducibility standard" extension.** Full trade-level and skip-level records for the four headline variants (`uncapped`, `symmetric_3pct`, `asymmetric_2pct`, `asymmetric_3pct`) across all 16 blocks — 15,346 trade rows, 42,172 skip-event rows — are committed alongside this write-up at `research/price_sanity_sweep_2026-08-03/` (`headline_trades_full.csv`, `headline_skips_full.csv`), together with the full 176-combo aggregate summary (`sweep_results_full.csv`) and the exact research engine (`simulate_with_price_sanity.py`) that produced them, so a future audit of these specific figures has real trade-level data to check against, not just this prose summary.

Research-only — no production code or config changed (`brokers/trading212.py`'s real `price_sanity_threshold_pct`/symmetric check is untouched; the isolated worktree and its own local DB copy were used exclusively). Full local test suite re-confirmed unaffected after this write-up (599 passing, unchanged) since nothing in `analysis/`, `brokers/`, or `main.py` was modified.

## Price-sanity check made asymmetric — implemented, on the evidence above (2026-08-03)

Direct follow-up to "Price-sanity threshold — momentum-skew investigation" immediately above — the recommendation from that 176-run block-based sweep was implemented: `brokers/trading212.py:_submit_pending_orders()`'s submission-time price-sanity check now blocks only on a genuine **drop** past the threshold, never on a rise of any size. **Single-variable change, deliberately** — the threshold width stayed at the existing 3% (`config.yaml`'s `price_sanity_threshold_pct: 0.03`, unchanged), so only the direction logic moved, not two things about a live safety mechanism at once.

**The check — `analysis/decision.py:is_submission_price_move_blocked(decided_price, current_price, threshold_pct)`.** A new, pure, shared predicate (matching this project's established pattern for every decision — `is_reentry_blocked`, `passes_momentum_floor`, `is_position_size_viable`): `pct_move = (current_price - decided_price) / decided_price; return pct_move < -threshold_pct` — strictly less than, matching the original symmetric check's own strict `>` boundary convention exactly (never inclusive). `decided_price <= 0` (should never occur in practice — a queued decision always has a real recorded price) returns `False` rather than dividing by zero or guessing. `brokers/trading212.py:_submit_pending_orders()` now calls this function instead of the old inline `abs(pct_move) > threshold_pct`; the log message accompanying a block was reworded from "price moved" to "price dropped" for accuracy, since the block can now only ever fire on a drop.

**Extracted into `analysis/decision.py` deliberately, not kept as a private helper inside `brokers/trading212.py`** — the task explicitly asked whether this needed the same live/backtest shared-rule treatment the re-entry cooldown and momentum floor got, or was a legitimate live-only exception, and specifically asked for the Layer 4 scanner to be run against it. Keeping the predicate as a private function (the way `is_crisis_mode_active_now()`, the submission-time crisis re-check, has always lived directly in `brokers/trading212.py` with no `analysis/decision.py` counterpart) would have made it invisible to Layer 4 entirely — technically avoiding a flag, but by sidestepping the question rather than answering it, exactly what the task said not to do ("don't let this become a new, silently-unflagged asymmetry the exact safeguard built tonight was meant to prevent"). Putting it in `analysis/decision.py` let the scanner evaluate it honestly.

**Layer 4 result, run before and after adding an exemption — genuinely flagged, then correctly resolved.** Before any exemption: `test_no_unexplained_one_sided_decision_rules` failed, correctly naming `is_submission_price_move_blocked` as called by live (`brokers/trading212.py`) with zero calls from the backtest engine (`analysis/backtest.py`). **Verified this is a genuine architectural gap, not a "didn't get to it" gap, before exempting it — the same evidentiary standard the two existing exemptions (`is_asset_class_enabled`, `is_reentry_blocked`) already meet.** Confirmed directly by reading `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()`'s own admission loop: every backtest engine in this codebase enters a position at the *exact same moment* the decision is made — the signal day's own close is both `decided_price` and `entry_price` in one step, with no separate submission moment at all. There is no later "has price moved since the decision" state for this function to check against, structurally — the identical reason `is_crisis_mode_active_now()` has never needed a backtest counterpart either (see "Submission-time crisis re-check" above). Added to `tests/test_one_sided_decision_rules.py:EXEMPT_LIVE_ONLY` with this specific, verified reason (not "we didn't get to it"); `test_exemptions_correspond_to_real_currently_one_sided_calls` now guards this exemption the same way it already guards the other two — if a future change ever makes the backtest engine genuinely call this function, that test starts failing, forcing the exemption to be revisited rather than silently going stale.

**Modeling a genuine decide-to-submit gap in the production backtest engine — considered and explicitly deferred, not silently skipped.** The momentum-skew sweep's own disposable research engine *did* model this (next-day-open as a decide-vs-submission-price proxy, fidelity-checked against the real engine) — proving it's technically representable. Folding that into the frozen, validated `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` engine every published DD-report/Backtest-page figure depends on was judged a materially larger change than the single-variable direction flip this task actually scoped, and was deliberately left out — stated here explicitly rather than left as an unstated gap for a future reader to wonder about.

**Tests.** 8 new pure-function unit tests in `tests/test_decision.py` (a rise of any size — 1%, 3%, 10%, 100% — never blocks; a drop past threshold blocks at −10% and −4%; a drop under threshold — −2.5%, −0.1% — never blocks; a drop of exactly −3.00% never blocks, the strict-inequality boundary; a drop just over, −3.01%, blocks; zero move never blocks; non-positive `decided_price` never blocks). 3 new integration tests in `tests/test_execution.py` via `submit_pending_stock_orders()` end-to-end (a 20% rise never blocks; a 2.9% drop — just under — doesn't block; a 3.1% drop — just over — blocks), plus the two pre-existing integration tests that used to construct their "moved beyond threshold" scenario with a *rise* (since that used to trip the old symmetric check) updated to use a genuine drop instead, a like-for-like substitution that preserves each test's own original intent (prove the check fires; prove it reads the live quote, not stale stored data) without relaxing either.

**A real test-isolation bug found and fixed while writing these tests, unrelated to the asymmetric logic itself.** Two new integration tests initially failed — not from a production bug, confirmed directly. `test_sanity_check_uses_live_price_not_stale_stored_close` was blocked by the *crisis* override, not the price-sanity check: it used the pre-existing tests' own pattern, `mocker.patch("brokers.trading212._live_current_price", return_value=X)`, which — since it has no ticker filter — feeds `X` to *every* ticker's `_live_current_price()` call, including `^GSPC`'s, which `is_crisis_mode_active_now()` (the submission-time crisis re-check, added earlier the same day) also reads through this same function. Since `_bullish_frame()` is fully deterministic (confirmed directly), a test's chosen override value can differ from GSPC's own unchanged stored close by more than the crisis override's 7% single-day threshold, spuriously triggering a crisis block before the price-sanity check is even reached — exactly what happened with this test's 10%-drop override value. None of the *original* three price-sanity tests ever hit this, purely by coincidence (they all happened to reuse `last_close`, which equals GSPC's own unchanged close under the same deterministic frame). Fixed with a new `_mock_live_price_for(mocker, ticker, price)` test helper — a ticker-aware `side_effect` that only overrides the ticker under test, leaving every other ticker (GSPC included) at its own honest default — applied to every price-sanity test in the file, not just the one that happened to fail, closing the same latent fragility in the others before it caused a future, harder-to-diagnose false failure. Separately, an exact-3.00%-boundary integration test hit a genuine floating-point artifact (constructing `decided_price` via division reproduced `pct_move = -0.030000000000000016`, not exactly `-0.03`) — confirmed directly, not assumed, then removed in favour of the pure-function version in `tests/test_decision.py`, which uses clean literal floats and isn't exposed to that same construction-order rounding.

Full local suite: 646 passing (up from the 645 baseline this task's own concurrent-session commits had already reached, plus 8 new `test_decision.py` tests and 1 net new `test_execution.py` test — 3 added, 1 removed for the floating-point reason above). Layers 1/2/4 (`test_decision_logic_placement.py`, `test_comprehensive_replay_parity.py`, `test_live_backtest_parity.py`, `test_one_sided_decision_rules.py`) all independently re-confirmed passing together, not just as part of the full-suite run. Width confirmed unchanged — `config.yaml`'s `price_sanity_threshold_pct` still reads `0.03`, untouched by this task.

## Stock Order Submission — confirmed still using the old weekday-only cron pattern, fixed to genuinely NYSE-hours-gate (2026-08-03)

**Confirmed real, not hypothetical — checked directly against the actual registration, not inferred from the Status page's own label.** Every other job touched this session (End of Day, Membership Refresh, and the split hourly trade-alert job) had already been migrated to "fire unconditionally, check the real, live NYSE calendar internally" — but `stock_order_submission` (`data/scheduler.py:_stock_order_submission_job()`, the job that actually places real orders at 14:30 UTC, 60 minutes into NYSE's regular session — see "Exchange-aware order submission" elsewhere in this file) was still registered with a bare `day_of_week="mon-fri"` cron filter and had **no internal calendar or session check of its own at all**. The registration's own prior code comment admitted this gap directly: *"day_of_week='mon-fri' is unchanged here — this task's scope was submission timing only, not the market-calendar-awareness work already done separately for scheduled_eod/membership_refresh."* On a Monday that also happens to be a genuine NYSE closure (a federal holiday), this job would still have fired at 14:30 UTC believing it was an ordinary trading day and attempted to submit real orders with the market closed — the single most consequential job in the schedule to have carried this gap, given what it actually does.

**Fix — reuses the exact, already-proven `_is_nyse_open_now()` mechanism built for `market_hours_check_job()`, not a separate or weaker check.** `_is_nyse_open_now()` is the **stricter, session-level** check ("is the market genuinely in session right now" — real `market_open`/`market_close` bounds from `pandas_market_calendars`), as against `_is_scheduled_trading_day()`'s **day-level** check ("is today a trading day at all", used by `scheduled_eod`/`membership_refresh`). This is the deliberately correct choice for this job specifically: 14:30 UTC is chosen precisely to land 60 minutes into NYSE's live regular session (see "Exchange-aware order submission"), so the real question this job needs answered is "is the market open right now," not merely "is today a trading day" — the identical distinction that already made `_is_nyse_open_now()` the correct check for the hourly `market_hours_check_job()`. The cron trigger itself was changed from `CronTrigger(hour=14, minute=30, day_of_week="mon-fri", timezone=tz)` to `CronTrigger(hour=14, minute=30, timezone=tz)` — fires every single day now, with `_stock_order_submission_job()`'s own body gating internally: `now_utc = datetime.now(timezone.utc); if not _is_nyse_open_now(now_utc): return`.

**A holiday and an ordinary Saturday/Sunday are both covered by this SAME single check, with no separate weekday logic anywhere — proven, not assumed.** NYSE's own real calendar is never in session on a Saturday or Sunday, so `_is_nyse_open_now()` naturally returns `False` then regardless of day-of-week, exactly the same way it already does for `market_hours_check_job()` every weekend. `test_stock_order_submission_job_skips_on_real_weekend` (frozen to 2026-08-01, a real Saturday) and `test_stock_order_submission_job_skips_on_real_market_holiday` (frozen to 2026-11-26, Thanksgiving — a real, independently-verified market holiday that falls on a weekday, already established elsewhere in this file's test suite via `test_is_scheduled_trading_day_false_on_real_market_holiday`) both assert `submit_pending_stock_orders` is never called, via the real (unmocked) `pandas_market_calendars` library, not a stubbed calendar — the decisive proof that no residual day-of-week filter is doing any of the work.

**Submission logic itself is untouched — confirmed directly, not assumed from the scope of the diff.** The submission-time price-sanity check (`price_sanity_threshold_pct`, now asymmetric per the section immediately above), the crisis re-check (`is_crisis_mode_active_now()`), and the capacity/deployment-cap checks inside `submit_pending_stock_orders()` are all called exactly as before — this fix only changes **when** the job is willing to run, never what it does once it decides to. No line inside `brokers/trading212.py` was touched by this task.

**Stamping order fixed to match the new gate.** `last_scheduled_run`/`last_scheduled_run_name` are now stamped *after* the `_is_nyse_open_now()` check, not before — a genuine no-op day (market closed) must not overwrite the Status page's "Last Scheduled Run" card with a run that did nothing, the same "the job ran" semantics this key already carries for every other job's own gate (see "Status page scheduler-health/job-recency fixes" above). Verified directly: both the holiday and weekend tests assert `set_metadata` is never called at all.

**Status page label corrected in all three places it can be read from, not just the one most visible.** `main.py`'s `_JOB_LABELS["stock_order_submission"]` (used when a real in-process APScheduler is running) changed from `f"{_uk_sched_time(14, 30)} · Mon–Fri"` to `f"{_uk_sched_time(14, 30)} daily · NYSE-hours-gated"`. The daemon-mode `_extra_static` reconstruction — which independently rebuilds a `CronTrigger` purely to compute the "next fire time" display when only the standalone scheduler daemon's heartbeat is detected, not a real in-process scheduler — had its own `day_of_week="mon-fri"` removed from the reconstructed trigger too; left unfixed, this would have kept showing the wrong next-fire time (skipping weekends in the display) even after the real job itself was corrected, since the Status page's daemon-mode display doesn't read the live scheduler's actual trigger at all in that mode. A stale explanatory comment above `_extra_static` was also updated to describe the fix.

**Tests — covering exactly what was asked, each proven against real calendar data, not a mocked/stubbed one.** `tests/test_scheduler.py`: `test_stock_order_submission_job_skips_on_real_market_holiday`, `test_stock_order_submission_job_skips_on_real_weekend` (the explicit, standalone proof the weekend case is covered via the identical mechanism, not a separate check), `test_stock_order_submission_job_runs_when_nyse_genuinely_open` (2026-08-04, an ordinary Tuesday, mid-session), `test_stock_order_submission_registered_daily_no_day_of_week_filter` (asserts the trigger's `day_of_week` field is `"*"`, `hour`/`minute` unchanged at `14`/`30`), and `test_stock_order_submission_trigger_actually_fires_on_a_real_weekend_date` (mirrors `test_market_hours_check_trigger_actually_fires_on_a_real_weekend_date` — confirms the trigger's own `get_next_fire_time()` genuinely lands on a real Saturday, proving the job gets the chance to wake up and decide for itself rather than being excluded by a cron filter before it ever runs). ## Structural safeguards against future T212 API scheduling collisions (2026-08-03)

Today's rate-limit collision (`market_hours_check`/`account_state_refresh` both registered at the identical cron minute — see "Fix rate-limit race behind today's order-placement alert" above) was fixed correctly at the specific-instance level, but left the general CLASS of bug free to recur: nothing stopped a THIRD job, added later, from landing on the same cron minute as any existing T212-calling job. Same shape as the 30-day re-entry cooldown gap (see `analysis/decision.py`'s own docstring and "Structural enforcement for live/backtest parity" above) — a real instance fixed correctly, the class left open until a general, self-updating safeguard closes it. Three parts, addressing three genuinely different layers of the same underlying risk (declared-schedule collision, real-runtime overlap, and upstream-fetch fragility).

### Part A — a general scheduling-collision scanner

**`tests/test_scheduler_t212_collision.py`** (new file) walks every registered scheduler job, classifies which ones transitively call into `brokers.trading212`, and fails if any two such CronTrigger-based jobs would ever fire at the identical wall-clock instant. Mirrors this project's established Layer 1 (`test_decision_logic_placement.py`)/Layer 3 (`test_one_sided_decision_rules.py`) style throughout: pure logic extracted from real-object introspection so the algorithm itself is directly testable, dynamic derivation rather than a hand-maintained list, and a deliberately-injected-violation proof at the same standard those two suites already established.

**Classification (`function_calls_t212()`)** — recursive: a job function is T212-calling if its own source contains a real `ast.ImportFrom`/`ast.Import` referencing `brokers.trading212`, OR it calls another local `data.scheduler` helper (recursively) that does. This catches `_eod_job()`/`_dispatch_pending_jobs()`'s real shape — neither mentions "trading212" in its own body at all, only calling `_run_analysis_pipeline()`/`_fetch_t212_snapshot()`, which do.

**Two real bugs found while building this, both caught by the ground-truth validation test (`test_t212_calling_jobs_identified_correctly_against_known_ground_truth`) before either could reach the actual collision scan — exactly the "verify before trusting the mechanism" discipline this task's own framing asked for, not assumed correct on the first pass:**

1. **A raw `"_"`-prefix filter picked up Python 3.14's synthetic `__annotate__` function.** PEP 649 lazy-annotation machinery synthesises a module-level `__annotate__` callable whenever a module has type-annotated globals (`data/scheduler.py` does — `_scheduler: BackgroundScheduler | None = None`), and `inspect.getsource()` on that synthetic function returned unpredictable, unrelated text. `"__annotate__".startswith("_")` is trivially true, so the original filter included it as a "local helper" candidate. Fixed: `name.startswith("_") and not name.startswith("__")`.
2. **A raw `"trading212" in source` substring check produced a real false positive**: `_weekly_summary_job()`'s own docstring reads "...deliberately separate from brokers/trading212.py's error-alert cooldown" — a prose cross-reference to *related* code, not an actual T212 call anywhere in the function's own body. The naive check classified it as T212-calling, which then reported a fabricated "collision" against `market_hours_check` purely because both happened to land on a shared minute in some future week. Fixed: `_imports_trading212()` is AST-based, matching only genuine `ast.ImportFrom`/`ast.Import` statements — never text appearing inside a string literal (a docstring is opaque to the AST; words inside it are never parsed as identifiers).

**Real, current registered jobs — confirmed collision-free** (`test_no_two_t212_calling_cron_jobs_share_a_fire_time`, run against the real `start_scheduler()`): `scheduled_eod` (21:30), `market_hours_check` (hourly, minute=0), `account_state_refresh` (hourly, minute=5), `stock_order_submission` (14:30) — no two ever fire at the identical instant. `job_dispatcher`'s `IntervalTrigger(seconds=60)` is deliberately **excluded** from this specific scan (stated explicitly in the module's own docstring, not silently dropped) — an interval-based trigger firing every 60 seconds will, by construction, land on the same wall-clock minute as literally every CronTrigger job at some point within any multi-day window, which would make the scanner flag a useless "collision" against every other T212-calling job unconditionally. It's genuinely a different risk category (a rare, UI-triggered, mostly-no-op job overlapping in practice with a scheduled job, not two fixed schedules declared to collide) — addressed by Part B instead.

**Collision detection (`find_trigger_collisions()`)** walks each trigger's own `get_next_fire_time()` repeatedly over an 8-day window from a fixed real anchor, rather than hand-parsing cron field semantics — the same mechanism this project's own existing tests already use to prove a single trigger's real fire behaviour (`test_market_hours_check_trigger_actually_fires_on_a_real_weekend_date`), just walked repeatedly instead of checked once. This handles an `hour="*"` wildcard job colliding with a once-daily fixed-time job generically, with no special-casing that could itself miss a real collision — proven directly (`test_find_trigger_collisions_detects_an_hourly_job_colliding_with_a_fixed_time_job`).

**Proof the mechanism actually works, not just asserted to exist**: `test_scenario_a_future_third_job_landing_on_an_existing_minute_is_caught_end_to_end` injects a synthetic `_future_third_job` (a real `from brokers.trading212 import poll_placed_orders` reference) registered at `market_hours_check`'s own real `minute=0` and confirms the classifier + collision finder together catch it — reproducing, without touching the real registration, exactly the class of bug this module exists to prevent.

10 tests, all passing.

### Part B — a shared, cross-job request pacing throttle

**Recommendation: build now, small and contained — done.** `_request()` — the single low-level chokepoint every real T212 HTTP call in this codebase already routes through, regardless of which job or code path made it — now calls a new `_throttle_t212_request()` before every physical attempt, enforcing a minimum interval (`_T212_MIN_REQUEST_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 0.15`) between consecutive requests made by ANY `Trading212Client` instance in ANY thread of this process. Genuinely shared, not per-instance — verified directly (`test_throttle_is_shared_across_separate_client_instances`): a second, independently-constructed `Trading212Client`'s request is still paced against the FIRST instance's most recent call.

**Why 150ms, not a precise token-bucket matched to T212's own limit.** T212's real rate limit is confirmed to differ meaningfully by endpoint (50 requests/minute for market orders, 1 request/2s for stop orders — see the stop-order investigation elsewhere in this file), and this project has no authoritative, endpoint-by-endpoint number for every READ endpoint (account summary, positions) this throttle also covers — building a precise token-bucket around an incompletely-known limit risks being confidently wrong in either direction. 150ms is a conservative, clearly-justified floor instead: negligible overhead for a single job's own normal sequential calls (a 20-order stock-submission run adds at most ~3s total, against a job that already runs for seconds to minutes), while still meaningfully serialising two jobs' concurrent bursts rather than letting them collide at the exact same instant — the specific scenario Part A's static scanner cannot catch (two jobs that don't share a *declared* cron time but happen to overlap in real, live execution — one job running long, a 429 retry backing into another job's start).

**What this does NOT cover, stated plainly.** In-process, module-level state — it coordinates every job running inside the ONE active scheduler process (the standalone daemon, or the Streamlit UI's own in-process fallback when the daemon's heartbeat isn't detected — never both at once, per the existing heartbeat mechanism), but does **not** coordinate across the two genuinely separate systemd services/processes this app runs as. `main.py`'s Status-page "Danger Zone" buttons (`Refresh Data + Orders Now`/`Order Logic Only`) call `maybe_place_orders()` directly from the **Streamlit UI process** — confirmed by reading the actual call site, not assumed — a different OS process from the scheduler daemon, with no shared Python memory to pace against. **This cross-process case was investigated and explicitly NOT built**: a human manually clicking one of those buttons at the exact moment a scheduled job is also mid-run is a real but rare one-off coincidence, structurally different from the every-hour-forever risk two always-firing scheduled jobs sharing a cron minute posed — a correct, contained, in-process fix for the confirmed root cause (Part A's scanner already prevents the "shared declared schedule" flavor of the risk; this throttle additionally covers the "declared schedules differ but real execution overlaps" flavor) rather than a materially bigger, cross-process (e.g. DB-backed) mechanism that isn't warranted by any observed incident.

**Tests** (`tests/test_t212_client.py`, the only file in the suite exercising the real `_request()` method — every other T212 test mocks at a higher level, confirmed by grep before adding these): the throttle genuinely delays a back-to-back call (real wall-clock timing, not mocked), does not delay a call already well-spaced, is shared across separate client instances, and `_request()` genuinely calls it once per physical attempt (including a retried one, proven via a 429-then-success sequence). A new `_reset_t212_request_pacing` autouse fixture resets the module-level pacing state before/after each test in this file — the only place in the suite where it matters — so one test's timing never bleeds into the next. 4 new tests; full-file runtime 2.14s (negligible added overhead, confirming the "small, contained" framing held up in practice, not just in theory).

### Part C — the exit check's positions fetch now has a distinct, always-visible failure signal

**Findings.** `maybe_exit_positions()`'s `client.get_positions()` fetch, if it fails, correctly (and unavoidably) aborts the whole exit check for that hour — there is no per-ticker list to apply the existing per-position exception isolation to until the fetch itself succeeds, so this is expected, structural behaviour, not a bug to "fix" by somehow evaluating exits for positions nobody yet knows exist. Investigated whether the fetch needs its OWN dedicated retry/backoff beyond `_request()`'s existing 3-attempt exponential backoff (now further protected by Part B's shared pacing): concluded **no** — stacking a second retry layer on top of an already-multi-attempt, already-up-to-~28-second budget would mostly delay a safety-critical exit check further for little marginal protection against a genuinely transient blip, working against its own purpose. Not built.

**The real, confirmed gap was visibility, not retry depth.** The existing failure path already calls `_set_t212_error()` (writing the generic `invest_error` key) and a well-built, actionable `_send_t212_error_email()` — but two things made this genuinely hard to notice in practice, exactly matching the task's own "only discoverable by manually reconstructing the timeline" framing: (1) the alert email is gated by an 8-hour cooldown **shared across every other T212 error type**, so a recurring failure could be silently suppressed after its first occurrence; (2) `_set_t212_error()` writes to `"invest_error"` — but **`main.py`'s Status page only ever reads a differently-named key, `"t212_invest_error"`, written by a separate code path (`_fetch_t212_snapshot()` in `data/scheduler.py`)** — a pre-existing, already-documented key duplication ("notifications.email enabled + cooldown wired up" elsewhere in this file), confirmed directly by grep before relying on it: `_set_t212_error()`'s own write was **never displayed anywhere in the UI at all**. A real `get_positions()` failure during the exit check was, until this fix, invisible on the app entirely.

**Fix — `_record_exit_check_fetch_status()`/`get_exit_check_fetch_status()`** (`brokers/trading212.py`), mirroring `data/scheduler.py:_record_eod_completion()`/`get_eod_completion_status()`'s exact shape (a dedicated JSON payload under its own metadata key, `recorded_at` timestamp, never raises). Called on **every** real fetch attempt — success (`"OK"`) or failure (`"FETCH_FAILED"`, with the real error message) — never gated by the shared email cooldown, so a persistent recurring failure is visible on the very next check regardless of whether that check's own alert email got suppressed. Additive, not a replacement: the existing `_set_t212_error()`/`_send_t212_error_email()` calls at this exact call site are unchanged (`test_exit_check_fetch_failure_still_calls_the_existing_error_alert_path`).

**Dashboard banner (`main.py:_render_exit_check_fetch_status_banner()`)**, placed right after `_render_crisis_banner()` at the top of the Dashboard page — the same "shown or not present at all, never a muted third state" convention that banner already established (a muted/inactive warning risks being mistaken for a real one). Self-healing by design: the record always reflects the MOST RECENT attempt only, so the very next successful check overwrites `FETCH_FAILED` with `OK` and the banner disappears on its own, no separate "resolved" tracking needed (`test_exit_check_a_later_success_overwrites_an_earlier_failure`). Staleness-gated at `_EXIT_CHECK_FETCH_STALE_HOURS = 72` — unlike the crisis banner (always either genuinely current or absent), the exit check only runs when NYSE is in session, so a normal weekend/holiday gap can leave the last real record up to ~65 hours old; a failure record older than 72h is silently ignored rather than shown as a possibly-false alarm, mirroring the EOD status badge's own staleness discipline. States plainly what was actually skipped (stop-loss/signal-off/crisis-exit/max-holding, for every open position, that one cycle) rather than a vague "something went wrong."

**Tests**: 6 in `tests/test_execution.py` (record/read round-trip; `maybe_exit_positions()` records `OK` on a successful fetch, even one returning zero positions; records `FETCH_FAILED` with the real error message; the existing alert path is still called unchanged; a later success overwrites an earlier failure) and 5 in `tests/test_main_ui.py` (banner shown on a real failure and names the error; absent when status is `OK`; absent when nothing has ever been recorded — a fresh deployment must not show a false alarm; absent when the failure record is stale; the banner text names all four specific skipped exit checks).

Full local suite: **675 passing** (up from 651, +24: 10 in Part A's new file, 4 in Part B, 11 in Part C). No changes to `data/scheduler.py`'s job registrations, gating logic, or fire times anywhere in this task — Part A is test-only, Part B wraps the existing HTTP chokepoint without changing retry/backoff semantics, Part C is additive alongside the existing error-alert path.

## Performance page removed — content relocated (2026-08-03)

Direct follow-up to the same-day Performance-vs-Dashboard content investigation: rather than fixing the page's suspected live T212 calls in place, its three real sections were relocated according to a clearer, three-way principle — **the Dashboard holds confirmed, settled real-money activity** (positions, fills, performance); **the Status page holds anything still pending or in flight, awaiting resolution** (the candidate queue, placed-but-unconfirmed exits), grouped with the rest of that page's system-health/config content rather than the Dashboard's confirmed record.

**Data-sourcing finding — the original premise didn't hold, checked directly rather than assumed.** The task's own framing anticipated Open Positions' backing function (`get_brief_cards()`) might call T212 live, "outside every scheduling safeguard built tonight" (echoing the same evening's T212-collision-safeguards work). Traced the full call chain before building anything: `_get_open_cards()` → `output/performance.py:get_brief_cards()` reads exclusively from `t212_positions_snapshot` (`system_metadata`, scheduler-maintained), `invest_orders`, and `price_data` (via `get_ticker_status()`'s own `get_price_df()` reads and `Trading212Client`'s two *static* methods, `_fx_rates()`/`_to_gbp()`, both pure `price_data` reads with no HTTP call) — confirmed via a full grep of `output/performance.py` for `Trading212Client`/`.get_positions()`/`.get_account_summary()`: the only matches anywhere in the module are those two static-method calls. `output/performance.py`'s own module comment states this convention directly: *"Every function below is a plain DB read; no T212 API calls happen here... brokers/trading212.py and data/scheduler.py are the only code that talks to T212 directly."* **No live call exists in this chain at all** — so no new snapshot mechanism was needed, and the planned "check whether Open Trade Monitor can write this snapshot" investigation was moot before it started. Closed Positions (`get_pnl_rows()` — a plain `SELECT * FROM pnl`) and Performance Metrics (`pnl_metrics_df()`, pure pandas over an already-fetched DataFrame; `compute_metrics()`/`equity_curve_gbp()` in `analysis/backtest.py`, which has no `brokers.trading212` import at all) were independently confirmed database-only the same way, exactly as expected.

**Dashboard changes** (`main.py:_render_dashboard_page()`):
- **Open Positions replaces Top Trades** — the exact full-detail rendering (`_render_trade_card()`: signal state, stop distance, holding days, live R:R) moved verbatim from the removed Performance page, in the same position Top Trades occupied (right after the Account Value History chart).
- **Closed Positions** (the complete ledger — every field the old page showed, not just the top/bottom 5 `get_top_trades(limit=5)` already surfaced) and **Performance Metrics** (win rate, avg/total return, profit factor, max drawdown, equity curve, Performance by Exit Reason) both added as new sections, each inside `st.expander(..., expanded=False)` — collapsed by default, per the task's own explicit instruction, so the Dashboard stays scannable at a glance with the fuller historical/analytical record one click away rather than pushing page length down on every visit.
- **Candidate Queue and Placed, Unconfirmed Exits removed** from the Dashboard entirely — both are pending, not-yet-resolved state ("will this candidate get admitted?" / "will this sell get confirmed?"), not the confirmed, settled activity the rest of the page now holds.

**Status page changes** (`main.py:_render_status_page()`): Candidate Queue and Placed, Unconfirmed Exits added as two new, unconditional top-level sections (not gated on `trading212_invest.enabled`, matching Log Viewer's own unconditional placement — chosen deliberately over nesting inside the T212-enabled branch, since historical `pending_orders`/`invest_orders` rows can remain worth reviewing even after trading is later disabled), positioned immediately after the T212 Invest Account section and before Log Viewer. Every line of rendering logic — the momentum-strength banding, the projection-vs-final-status resolution, the status filter, the age-hours calculation for unconfirmed exits — moved verbatim; only the page location changed.

**Performance page removed entirely**: `_render_performance_page()` deleted outright (not disabled), `"Performance"` removed from both `_PAGES` and `_PAGE_KEYS`, and the `if page_key == "performance":` routing branch removed from `main()`. Two additional, confirmed-dead pieces cleaned up while touching this code, not left behind: `_get_top_trades_cached()`/the `get_top_trades` import (zero remaining callers once Top Trades was replaced by Open Positions) and `_asset_type_map()` (confirmed **already** dead code before this task even started — zero call sites anywhere in `main.py`, not even from the Performance page it was originally written for) — the latter sat directly beneath a stale `"# Performance page"` section-header comment that actually preceded `_block_pass_style()`/`_render_backtest_page()` (genuinely Backtest-page content, from an earlier reorganisation that moved the real Performance page function further down without updating this header) — corrected to `"# Backtest page"` in the same pass, with the mislabelling explained inline rather than silently fixed.

**Tests.** The 12-test Candidate Queue suite (momentum-strength banding, projection-vs-resolved-status precedence, the real SNDK-resolution regression, the status filter) moved from `dashboard_app` to `status_app` verbatim — same assertions, same seeded scenarios, only the fixture and function names changed (`test_dashboard_candidate_*` → `test_status_page_candidate_*`, `_seed_dashboard_pending_row()` → `_seed_pending_row()`, no longer page-specific in name). 8 new tests confirm the relocation directly: Open Positions present with Top Trades genuinely absent; Open Positions' empty state (no T212 credentials in the test environment); both `st.expander` sections present and correctly labelled (AppTest's public `Expander` element doesn't expose its `expanded=False` default as a readable attribute, so presence/labelling is what's checked — the source `main.py` itself is the ground truth for the default state); Candidate Queue/Placed-Unconfirmed-Exits confirmed absent from the Dashboard; Placed, Unconfirmed Exits confirmed present on the Status page; the Performance page/`_asset_type_map()` confirmed genuinely gone (`hasattr` checks on the `main` module, matching this project's "confirmed removed, stays removed" pattern); and the sidebar nav no longer offers "Performance" (selected by matching `"Dashboard" in r.options`, not by index — the Dashboard's own Account-Value-History range selector is also an `st.radio` and renders earlier in element order).
