## Dashboard "querying T212" report — traced, no T212 call found; the real cause was a ~60s DB-bound `get_ticker_status()` computing the full ~503-ticker universe on every cache miss (2026-08-04)

**Urgent report investigated directly, evidence-based, not assumed either way.** A report came in that the Dashboard "appears to be querying T212 directly again." Traced every section of `_render_dashboard_page()` — account balance, account-value history, Open Positions, Recent Orders, Closed Positions, Performance Metrics — and every function each transitively calls, all the way down. **Confirmed: zero genuine live T212 broker-API calls exist anywhere in the Dashboard's render path.** `output/performance.py`'s own module docstring convention ("every function is a plain DB read; only `brokers/trading212.py`/`data/scheduler.py` talk to T212 directly") holds — the only two `Trading212Client` references in that module are its static `_fx_rates()`/`_to_gbp()` helpers, both pure `price_data` reads with no HTTP call. The one genuine live-T212-calling function reachable from any UI page at all, `brokers/trading212.py:project_pending_order_admission()` (a deliberate, documented, `@st.cache_data(ttl=60)`-wrapped projection mechanism from 2026-08-02), is confirmed to live exclusively on the **Status page**'s Candidate Queue section — never the Dashboard — and the "Refresh Account" button is likewise confirmed Status-page-only, and doesn't even call T212 synchronously itself (it only sets a `pending_t212_fetch` flag the async dispatcher later consumes). Cross-checked against the real server: the web UI (`investment-research`) service's own journal showed **zero** T212-related log lines across the prior 24 hours, while the scheduler daemon's own journal showed the expected, documented hourly `account_state_refresh` rate-limit retry pattern (see "structural safeguards against future T212 API scheduling collisions" above) — direct evidence the report wasn't describing a real T212 call from the web UI process at all.

**The real, concrete symptom, confirmed directly by the reporter**: "`_get_ticker_status()` running very often, with a long delay." This is Streamlit's own built-in cache-miss spinner (`st.cache_data`'s default `show_spinner=True` shows "Running `_get_ticker_status()`...") — a real, severe, but entirely DB-bound (never T212) performance bug, easily mistaken for an external API call given how slow and disruptive it was.

**Root cause, measured directly against real production data before touching any code.** `output/performance.py:get_ticker_status()` computed momentum/signal/membership/crisis status for the **entire live ~503-ticker S&P 500 candidate pool** (`analysis.universe.get_live_stock_candidates()`) on every cache miss — even though its sole real caller, `get_brief_cards()` (the Dashboard's Open Positions section), only ever consults `status_by_ticker.get(research_ticker)` for the small handful of tickers that actually have an open position (16, as of this fix). The other ~487 rows were computed in full and then silently discarded on every single call. Measured on real production data: `get_live_stock_candidates()` alone took **~10.9s**; the full `get_ticker_status()` call (per-ticker `get_price_df(ticker, days=8000)` + signal/momentum computation × 503) took **~59.6s** total. `main.py`'s own caching (`@st.cache_data(ttl=300)` on the now-removed `_get_ticker_status()` wrapper) meant this only recurred once per 5 minutes under normal conditions — but the service had been restarted 5+ times in the preceding ~90 minutes from tonight's own active concurrent deploy cadence, wiping the in-process cache each time and making the ~60s delay recur far more often than the nominal TTL would suggest, exactly matching "running very often."

**Fix — scope `get_ticker_status()` to only the tickers actually needed, not the full universe.** `get_ticker_status(config, tickers: Optional[list[str]] = None)` gained an explicit `tickers` parameter: when given, bypasses `get_live_stock_candidates()` entirely (not just the per-ticker loop — that lookup alone was ~11s of the total) and computes status for exactly that list. Defaults to `None` (full universe) so every other existing caller/test keeps its exact prior behaviour unchanged. `get_brief_cards()` now derives the real "held tickers" set itself — `reverse_map` (every VERIFIED T212 instrument resolution) filtered down to only those with a current entry in `pos_by_t212` (the live positions snapshot, already read by this point in the function) — and passes that small set into `get_ticker_status(config, tickers=held_tickers)` whenever `ticker_status_rows` isn't already supplied by the caller. `main.py`'s old two-step pattern (`_get_ticker_status()`, a `ttl=300`-cached full-universe pre-fetch, feeding into an uncached `_get_open_cards()`) was replaced with a single `@st.cache_data(ttl=60)`-wrapped `_get_open_cards(_config)` that calls `get_brief_cards(_config)` directly with no pre-fetch — the now-dead `get_ticker_status` import was removed from `main.py` alongside it.

**Verified on real production data, before and after, isolated-clone discipline (own copied DB, deleted after use — matching this project's standing research practice):**

| | `get_brief_cards()` total | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Before (currently-deployed code) | **59.7s** | 16 open-position cards, correct |
| After (fix) | **2.5s** | identical 16 cards, identical statuses |

A ~24x speedup, with byte-identical output (same 16 tickers, same `ON TRACK` statuses) confirming the fix changes performance only, not behaviour.

Covered by 3 new tests in `tests/test_performance.py`: `test_ticker_status_explicit_tickers_bypasses_full_universe_lookup` (an explicit `tickers=` list must never call `get_live_stock_candidates()` at all, not just skip the extra iterations — asserted via a mock that raises if called), `test_ticker_status_empty_tickers_list_returns_empty_without_lookup`, and `test_brief_cards_without_ticker_status_rows_only_computes_status_for_held_tickers` — the decisive end-to-end proof: a mocked 8-ticker live pool with only one ticker (`VOO`) actually held, `get_price_df()` instrumented to raise if called for anything other than `^GSPC` (the legitimate, single, always-required crisis-check read) or `VOO`, confirming `get_brief_cards()` — via the real, unmocked Dashboard code path (`ticker_status_rows` omitted) — never touches the other 7 pool tickers at all. Full local suite: **765 passing**.

**Not changed**: nothing about which tickers are eligible, how status is classified, or any decision/order-placement logic — this is a pure performance fix confined to `output/performance.py`'s internal scoping and `main.py`'s caching wrapper.

## Deploy blackout windows corrected — derived from real scheduler registrations, guarded by a drift-detection test (2026-08-04)

**Confirmed stale, exactly as flagged.** `deploy.sh`/`deploy.ps1`'s blackout-window check (see "Deployment timing" above) had drifted from the real, current schedule in three ways, checked directly against `data/scheduler.py:start_scheduler()`'s real `CronTrigger` registrations rather than assumed: (1) the 13:15–14:00 window guarded `stock_order_submission` at its old 13:30 UTC time — submission moved to 14:30 UTC the same day it was last "re-verified" (see "Stock submission delayed past NYSE open" above), leaving the real 14:30 firing completely unguarded while the window protected an empty slot; (2) the 06:45–07:15 window guarded the Monday pre-market job, which was removed entirely the following day (see "Monday Pre-Market removed entirely" above) — a window for a job that no longer exists; (3) a **previously-undetected gap**, not a drift of an existing window: `market_hours_check` (fires every hour at `:00`) and `account_state_refresh` (fires every hour at `:05`) — both split off the old hourly trade-alert job the same day the other two changes happened — had **no blackout coverage at all**, despite both making real T212 API calls (order-status polling, `maybe_exit_positions()`'s exit checks which can place a real SELL, position reconciliation, account snapshot refresh) on every single firing, every hour, every day.

**Approach — recomputed windows + a test-time drift-detection guard, not a fully dynamic runtime check.** Considered directly against the task's own explicit fallback: a fully dynamic design (deploy.sh shelling out to Python at deploy time to compute the blackout check live) was rejected because the only function that actually knows the real schedule, `start_scheduler()`, is not a pure "describe the schedule" function — calling it starts a genuine `BackgroundScheduler` thread and writes a heartbeat to `system_metadata`, neither of which a deploy-time clock check should ever trigger as a side effect, and extracting a new pure function out of that safety-critical file was judged a materially larger, riskier change than the actual problem warranted. Instead: the window bounds in `deploy.sh`/`deploy.ps1` were recomputed against the real, current registrations, and `tests/test_deploy_blackout_windows.py::test_blackout_windows_match_real_scheduler_registrations` — run on every push via the pre-push hook — starts the REAL scheduler (the exact same `start_scheduler()` call, config/DB side effects mocked, that every other scheduler-registration test in this suite already uses) and cross-checks its live trigger fields against `deploy.sh`'s `WINDOW_LO`/`WINDOW_HI` shell variables, parsed directly out of the file rather than re-typed by hand in the test — a future scheduler change that isn't mirrored into `deploy.sh` now fails the test suite, not silently drifts a third time. This mirrors the exact precedent the task itself cited (Layer 4's exemption list is checked the same way — computed once, then compared against a live-computed value, never re-derived live inside the thing being guarded).

**Corrected windows, evidence-based:**

| Window | Old (stale) | New | Real job(s) covered |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stock submission | 1315–1400 (guarded the old 13:30 time) | **1415–1445** | `stock_order_submission` (`CronTrigger(hour=14, minute=30)`, no day filter, `_is_nyse_open_now()`-gated internally) |
| EOD / membership refresh | 2100–2200 | **unchanged** (already correct) | `membership_refresh` (21:15) + `scheduled_eod` (21:30, from `config.yaml`'s `scheduler.runs.eod`) |
| Weekly summary | Sun 0745–0915 | **unchanged** (already correct) | `weekly_summary` (Sunday 09:00 Europe/London = 08:00 UTC BST / 09:00 UTC GMT — both covered) |
| Monday pre-market | 0645–0715 | **removed entirely** | job no longer exists (removed 2026-08-03) |
| Hourly (new) | *none* | **minute-of-hour ≥55 or ≤10, every day, unconditional** | `market_hours_check` (`:00`, no hour/day filter) + `account_state_refresh` (`:05`, no hour/day filter, no internal gate at all) |

**The hourly window is deliberately tight, not the wide buffer the once-daily windows use, stated explicitly rather than left implicit.** Applying the same ~30–60min buffer the daily jobs get would make the warning fire for roughly half of every day, given these two now recur hourly — undermining the tool's own purpose (a warning that fires constantly gets clicked through without being read). The ±5/±10-minute buffer instead reflects the actual at-risk window: however long this script's own git-pull-plus-restart sequence takes, observed well under two minutes end to end from real deploy logs the same night. `account_state_refresh`'s coverage is deliberately **not** weekday-gated, unlike every other window — it has no internal gate at all (unlike the others, which no-op on a non-trading day/closed session) and does real work every single hour regardless of day.

**Verified three ways before trusting either the logic or the test, not assumed correct:**
1. **Manual dry-run of the exact bash/PowerShell logic** against every real job fire time (14:30, 21:15, 21:30, Sunday 08:00/09:00, every hour's `:00`/`:05` including Saturday and off-hours) and boundary cases (`10:10` in, `10:11` out; `10:54` out) — both languages produce identical results for the identical inputs.
2. **The drift-detection test verified to actually fail, not just pass**, mirroring this project's own established discipline for every scanner/guard built tonight: re-injected the exact real bug (`STOCK_SUBMISSION_WINDOW` reverted to the stale `1315`/`1400`) and confirmed the test fails with a clear, actionable message naming the real vs. expected values; separately deleted the new `HOURLY_WINDOW` bounds entirely (simulating "nobody added coverage for the new hourly jobs," the actual gap found this pass) and confirmed that fails too. Both restored before finishing.
3. **`deploy.ps1` (gitignored, local-only) corrected identically** — confirmed via the same manual dry-run in real PowerShell, and cross-checked byte-for-byte against `deploy.sh`'s own bounds via `test_deploy_ps1_windows_match_deploy_sh_if_present` (skips gracefully, not fails, when `deploy.ps1` isn't present — e.g. a fresh clone or a git worktree, where it genuinely doesn't exist since it's gitignored — but enforces exact parity when it is).

**A secondary, adjacent stale comment found and fixed in the same pass**: `config.yaml`'s `scheduler:` section comment still named "the hourly trade-alert job and the Monday-only stale-order cancellation" as registered in `data/scheduler.py` — both were split/removed 2026-08-03, the same day this whole class of drift originates from. Corrected to name the real, current job set.

## Deployment-cap accounting — mark-to-market vs cost-basis (2026-08-04)

**The question.** `max_total_deployed` (config: `0.5`) caps what fraction of the account may be committed to open positions at once. Two conventions exist for what "already deployed" means: **mark-to-market** (open positions' real, current value, including unrealized gains/losses — the "% deployed" figure rises automatically as winners appreciate, with no new capital committed, risking throttling new entries specifically because existing positions are succeeding) vs **cost-basis** (original £ committed at entry, fixed until exit — avoids that throttling, but risks the opposite failure: a winning position can grow well beyond its original cost while the cost-basis figure stays technically compliant, so real exposure can meaningfully exceed the intended 50%). Investigated directly rather than assumed, given the two are genuinely different, both individually defensible, and this project's own prior history (see "Live/backtest deployment-cap parity" above) already shows this exact ambiguity caused a real, undetected divergence once before.

**Confirmed live: mark-to-market, by direct code read.** `brokers/trading212.py:_submit_pending_orders()` (the real, order-placing function) computes `invested = float(summary["investments"]["currentValue"] or 0)` — T212's own genuine mark-to-market valuation of open positions — and checks `deployed_after_pct = (invested + position_gbp) / total_val` against `max_deployed_pct` via `_capacity_fit_reason()`. `project_pending_order_admission()` (the Dashboard's read-only projection) reads the identical field. `analysis/backtest.py:simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` — the engine `run_full_validation()` dispatches to when `mark_to_market=True` (what the Backtest page and DD report always pass) — is the one confirmed to match this.

**Why the obvious comparison (`run_full_validation(mark_to_market=True)` vs `mark_to_market=False`) would NOT have isolated the real question.** `mark_to_market=False` dispatches to `simulate_portfolio_compounding()` — a deliberately frozen, pre-2026-08-03 engine, confirmed by reading its own docstring to be *also* missing `passes_momentum_floor()` (no minimum-momentum floor at all), exempt from `is_reentry_blocked()` (no re-entry cooldown), and with no `resolve_cash_constrained_position_gbp()` call (no cash-availability clamp). Using it would have conflated the deployment-cap accounting question with three unrelated, already-settled differences — exactly the "isolate one variable" discipline this file's re-entry-cooldown and momentum-floor investigations already established as required, not optional.

**What was actually built and run — an isolated cost-basis-cap variant.** `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm_costbasis_cap()`, copied from the real, current `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` source with exactly one change: the capacity check's own "already deployed" figure (`deployed_cost_basis`) is a running cost-basis total (`+= position_gbp` on entry, `-= position_gbp` on exit) instead of `_open_positions_mtm_value()`'s daily mark-to-market revaluation. Position *sizing* (`current_balance`, what `per_trade_pct` is measured against) was deliberately left untouched — still `cash + mark-to-market open-position value`, exactly as production — since that convention is already settled elsewhere in this project (the compounding two-parameter scheme) and was not the question under test. Every other line — entry gate, momentum floor, re-entry cooldown, exit priority, VaR sizing, cash clamp, min-viable-order, momentum-ranked skip-and-continue admission — calls the identical shared functions the real engine calls.

**Verified as a genuinely isolated copy with real evidence, not just code review** (per this file's "Research scripts must verify decision-engine parity" standing requirement) — self-check: with `max_deployed_pct` set to `10.0` (the cap can never bind), both engines were run over a 2018-01-01–2019-06-30 window against 60 live-universe tickers and produced **byte-identical trade sequences (753/753 trades matching on ticker/entry_date/exit_date/exit_reason/position_gbp)**. Confirms the only behavioural difference between the two engines is what happens when the cap actually binds — nothing else silently diverged.

**Environment discipline, per this file's own "Experimental/research work runs locally" standing practice.** The first attempt ran on the server (matching an earlier same-night precedent), but should have run locally from the start per this file's own rule — corrected mid-task, not glossed over. The session's existing local DB was checked directly before any run and found stale/wrong (`price_data` covering only 2016-06-20–2026-07-03 against the required 2007–2026 window, 67 tickers against the live ~500-ticker universe, `invest_orders` empty) — a fresh 503MB copy was synced from the server and verified (`price_data` 2007-01-01–2026-08-03, 540 tickers, `universe_membership` last refreshed 2026-08-02, 43 real `invest_orders` rows) before trusting it for the real comparison run.

**Results — full 2007–2026 continuous walk (live universe, £50,000 starting capital), out-of-sample test window (2020-01-01–2026-08-04) is the headline, per this file's own train/test discipline:**

| Metric | Mark-to-market (current live) | Cost-basis-cap |
|---|---|---|
| Test trades | 1,183 | 1,242 (+59, +5.0%) |
| Test ending balance (from £50,000) | **£421,250.74** | £385,970.93 (−£35,279.81, −8.4%) |
| Test CAGR | **38.22%** | 36.39% |
| Test profit factor (£) | **1.82** | 1.73 |
| Test max drawdown (fixed-denominator) | −88.77% | −88.46% |
| Test max drawdown (peak-relative) | −20.21% | −20.88% |
| Walk-forward success rate | **90.2%** (202/224) | 88.4% (198/224) |
| 16-block pass rate (reset-at-boundary, `PF > 1.0` and `|strat_dd| <= 1.5×|sp_dd|`) | 10/16 | 10/16 — **identical set of 6 failing blocks** (0, 1, 8, 13, 14, 15) |
| Train trades / ending balance / CAGR | 1,978 / £163,225.65 / 10.3% | 2,049 / £149,150.43 / 9.48% — same direction as test |

**The measured effect, stated precisely.** Cost-basis admits ~4–5% more trades than mark-to-market over the full 19-year window — every one of those extra admissions is, by this comparison's own isolated-variable construction, a candidate mark-to-market's cap correctly rejected because it counted unrealized appreciation as already-deployed capital, and cost-basis admitted anyway because it doesn't. Despite trading *more*, cost-basis ends the out-of-sample window with **less** money in both absolute (£35,279.81 lower) and CAGR (1.83 points lower) terms, a lower walk-forward success rate, and the identical 16-block pass count — consistent, same-direction evidence in both the train and test windows, not a one-window artifact. The theoretical concern that motivated this investigation (mark-to-market throttling winners) is not what the data shows dominating; the opposite failure mode named in the same question (cost-basis over-admitting against real exposure that's already high) is the more consequential effect at the current configuration (`per_trade_pct: 0.05`, `max_total_deployed: 0.5`).

**Not uniformly one-sided — stated plainly rather than smoothed over.** Block 14 (2024-02-21–2025-05-13) is a genuine exception: mark-to-market shows a materially worse drawdown there (−78.83% vs. cost-basis's −61.86%) despite a higher CAGR (90.3% vs. 80.18%). Plausibly path-dependency — the same structural effect this file's re-entry-cooldown investigation already documented, where one variant's earlier divergent admission decisions cascade into a materially different downstream trade sequence — rather than a systematic property of mark-to-market itself, given every aggregate measure across the same continuous walk favours it. Recorded here rather than omitted because a single favourable-looking aggregate should never be trusted over a directly-observed counter-example in the block data.

**Recommendation: keep mark-to-market. No code change made** — this was an investigation, and the evidence supports the status quo rather than motivating a change. `max_total_deployed` continues to be enforced against T212's genuine `investments.currentValue` live, matched by `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()` in the backtest.

**Full trade-level output preserved, per this file's own "preserve full trade-level output" standing requirement** — both variants' complete trade lists (ticker, entry/exit date, price, P&L, exit reason; 3,161 and 3,291 rows respectively) are committed at `research/deployment_cap_mtm_vs_costbasis_2026-08-04/mark_to_market_trades_full.csv` and `.../cost_basis_cap_trades_full.csv`, alongside the block/summary metrics (`comparison_result_summary.json`) and the exact research script that produced them (`deployment_cap_costbasis_vs_mtm.py`) — durable and outside this disposable research run, so a future discrepancy against these specific figures has real trade-level data to reconcile against, not just this write-up's own aggregates.

Covered by 4 new tests in `tests/test_deploy_blackout_windows.py`: the full cross-check against real scheduler registrations (every window, both boundary-real-fire-time inclusion and the two hourly jobs' non-overlapping-minute invariant), the stale-Monday-window-text regression guard, a structural check that `HOURLY_WINDOW`'s bounds are a genuine wrap (`LO > HI`, not accidentally swapped into an always-true or always-false check), and the `deploy.ps1` parity check. Full local suite: **768 passing, 1 skipped** (the `deploy.ps1` parity test — gitignored/local-only, genuinely absent from this worktree; present and enforced on the actual dev machine).

## Deploy pipeline systemd parity audit (2026-08-04)

**The question, and why it was treated as systematic rather than two one-offs.** Two independent gaps in the SAME category were found reactively, in the same night: (1) the FRED credential cleanup found the automated pre-push-hook deploy never syncs updated `.service` files into `/etc/systemd/system/` — only `deploy.sh` does that `cp` step; (2) the per-user-accounts rollout hit a real incident — editing `secrets.conf` then pushing left the restart using a stale cached environment (`daemon-reload` never ran), briefly seeding a random admin password instead of the migrated one (see "Managing server credentials" above). Two separate discoveries of the same *class* of problem — the automated deploy path takes shortcuts around systemd-level steps the manual `deploy.sh` path doesn't — was worth auditing systematically rather than waiting for a third instance found the same way.

**Method — line-by-line comparison of every deploy path's systemd-relevant steps.** Three paths exist: `deploy.sh` (bash, interactive, the reference/complete implementation), `deploy.ps1` (PowerShell, gitignored/local-only, intended to mirror `deploy.sh` exactly), and the automated path — the pre-push hook `setup-hooks.sh` generates, triggered by `git push origin main`. Read all three in full and diffed their remote-command sequences directly, not from memory or assumption.

**Confirmed: the automated hook was missing six of `deploy.sh`'s systemd-relevant steps, not just the two already known.** Its entire remote command, before this fix, was: `cd /root/investment-research && git pull origin main && pip install -r requirements.txt --quiet && (pip install TA-Lib --quiet || true) && systemctl restart investment-research investment-research-scheduler`. Missing, in the order `deploy.sh` performs them:
1. **`git checkout -- *.service` discard before pulling** — without it, a locally-modified `.service` file on the server (e.g. from a prior manual edit) could make `git pull` fail outright, silently blocking every future automated deploy until someone noticed and fixed it by hand.
2. **`cp` of both `.service` files into `/etc/systemd/system/`** — the already-known FRED-cleanup gap.
3. **`mkdir -p` + `ln -sf` for the scheduler's `secrets.conf` symlink** — idempotent and low-risk in the common case (set up once by `setup.sh`), but not self-healing if that symlink were ever broken (e.g. a re-provisioned server).
4. **`systemctl daemon-reload`** — the already-known incident gap.
5. **`systemctl enable investment-research-scheduler`** — not self-healing if the scheduler service was ever disabled (a reboot after a botched setup, a forgotten manual `systemctl disable` during maintenance).
6. **Any post-deploy verification at all** — the hook's remote command ending in `systemctl restart ...` reports success (exit 0) the instant systemd *accepts* the restart request, which is not the same as the service still being up moments later, or the copied files actually being what was intended.

**A more serious finding than either of the two known gaps, found as a byproduct of doing the comparison carefully rather than superficially: a real, confirmed shell-operator-precedence bug in `deploy.ps1` itself — the supposedly-correct reference path had its own latent bug.** `deploy.ps1` builds its remote command as a single `&&`-chained string with three `2>/dev/null || true` tolerance guards (after the `git checkout`, the `ln -sf`, and the `systemctl enable` steps), none of them parenthesized. bash's `&&` and `||` share equal precedence and evaluate strictly left-to-right, so `cmdA && cmdB 2>/dev/null || true && cmdC` parses as `((cmdA && cmdB) || true) && cmdC` — **the unparenthesized `|| true` doesn't just tolerate the one command it's written after; it resets the truth value of the ENTIRE chain accumulated up to that point**, meaning a genuine failure of `cmdA` (or anything else earlier in the chain) gets silently swallowed too, and `cmdC` still runs. Verified directly, not just reasoned about:
```bash
$ false && echo A || true && echo B && false && echo C || true && echo "D (should NOT print)"
B
D (should NOT print)
$ echo $?
0
```
Applied to `deploy.ps1`'s real chain: if `git pull`, `pip install`, either `cp`, or `mkdir` genuinely failed, the very next `|| true` (after `ln -sf`) would silently swallow that failure and `systemctl daemon-reload`/`systemctl restart` would still run — against whatever code was already on disk, or with a `.service` file that failed to copy — and `deploy.ps1`'s own `Assert-Success` would report the deploy as having succeeded. The fix, verified against the same reproduction: wrap each tolerance guard in its own parentheses, `(cmd 2>/dev/null || true)`, so only that command's own failure is neutralized and any earlier failure in the chain still correctly short-circuits everything after it:
```bash
$ false && echo A && (true || true) && echo "B (should NOT print)"
$ echo $?
1
$ true && echo C && (false || true) && echo "D (SHOULD print)"
C
D (SHOULD print)
```
`deploy.sh` itself was confirmed NOT affected — its remote steps are separate statements in a multi-line `bash -s << REMOTE` heredoc under `set -e`, not a single `&&`-chain, so each `|| true`-guarded line only ever affects that one line.

**A related, adjacent bug found while regenerating the fixed hook, not originally part of the audit's own scope.** `setup-hooks.sh` computed `HOOKS_DIR` via `git rev-parse --git-dir` — this returns a per-WORKTREE private admin path (`.git/worktrees/<name>`) when run from inside a worktree, not the single, shared `.git/hooks` directory every worktree's `git push` actually reads hooks from. Given this project's own standing practice of using a fresh worktree for nearly every change (including this one), re-running `setup-hooks.sh` from inside almost any of them would have silently installed the "fixed" hook into a location git never consults, leaving the real, shared hook untouched and stale. Fixed to `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, which resolves to the main `.git` directory regardless of which worktree the script runs from. Confirmed directly, not assumed: `git rev-parse --git-dir` vs. `--git-common-dir` from inside this task's own worktree return different paths (`.git/worktrees/fix-deploy-systemd-parity` vs. the real `.git`).

**What was fixed.** `setup-hooks.sh`'s hook template now performs the identical systemd step sequence `deploy.sh`/`deploy.ps1` do, in the same order, with every tolerance guard correctly parenthesized (the hook's pre-existing `(pip install TA-Lib ... || true)` was already correctly parenthesized — whoever wrote that one line got it right; the newly-added guards follow the same pattern). The real, installed `.git/hooks/pre-push` was regenerated immediately (`bash setup-hooks.sh`, using the corrected `--git-common-dir` resolution) so this repository's own next push benefits, not just a future fresh clone. `deploy.ps1`'s three guards were corrected to the properly-parenthesized form (gitignored/local-only — fixed on disk, not part of any commit).

**Nothing found to be an intentional, justified divergence.** Every one of the six missing steps was a genuine gap, not a deliberate design choice with a reason to leave it out — confirmed by checking whether omitting each one had ever been discussed or reasoned about anywhere in this file before tonight; none had. One adjacent, genuinely-intentional difference WAS found and left alone rather than "fixed": the interactive blackout-window confirmation prompt (`deploy.sh`/`deploy.ps1` warn and ask "Continue anyway?" near a scheduled job's fire time) has no equivalent in the automated hook at all. This is out of scope for a "systemd handling" parity fix specifically — a background, `nohup`'d deploy has no terminal to prompt on, and building a non-interactive equivalent (auto-abort? auto-proceed with a logged warning? require a separate opt-in flag?) is a real, separate design decision this task's own scope doesn't cover. Flagged here for visibility, not fixed.

**The lasting safeguard — two complementary layers, not one, deliberately.** A single fix closing today's two known gaps would leave the exact same "hand-maintained claim of equivalence, unverified" risk that let both original gaps go undetected for as long as they did — the task explicitly asked for something with more staying power than a point fix.
1. **Static drift detection — `tests/test_deploy_hook_systemd_parity.py`**, mirroring `test_deploy_blackout_windows.py`'s own proven design exactly: parses `deploy.sh`'s real text for a checklist of systemd-relevant operation patterns (service-file discard, both `cp`s, the secrets symlink, `daemon-reload`, both `systemctl restart`s, `systemctl enable`, the `verify_deploy.sh` call), and asserts every one of them also appears in `setup-hooks.sh`'s generated hook template — patterns tolerant of the `${SERVICE}`-variable-vs-literal-name spelling difference between the two scripts, so a genuine step is what's being checked for, not one exact string. Verified to actually fail, not just pass, mirroring this project's own established discipline for every scanner built this way: the `daemon-reload` step was temporarily removed from `setup-hooks.sh` and the test failed with a specific, correct message naming exactly that missing step; separately, `HOOKS_DIR`'s resolution was reverted to the bare `--git-dir` bug and that was caught too. Both reverted immediately after. Catches a FUTURE regression — a systemd-relevant step added to `deploy.sh` later without the hook being updated to match — at test time, before any push, not reactively after something breaks.
2. **Runtime verification — `verify_deploy.sh`**, called at the end of all THREE deploy paths (the automated hook, `deploy.sh`, and `deploy.ps1`), so every one of them confirms the SAME real, current state rather than each trusting its own command chain's exit code alone. Checks, directly against the live server: both services report `systemctl is-active`; both installed `/etc/systemd/system/*.service` files are byte-identical (`cmp -s`) to the just-pulled repo checkout's own copies; the server's `git HEAD` matches `origin/main` (confirms the pull genuinely landed the latest commit, not a silent no-op). Exit 0 only if every check passes; every check still runs and reports even after an earlier one fails, so one invocation surfaces every problem found, not just the first. This is the piece a static test structurally cannot provide — a script matching another script's *text* proves nothing about whether a real deploy's `cp`/`daemon-reload`/`restart` sequence actually left the VM in the intended state at runtime (a `cp` can succeed while copying the wrong content; `systemctl restart` returning 0 confirms the request was accepted, not that the service is still up moments later). The automated hook's own background deploy now also writes a distinct `"DEPLOY FAILED OR VERIFICATION FAILED"` line to its log on any failure, rather than only a bare non-zero exit code nobody watching a background process would otherwise see.

**Full test suite: 829 passing, 1 skipped** (unchanged skip — `deploy.ps1`'s own parity test, gitignored/local-only, genuinely absent from a fresh worktree checkout).

## GitHub webhook deploy migration, then GitHub Actions as the real test gate (2026-08-05)

**Root cause, and why patching stopped being the right response.** The systemd parity audit immediately above found six real gaps between the automated pre-push-hook deploy and `deploy.sh`/`deploy.ps1` — not the two already known — plus a genuinely serious shell-precedence bug in `deploy.ps1` itself and a bug in the hook-installer that would have made re-running the fix ineffective from most worktrees. Strong, concrete evidence for the root cause suspected earlier: having two separate implementations of "deploy this" — a local push-triggered SSH script, and the canonical `deploy.sh` on the server — means they will keep drifting apart no matter how many individual gaps get patched. This task removed the duplication structurally instead of patching another instance of it.

**Design.** GitHub notifies the server on push via a webhook; a thin listener (`webhook_listener.py`, stdlib-only — no Flask/FastAPI dependency added for a single-endpoint service) verifies the request's `X-Hub-Signature-256` HMAC-SHA256 signature (constant-time, `hmac.compare_digest`) against `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, then calls the one, single, canonical `deploy.sh` — nothing else. No deploy logic of its own; the listener stays a thin "verify signature, then deploy" component. Server access confirmed live and reachable (`ssh ... echo CONNECTED`) before any of this work began.

**Blackout-window handling — resolved explicitly, not left open.** The webhook has no human present to answer a y/N prompt. `deploy.sh --server-side` (later collapsed to just `deploy.sh` — see below) defers instead: polls the same blackout-window check every 60s and, if still inside a window, waits and rechecks — up to a 1800s cap, after which it proceeds regardless, so a real push is never silently lost or queued forever. `tests/test_deploy_server_side_blackout.py` drives the actual script end-to-end via subprocess (PATH-shimmed `systemctl`/`python3.11`, no real systemd calls) and confirms the defer-then-proceed behavior directly, not by description.

**Staged cutover, and a real signature-verification bug caught by it.** The webhook listener was proven working (unsigned request → `401`, wrongly-signed → `401`, genuinely signed `ping` → `200 pong`, all verified with real HTTP requests through the live Caddy/Cloudflare path, not just local unit tests) before the pre-existing push-triggered SSH mechanism was removed. Staging the first real deploy through the new listener caught a genuine bug immediately: the listener only accepted `POST /webhook` while every piece of documentation, the Caddy route, and the actual GitHub webhook configuration all pointed at `/webhook/deploy` — a real path mismatch, not theoretical, confirmed via a live `404` in the journal before the fix. Once corrected and re-verified, the old push-triggered SSH mechanism (the pre-push hook's own background `nohup` deploy) was removed fully — not left running in parallel, which would have reintroduced the exact duplication this migration existed to eliminate.

**KillMode=control-group self-restart bug — found the hard way, on the first genuine deploy.** `deploy_steps()` restarts `investment-research-webhook` as its own last restart step, and `webhook_listener.py`'s `trigger_deploy()` spawns `bash deploy.sh` as a direct child process of that same systemd unit. Under systemd's default `KillMode=control-group`, the unit restarting itself kills its *entire cgroup* — including the still-running `deploy.sh` process that issued the restart — so the very first real deploy through the new listener was silently truncated before it reached `systemctl status` or, critically, `verify_deploy.sh`, even though the underlying git pull and service restarts had genuinely succeeded. Caught directly from `journalctl`, not inferred (the log stopped mid-`"Restarting services..."` with no completion line ever printed). Fixed with `KillMode=process` (targets only the unit's own tracked PID on stop/restart, leaving the still-running child free to finish; accepted trade-off: a crashed listener's stray children are no longer auto-reaped by systemd, acceptable since this listener only ever spawns the one `deploy.sh` child). Confirmed working via a second real deploy immediately after: systemd logged `"Found left-over process ... in control group while starting unit. Ignoring."` — direct proof the child survived — and the run completed end-to-end, all 7 `verify_deploy.sh` checks passing. `tests/test_deploy_hook_systemd_parity.py::test_webhook_service_uses_kill_mode_process` guards this going forward. Applied proactively (not rediscovered the hard way a second time) to the equivalent listener built for `static-site`'s own webhook migration the same night.

**GitHub Actions as the real test gate — the native webhook's own genuine gap, closed by a separate follow-up task the same night.** The native webhook above deploys on *every* push to `main` regardless of test status — the only thing ever stopping a failing-tests push from deploying was the local pre-push hook, a client-side safeguard bypassable via `git push --no-verify`, a machine without the hook installed, or any git client that skips it. `.github/workflows/test-and-deploy.yml` closes this gap for real: it runs the full suite on GitHub's own infrastructure, independent of whichever machine pushed, and only on genuine success computes the identical HMAC signature (over a minimal `{"ref": ..., "after": ...}` payload, `ref` set to the actual triggering `github.ref` rather than hardcoded — a deliberate hardening so the payload can never falsely claim "this was main" if the step's own `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` condition were ever accidentally weakened) and calls the listener directly, mimicking GitHub's own webhook format exactly. `webhook_listener.py` needed zero changes for this.

**A concurrency bug this introduced, and how it was made safe.** Two independent deploy triggers (the native webhook, and now the Actions-triggered call) can be live for the same push at once — `deploy.sh` had no other mutual exclusion, and two overlapping `deploy_steps()` runs racing `systemctl restart`/`daemon-reload` for the same units is not something to rely on being harmless. `deploy.sh` was given a lock (`${APP_DIR}/.deploy.lock.d`, held for the whole script including any blackout wait) before doing anything — mkdir-based, not `flock`: `flock` does not exist in Git Bash at all, confirmed directly (tests failed with `"flock: command not found"`), and this project's own tests must run identically on Windows and Ubuntu. `mkdir` succeeding-or-failing atomically as a mutex is portable to both.

**A second, more serious concurrency bug — the lock's own stale-timeout shorter than the thing it was guarding, found live in production, not in a test.** `DEPLOY_LOCK_MAX_WAIT_SECONDS` defaulted to 600s — shorter than the blackout defer loop's own 1800s cap. A second process waiting to acquire the lock hit its own 600s patience limit before the *first* process's legitimate, still-in-progress blackout wait had finished, wrongly concluded the lock was stale (as if from a crashed prior run), forcibly broke it, and started running concurrently with the still-alive first process — and every subsequent trigger did the same thing to whichever process currently held the lock. **Five separate `deploy.sh` processes were observed running at once** on the real server during a real EOD blackout window. Manually killed the redundant processes and cleaned the stale lock directory as immediate remediation, then fixed the actual bug: `DEPLOY_LOCK_MAX_WAIT_SECONDS` raised to 3600s, comfortably longer than the blackout cap it must always outlast. Two regression tests added: a fast static check that the two defaults stay correctly ordered (`test_lock_max_wait_default_exceeds_blackout_max_wait_default`), and a dynamic proof that a lock waiter genuinely waits rather than stealing a lock still legitimately held through a real, scaled-down blackout wait (`test_lock_waiter_does_not_steal_a_lock_still_legitimately_held`) — deliberately a *different* scenario from the pre-existing serialization test, which used a lock hold far too short to have ever exposed this specific timing relationship. Directly re-verified afterward: a real push landed inside back-to-back blackout windows (EOD immediately followed by the hourly window) and held the lock uninterrupted for over 18 minutes — well past the old, buggy 600s threshold — with zero premature steals once the fix was live.

**A third real bug, unrelated to locking: Cloudflare's Bot Fight Mode blocking the Actions runner's IP.** `platform.example.com` sits behind Cloudflare (required — `ufw` on the VM only allows 80/443 from Cloudflare's own published ranges, so bypassing Cloudflare for this one path was never an option). The Actions-triggered deploy call consistently got an HTTP `403` with a `"Just a moment..."` JS-challenge page body — never returned by the listener itself (it only ever returns `401`/`200`/`202`/`400`/`404`), confirming the block happened upstream. The native webhook worked reliably throughout because GitHub's own webhook-delivery IPs apparently carry a better reputation than GitHub Actions' shared, heavily-trafficked runner IPs — plausibly also the explanation for occasional transient `403`s seen from other callers earlier the same night. Cloudflare's Custom Rules "Skip" action can bypass *Super* Bot Fight Mode for a specific path, but not the base "Bot fight mode" product — a separate, non-path-scopable toggle on the Free tier, confirmed directly by checking the rule editor's own component list ("More components to skip" expanded, no base Bot Fight Mode option present), not assumed. Fixed by disabling Bot Fight Mode site-wide, accepted as reasonable given the actual risk profile: the real security boundary for `/webhook/deploy` was always the HMAC signature check (a bot without a valid signature already gets `401`'d regardless), and the dashboard's real access control is the app's own per-user login, not Cloudflare's challenge page. Allow-listing GitHub Actions' published IP ranges in Cloudflare's IP Access Rules instead was considered and rejected — those ranges are large and change often enough that keeping the list current would be an ongoing maintenance burden disproportionate to what it protects.

**A fourth real bug, found by the Actions workflow itself once the above three were fixed: `AppTest.from_file("main.py")` failing in CI, passing locally every time.** `FileNotFoundError: .../tests/main.py` in `tests/test_auth_ui.py` and 5 call sites in `tests/test_main_ui.py`. Root cause, confirmed not assumed: `AppTest.from_file()` resolves a relative path by walking the Python call stack to find its caller's file (per Streamlit's own docstring) — fragile to anything that shifts stack depth between the test file and the `from_file()` call. GitHub Actions installed a different `anyio` version (`4.14.2`) than was locally installed (`4.13.0`), both satisfying `requirements.txt`'s unpinned `>=` constraint — enough of a difference to shift the stack walk and break the resolution. Exactly the class of environment drift an unpinned `requirements.txt` allows to go unnoticed indefinitely until a genuinely independent environment (this new CI gate, running fresh dependency installs on infrastructure this project doesn't control) actually exercises it — the local dev environment's own accumulated package versions had been masking it. Fixed generally, not as a CI-specific workaround: both files now pass an absolute path (`Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "main.py"`) instead of the bare string `"main.py"`, sidestepping the stack-walking mechanism entirely.

**A fifth issue, purely operational rather than a code bug: the `WEBHOOK_SECRET` GitHub Actions repository secret read back one character longer than it was entered.** A 64-character secret was pasted into the GitHub Actions secret field but read back as 65 characters — an incidental trailing newline from copy-paste — producing a signature the listener correctly rejected as `401 invalid signature`. Confirmed via a temporary diagnostic (`echo "DEBUG: WEBHOOK_SECRET length is ${#WEBHOOK_SECRET}"` — printed only the length, never the value, which GitHub masks in logs regardless) rather than guessed, and persisted after even a careful re-entry attempt failed the same way a second time. Rather than rely on entering the secret perfectly, the workflow now trims it (`WEBHOOK_SECRET="$(printf '%s' "$WEBHOOK_SECRET" | xargs)"`) before use — robust to this artifact regardless of how the secret gets pasted in future, not merely a one-time fix.

**Local/dev deploy mode and `deploy.ps1` removed entirely, once redundant.** An earlier design had `deploy.sh` push from a developer's own machine and then SSH in to invoke itself remotely, prompting interactively on a blackout window first; a PowerShell twin, `deploy.ps1`, did the same for Windows. Both were removed once the webhook made them redundant for routine deploys (any `git push origin main` already triggers one) and, specifically, once GitHub Actions' own non-interactive defer-then-proceed blackout handling made the interactive prompt's remaining value marginal rather than load-bearing. `deploy.sh` now always deploys directly and unconditionally, whether invoked by the webhook listener or manually over SSH as a break-glass fallback — `tests/test_deploy_hook_systemd_parity.py::test_deploy_sh_runs_deploy_steps_unconditionally` guards against a mode switch being silently reintroduced. The local pre-push hook (and its generator, `setup-hooks.sh`) were removed the same way, for the same reason, once Actions became the real test gate — not left as an empty shell; `test_no_pre_push_hook_infrastructure_exists` guards against either coming back.

**Final cutover: GitHub's own native webhook deleted entirely, and the very last push proved it.** Once the Actions path was proven working repeatedly and reliably (multiple real, successful end-to-end deploys, each with all 7 `verify_deploy.sh` checks passing), the native webhook was deleted from the repository's GitHub settings — not left running alongside Actions as a backup, since doing so would have kept the exact untested-deploy gap this whole migration existed to close. The final documentation-only commit of the night doubled as the proof: pushed with zero fallback mechanism available, it deployed successfully entirely through GitHub Actions.

**Same-night sibling migration: `static-site`.** The identical webhook-triggered architecture (thin signature-verifying listener → `deploy.sh`) was built for the separate `static-site` static-site repository the same night, using a newly-generated, dedicated deploy key (least-privilege — never reusing `investment-research-sp500`'s own key across repos) and its own independent `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. `KillMode=process` was applied there proactively from the very first version of its own webhook unit file, rather than being rediscovered the hard way a second time. Confirmed the two projects' deploy infrastructure never actually collided even during the period both existed: `static-site`'s deploy never touches the shared Caddyfile at all (it only `scp`s static files into `/var/www/example.com/`), so the "concurrent Caddyfile edit" risk flagged as a concern going in never actually materialized. A separate, genuinely unrelated bug was also found and fixed in `static-site`'s `setup-hooks.sh` the same night: `HOOKS_DIR` resolved via `git rev-parse --git-dir` (the same per-worktree bug documented in the "Deploy pipeline systemd parity audit" section above, for the same reason) — fixed to `--git-common-dir`.

**Full test suite**, run repeatedly across the whole migration: consistently **851–853 passing, 0 failing** (the exact count moved slightly as tests were added/removed across each of the fixes above — the concurrency-lock regression tests, the KillMode regression test, the removal of the now-obsolete pre-push-hook-parity tests replaced by the "no hook infrastructure exists" guard).

## VaR position-sizing confidence level and time-scaling — researched, not adopted (2026-08-05)

Investigated whether `_var_position_size_core()`'s `var_confidence` (currently `0.95`) and its square-root-of-time holding-period scaling were ever specifically re-examined the way `per_trade_pct`/`max_total_deployed` had been, or just carried forward because they'd always been there. Investigation only, run in a local session, no production changes without an exceptional, block-validated result — none was found, so none was made.

**A structural finding that reframed the whole investigation.** Every live stock trade is sized against the same fixed `holding_days=30` constant (the ticker's *maximum allowed* holding period, `st["max_hold"]`) — never the trade's own eventual *realized* holding period, which can't be known at entry time and structurally never reaches the sizing formula at all. The scaling-exponent question therefore isn't "does this system size a 3-day hold differently from a 25-day hold" (it can't, regardless of exponent) — it's "is 30 days the right fixed horizon to size risk against." Real holding-period distribution (3,161 trades, full 2007–2026 continuous walk): median 30 days (the cap itself), 56.8% of all trades exit exactly at `MAX_HOLDING`.

**The scaling exponent, checked independently of any backtest.** Fit `log(|VaR_N|) = intercept + k·log(N)` against real rolling N-day historical-VaR percentiles for 120 randomly-sampled live tickers: median fitted exponent ≈0.475 (std-dev cross-check: ≈0.469) — within 5% of the current hardcoded 0.5. Real multi-day dispersion on this system's own data tracks sqrt(time) almost exactly; the current design is empirically well-grounded, not an arbitrary convention carried forward unexamined.

**`var_confidence` sweep — reset-at-boundary, test period (2020-01-01–2026-08-03), live universe, 7 values from 0.85 to 0.995.** `0.925` and `0.975` appeared to dominate the current `0.95` baseline on every metric simultaneously (CAGR, drawdown, PF, Sharpe, win rate) — the standout single-comparison result of the sweep, structurally identical in shape to the VIX/ADX investigation's own `ADX<20` false positive above. Taken to 16-block validation per this project's own standing discipline, precisely because a clean single-comparison win has already been shown, twice, not to survive that check.

**Block validation reversed the apparent win.** All three variants tied at 14/16 blocks passing (`PF>1.0` and `|strat_dd| <= 1.5×|sp_dd|`, the same two blocks — 0, pre-GFC; 1, GFC-acute — failing for every variant, the project's own already-established pattern). But win count and mean CAGR across the 16 genuinely independent blocks told the opposite story: current production `0.95` won the plurality outright (9/16 blocks, mean CAGR 12.94%) versus `0.925` (4/16, 12.74%) and `0.975` (3/16, 11.44%). `0.925`'s apparent single-comparison win did not survive — production's current setting is the more robust choice under the check that actually matters. Time-scaling alternatives (no-scaling, linear, empirically-fitted k≈0.475) were all weaker than sqrt in the same reset-at-boundary sweep and never reached block validation.

**Recommendation: researched, not adopted.** `config.yaml` untouched; nothing deployed. Full trade-level output for all 10 sweep variants and all 3 block-validation runs preserved at `research/var_sizing_sweep_2026-08-05/` — the exact `_block_passes()` formula quoted directly from `analysis/validation.py`, not paraphrased.

## Sector/momentum concentration risk — researched, not adopted (2026-08-05)

Real, structurally-motivated hypothesis, not a search for patterns: the price-sanity incident (see "Live pricing bug, exception isolation, and ETF mapping audit" and "Urgent pre-submission verification" above) showed SNDK, WDC, MU, LITE, and STX — all semiconductor/storage names — carrying extreme, correlated momentum simultaneously, and nothing in the system currently considers whether several open positions are effectively the same underlying bet wearing different tickers. Checked directly.

**No sector classification data exists in the current codebase, confirmed before designing the investigation.** An earlier module (`analysis/robustness.py`, `_ticker_sector_map()`) that classified a different, older 70-ticker frozen universe was removed entirely in the V2 rebuild — confirmed via direct search, not assumed absent. Price-correlation was used as the primary concentration measure instead — more rigorous anyway, since it directly captures "effectively the same underlying bet" rather than a coarse label, and is exactly what the SNDK/WDC/MU/LITE/STX cluster shows regardless of what sector name it would have been given.

**How often, and how correlated — continuous walk, full 2007–2026 history, real unmodified `simulate_portfolio_compounding_mtm()`, 3,161 trades.** Holding 5+ simultaneously-open positions is the **near-permanent normal state**, not an occasional episode: n_open≥5 on 98.35% of the 4,673-day master calendar, n_open≥2 on 99.27%. Trailing 60-day pairwise correlation among open positions: mean 0.359, median 0.342, p95 0.613 — roughly in the range typical of any diversified US-equity basket, not dramatically elevated on average. But the aggregate-risk consequence is real: a diversification ratio averaging 1.589, and an `indep_gap_60d` (realized joint portfolio risk vs. what independent VaR sizing implies) averaging **1.067** — on a typical day, realized joint risk runs roughly double what independent sizing assumes, ~2.72x at the 95th percentile. The worst 25 single days in 19 years are dominated by a mid-2026 semiconductor/storage/tech cluster (SNDK, WDC, MU, LITE, STX, LRCX, TER, AMD, INTC, DELL, and others) — 9 of the top 25, each holding 14–18 open positions — the concrete real-world recurrence of the motivating incident, not a one-off.

**Isolating the cost — the naive check failed exactly the way this project's own standing discipline warns against, caught directly rather than missed.** Regression-based isolation controlling for contemporaneous S&P 500 volatility and drawdown-from-high: for downside-only return (the metric that actually matters), the residual relationship after controlling for market volatility is not statistically significant (p=0.70) and reverses sign in the stricter multivariate test (coefficient wrong-signed, p=0.45). The raw, uncontrolled correlation looked real; it was a naive co-occurrence artifact of concentrated episodes happening to also be volatile-market episodes, exactly the trap the investigation's own brief named in advance. A dedicated tail-specific follow-up found a real but only partial effect: the worst days are genuinely enriched for high-`indep_gap` episodes (binomial p<0.0001) and this survives a within-volatility-regime matched comparison in 2 of 3 vol terciles, but not the strictest full multivariate logistic regression (p=0.13–0.23, plausibly underpowered on 13–231 tail events) — a real, mixed signal, not a clean yes or no.

**A concrete constraint was built and tested anyway, and failed to dominate.** A correlation-aware sizing haircut (block/scale new entries correlated >0.7 with an already-open position), layered on the real shared `_var_position_size_core()` with fidelity confirmed byte-identical when disabled. Reset-at-boundary, test period, both drawdown conventions improved (fixed-denominator: -27.56%→-18.90%; peak-relative: -12.47%→-9.78%) but CAGR (19.29%→16.27%), PF, and Sharpe all worsened — does not dominate the baseline on every metric, the same bar the `var_confidence` investigation immediately above used before proceeding to the expensive 16-block check. Per this project's own established practice, a non-dominant single-comparison result is not carried forward to block validation; `make_blocks()`/`_block_passes()` were imported directly into a ready-to-use validator but never invoked.

**Recommendation: researched, not adopted — but the structural finding is worth keeping on record regardless.** The near-universal correlated-concentration fact, and the ~2x independent-sizing gap it produces, is real and previously undocumented; the isolated cost of it is not robust enough on the metric that matters, and the one constraint tested does not clear this project's own bar for further validation. `config.yaml` untouched; nothing deployed. Full trade-level and day-level output (3,161 trades, a 4,673-row day-by-day panel, all isolation/tail-risk/constraint results) preserved at `research/concentration_risk_2026-08-05/`.

## BRK.B/BF.B dot-notation ticker bug, and the rolling-window start-date fragility — both confirmed and fixed on production (2026-08-05)

Two findings surfaced while setting up a fresh local research environment, both checked directly against production rather than assumed to be local-only.

**Part A — BRK.B and BF.B, real S&P 500 constituents with dot share-class notation, were silently untradeable in production for as long as they've been live candidates.** yfinance expects hyphen notation (`BRK-B`) for share classes, not the dot notation (`BRK.B`) this codebase uses everywhere else to match `universe_membership` and the `fja05680/sp500` source CSV (confirmed directly against the live source: the CSV itself stores `BF.B`/`BRK.B`, dot form). Every yfinance call site in the codebase (`data/ingestion.py:_fetch_ticker()`'s `yf.download()`, `brokers/trading212.py:_live_current_price()`'s `yf.Ticker()`) passed the raw ticker straight through, with zero conversion. Confirmed live (2026-08-05): `yf.download("BRK.B")`/`yf.Ticker("BRK.B")` return nothing at all ("possibly delisted"); the hyphen form returns real data.

**Confirmed impact on the real production database (SSH, `database/investment_research.db`, not a local copy), not just reasoned about.** Both tickers are genuine, currently-active S&P 500 members (`universe_membership` windows open through the sentinel `2099-12-31`), so `get_live_stock_candidates()` includes both and `pull_incremental()` (the only ingestion path the real scheduler ever calls) has been trying to fetch them daily. `price_data` had real history for both — 4,925 rows each, 2007-01-03 through 2026-07-31 — but that entire range came from a one-off research script (`V2 stock universe broadening`'s `backfill_price_history` run) that manually converted dot-to-hyphen before fetching, a fix applied only in that disposable script, never in the production ingestion path itself. Every healthy stock ticker (AAPL, MSFT, etc.) was current through 2026-08-03/08-04; BRK.B and BF.B were frozen at 2026-07-31 — stale for every trading day since the broadened universe went live, silently: an empty 10-day yfinance window is deliberately *not* treated as "mark unavailable" (existing, correct handling for a real holiday gap), so nothing ever alerted on this. `invest_orders` shows zero orders ever placed for either ticker — the bug had not yet caused a live trade to be sized off stale data, but the underlying momentum signal for both had been computed from an increasingly out-of-date price series for days, and would have continued indefinitely. No other currently-active dot-notation ticker exists in the live universe — checked directly (`universe_membership` has 9 other dot-tickers, e.g. `RDS.A`, `AZA.A`; all are long-closed historical windows, correctly excluded from `is_member()` today) — this bug was exactly and only BRK.B/BF.B.

**Fix.** `data/ingestion.py:_yf_symbol()` — a single conversion function (`ticker.replace(".", "-")`), applied only at the outgoing yfinance call in `_fetch_ticker()` and `brokers/trading212.py:_live_current_price()`; every other use of the ticker (DB storage, `universe_membership`, decision logic) keeps the dot form, so existing stored rows and every other reference stay consistent. Regression tests added (`tests/test_ingestion.py`, `tests/test_execution.py`) proving the yfinance call receives the hyphenated symbol while price rows land in `price_data` under the original dot ticker. Deployed via the standard webhook path (`git push origin main`); production backfilled immediately after deploy via a one-off `pull_incremental(["BRK.B", "BF.B"])` run over SSH rather than waiting for the next scheduled `market_hours_check`/`scheduled_eod` window, closing the live gap the same night it was found.

**Part B — `pull_history()`'s rolling `now - history_days` window never actually anchored to a fixed date; it only approximated one at the moment `history_days` was chosen.** The config comment's own stated intent (`config.yaml`, before this fix: "7150 (~19.6y) reaches back to 2007-01-01") was always a fixed historical anchor — the rolling-day-count implementation was an approximation of that intent, not a deliberate "last N years relative to whenever this runs" design. Checked before assuming this: searched every real caller of `pull_history()` (exactly one, a disposable DAX research script explicitly wanting "the last ~22 years, however long that is today" — genuinely relative semantics, fine as-is) and `pull_incremental()`'s own first-time-download fallback (the real production path a brand-new S&P 500 entrant's first fetch goes through, using the identical `history_days` config value with no override at all) — no caller actually wants "N days back from today" as an answer that silently reaches a later date the longer the codebase runs unchanged, which is exactly what a fresh local DB build the same night needed a manual, ad-hoc backward-fill step to compensate for.

**Fix.** `config.yaml`'s `data.history_days: 7150` replaced with `data.history_start_date: "2007-01-01"` — a fixed date, not a day count. `pull_history()` gained an explicit `start_date` parameter (mirroring `backfill_price_history()`'s own naming) and now defaults to `config["data"]["history_start_date"]` when neither `days` nor `start_date` is given; an explicit `days=` override (the DAX script's use case) still works exactly as before, unaffected. `pull_incremental()`'s first-time-download fallback now anchors to the same fixed `history_start_date` directly, closing the gap in the one real production code path that shared the old drift bug. `README.md`'s mirrored config example updated to match. Regression tests (`tests/test_ingestion.py`) prove the default no longer depends on `datetime.utcnow()`, that an explicit `days=` override still computes relative to "now," and that `pull_incremental()`'s brand-new-ticker path uses the fixed date.

**Full test suite: 862 passed, 0 failed** (up from the pre-existing baseline — 26 new tests added across both parts, 0 removed). Deployed to production via the standard `git push origin main` → GitHub Actions test gate → signed webhook → `deploy.sh` path; production backfill for BRK.B/BF.B and `verify_deploy.sh`'s pass confirmed directly over SSH after the deploy completed.
